The Epistle Dedicatory

Beloved in our dearest Lord,

Christ, the Scripture, your+ own hearts, and Satan’s devices are the four prime things that should be first and most studied and searched. If any cast off the study of these, they cannot be safe here, nor happy1 hereafter. It is my work as a Christian, but much more as I am a watchman, to do my best to reveal the fullness of Christ, the emptiness of created things, and the snares of the great deceiver; and this I have tried to do (in the following discourse) according to that measure of grace which I have received from the Lord. God once accepted a handful of flour for a sacrifice, and a fistful of goats’ hair for an offering; and I know that you+ have not so learned the Father as to despise the day of small things. Beloved, Satan, having fallen from light to darkness, from happiness to misery, from heaven to hell, from an angel to a devil, is so full of malice and envy that he will leave no means untried by which he may make all others eternally miserable with himself. Being shut out of heaven, and shut up under chains of darkness until the judgment of the great day, he uses all his power and skill to bring all the sons of men into the same condition and condemnation with himself. Satan has cast such sinful seed into our souls that now he no sooner tempts than we are ready to assent; he no sooner has a plot against us than he makes a conquest of us. If he only shows men a little of the beauty and splendor of the world, how ready they are to fall down and worship him!

Whatever sin the heart of man is most prone to, the devil will help it forward. If David is proud of2 his people, Satan will provoke him to number them, so that he may be prouder still. If Peter is slavishly3 fearful, Satan will drive him to rebuke and deny Christ, to save his own skin. If Ahab’s4 prophets are given to flattery, the devil will at once become a lying spirit in the mouths of four hundred of them, and they will flatter Ahab to his ruin. If Judas will5 be a traitor, Satan will quickly enter into his heart and make him sell his master for money, which some heathens would never have done. If Ananias will lie6 for gain, Satan will fill his heart so that he may lie (with a vengeance) to the Holy Spirit. Satan loves to sail with the wind, and to suit men’s temptations to their conditions and inclinations. If they are in prosperity, he will tempt them to deny God; if they are in adversity, he will tempt them to distrust7 God. If their knowledge is weak, he will tempt them to have low thoughts of God; if their conscience is tender, he will tempt them to over-scrupulousness; if it is lax, to carnal complacency. If we are bold-spirited, he will tempt us to presumption; if timid, to despair; if pliable, to inconstancy; if stiff, to impenitence, etc.

From the power, malice, and skill of Satan proceed all the soul-killing plots, devices, stratagems, and machinations that are in the world. He has various devices to draw souls to sin, and various plots to keep souls from all holy and heavenly services, and various stratagems to keep souls in a mourning, staggering, doubting, and questioning condition. He has various devices to destroy the great and honorable, the wise and learned, the blind and ignorant, the rich and the poor, the real and the nominal saints, etc. At one time he will refrain from tempting, so that we may think ourselves complacent and neglect our watch; at another he will seem to flee, so that he may make us proud of the victory. At one time he will fix men’s eyes more on others’ sins than on their own, so that he may puff them up; at another he will fix their eyes more on others’ graces than on their own, so that he may overwhelm them, etc. A man may as well count the stars and number the sands of the sea as reckon up all the devices of Satan. Yet those which are most important, and by which he does most harm to the precious souls of men, are uncovered in the following treatise, and the remedies against them prescribed, etc.

Beloved, I think it necessary to give you+ and the world a faithful account of the reasons moving me to appear in print in these days, in which we may say there was never more writing and yet never less practicing; and they are as follows, etc.

First, because Satan has a greater influence on men, and higher advantages over men (having, as it were, the wind and the hill), than they think he has; and the knowledge of his high advantages is the highway to frustrating him, and to making the soul strong in resisting and happy in conquering, etc.

Your+ urgent pleading, and the urgent pleading of many other precious sons of Zion, has, after much striving with God, my own heart, and others, made a conquest of me, and forced me to do at last what at first was not a little contrary to my inclination and resolution, etc.

The strange opposition that I8 met with from Satan in the writing of this following discourse has put an edge on my spirit, for I know that Satan strives mightily to keep from the light those things that tend most of all to shake and break his kingdom of darkness, and to lift up the kingdom and glory of the Lord Jesus Christ in the souls and lives of the children of men, etc.

Its exceeding usefulness to all sorts, ranks, and conditions of men in the world. Here you+ have a salve for every sore, and a plaster for every wound, and a remedy against every disease, especially against those that tend most to the undoing of souls and to the ruin of the state, etc.

I do not know of anyone who has written on this subject; all that I have ever seen have only touched on this string. This has been no small provocation to me to attempt something in this way, so that others who have better heads and hearts may be the more stirred to make use of their talents in a further uncovering of Satan’s devices, and in making known such choice remedies as may enable the souls of men to triumph over all his plots and stratagems, etc.

I have many precious friends in various parts of the country who are not a little desirous that my pen may reach them, now that my voice cannot. By the help of the mighty God of Jacob I have formerly been a weak instrument of good to them, and I cannot but hope and believe that the Lord will also bless these labors to them, since they are (in part) the fruit of their desires and prayers, etc.

Lastly, not knowing how soon my hourglass may run out, and how soon I may be cut off by the hand of death from all opportunities of doing further service for Christ or your+ souls in this world, I was willing to sow a little handful of spiritual seed among you+, so that when I lay aside this earthly tabernacle, my love to you+, and that dear remembrance of you+ which I have in my soul, may strongly move your+ minds and spirits to make this book your+ companion, and under all outward or inward changes to make use of this heavenly salve. I hope it will, by the blessing of the Lord, be as effectual for the healing of all your+ wounds as looking up to the bronze serpent was effectual to heal those who were bitten and stung by fiery serpents. I will leave this book with you+ as a legacy of my dearest love, desiring the Lord to make it a far greater and sweeter legacy than all those carnal legacies that are left by the high and mighty ones of the earth to their nearest and dearest relations, etc.

Beloved, I would not have affection carry my pen too far beyond my intention; therefore allow me only to express my desires for you+ and my desires to you+, and I will draw to a close.

My desires for you+ are “that out of the riches9 of His glory He may strengthen you+ with power through His Spirit in your+ inner10 being, so that Christ may dwell in your+ hearts through faith; that you+, being rooted and grounded in love, may11 have power, together with all the saints, to comprehend the length and width and height and depth12 of the love of Christ, and to know this love that surpasses knowledge; that you+ may be filled with all the fullness of God.” And “that you+ may walk13 in a manner worthy of the Lord and may please Him in every way, bearing fruit in every good work, growing in the knowledge of God, being strengthened with all power according14 to His glorious might, so that you+ may have full endurance and patience with joy.” “That you+ will not do anything wrong.” “That15 your+ love may abound more and more in knowledge and depth of insight,16 so that you+ may be able to test and prove what is best, and may be pure17 and blameless for the day of Christ.” And “that our God will18 count you+ worthy of His calling, and will fulfill every good desire and work of faith with19 power, so that the name of our Lord Jesus may be glorified in you+, and you+ in Him, according to the grace of our God and of the Lord Jesus Christ.” And that you+ may be eminent in20 holiness, holiness being Zion’s glory; that your+ hearts may be kept upright, your+ judgments sound, and your+ lives blameless. That as you+ are now my joy, so in the day of Christ you+ may be my crown. That I may see my labors in your+ lives; that your+ conduct may not be earthly when the things you+ hear are heavenly, but that it may be worthy of the gospel. That as the fish that live in the salt sea are yet fresh, so you+, though you+ live in an uncharitable world, may yet be charitable and loving. That you+ may, like the bee, suck honey out of every flower. That you+ may shine in a sea of troubles, as the pearl shines in the sky, though it grows in the sea. That in all your+ trials you+ may be like the stone in Thrace that neither burns in the fire nor sinks in the water. That you+ may be like the heavens, excellent in substance and beautiful in appearance, so that you+ may meet me with joy on that day when Christ will say to his Father, “Here am I, and the children You have given Me.”

My desires to you+ are that you+ would make it your+ business to study Christ, his Word, your+ own hearts, Satan’s plots, and eternity more than ever. That you+ would strive more to be inwardly sincere than outwardly glorious; to live, rather than to have a name for being alive. That you+ would labor with all your+ might to be thankful under blessings, and faithful in your+ places, and humble under divine appearances, and fruitful under precious ordinances; that as your+ means and blessings are greater than others’, so your+ account before God may not prove worse than others’. That you+ would pray for me, who am not worthy to be named among the saints, that I may be a precious instrument in the hand of Christ to bring in many souls to him, and to build up those who are brought in, in their most holy faith; and that utterance may be given to me, that I may make known all the will of God. That21 I may be sincere, faithful, frequent, fervent, and constant in the work of the Lord, and that my labor may not be in vain in the Lord; that my labors may be accepted by the Lord and his saints, and that I may daily see the travail of my soul, etc.

But above all, pray for me, that I may more and more find the power and sweetness of those things on my own heart that I give out to you+ and others; and that my soul may be so visited with strength from on high that I may live fully and constantly up to those truths that I hold out to the world; and that I may be, both in life and doctrine, a burning and a shining light; so that when the Lord Jesus appears, I may receive a crown of glory, which he will give to me on that day, and not only to me, but to all who love his appearing, etc.

To close, remember this: your+ life is short, your+ duties many, your+ help great, and your+ reward sure. Therefore do not lose heart; hold on, and hold up in ways of well-doing, and heaven will make amends for all.

I will now take leave of you+, now that my heart has, by my hand, signed that I am,

Your+ loving pastor under Christ, in all pastoral affection and commitment, in our dearest Lord.

THOMAS BROOKS.

A Word to the Reader

Dear friend!

Solomon bids us buy the22 truth, but does not tell us what it must cost, because we must get it however dear it may be. We must love it both23 shining and scorching. Every scrap of truth is precious, like the filings of gold; we must either live with it or die for it. As Ruth said to Naomi, “Wherever you go, I will go, and24 wherever you lodge, I will lodge, and nothing but death will part you and me,” so gracious spirits must say, “Where truth goes, I will go, and where truth lodges, I will25 lodge, and nothing but death will part me and truth.” A man may lawfully sell his house, lands, and jewels, but truth is a jewel that exceeds all price, and must not be sold. It is our heritage: “Your testimonies are my heritage26 forever.” It is a legacy that our forefathers bought with their blood, which should make us willing to lay down anything and to lay out anything, so that, with the wise merchant in the gospel, we may purchase this precious pearl,27 which is worth more than heaven and earth, and which will make a man live happily, die comfortably, and reign eternally.

And now, if you please, read the work, and take this counsel from me.

First, you must know that a man may be useful even though he cannot be excellent. An iron key may unlock the door of a golden treasure; indeed (ferrum potest quod aurum non potest) iron can do some things that gold cannot, etc.

Secondly, remember that it is not hasty reading, but serious meditating on28 holy and heavenly truths, that makes them prove sweet and profitable to the soul. It is not the bee’s touching of the flower that gathers honey, but her staying a while on the flower that draws out the sweetness. It is not he who reads most, but he who meditates most, who will prove the choicest, sweetest, wisest, and strongest Christian, etc.

Thirdly, know that it is not the knowing man, nor the talking man, nor the reading man, but the doing man, who in the end will be found the happiest man. “If you+ know these things, you+ will be blessed29 and happy if you+ do them.” “Not everyone who says to Me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the30 kingdom of heaven, but only he who does the will of My Father in heaven.” Judas called Christ Lord, Lord, and yet betrayed him, and has gone to his own place. Ah, how many Judases we have in these days, who kiss Christ and yet betray Christ; who profess him in their words but deny him in their works; who bow31 their knee to him and yet despise him in their hearts; who call him Jesus and yet will not obey him as their Lord!

Reader, if it is not strong on your heart to practice what you read, to what end do you read? To increase your own condemnation? If your light and knowledge are not turned into practice, the more knowing a man you are, the more miserable a man you will be in the day of recompense; your light and knowledge will torment you more than all the devils in hell. Your knowledge will be the rod that will eternally lash you, and the scorpion that will forever bite you, and the worm that will everlastingly gnaw you. Therefore read, and labor to know, so that you may do, or else you are undone forever. When Demosthenes was asked what was the first part of an orator, what the second, and what the third, he answered, “Action.” I may say the same: if anyone should ask me what is the first, the second, the third part of a Christian, I must answer, “Action.” For the man who reads so that he may know, and labors to know so that he may do, will have two heavens: a heaven of joy, peace, and comfort on earth, and a heaven of glory and happiness after death.

Fourthly, and lastly, if in your reading you will cast a serious eye on the notes, you will find many sweet and precious notes that will often give light to the things you read, and repay your pains with much comfort and profit. So, desiring that you may find as much sweetness and benefit in reading this treatise as I have found (by the overshadowings of heaven) in studying and writing it, “I commit you to God and to the word of His grace, which can32 build you up and give you an inheritance among all who are sanctified.” And I remain,

Reader,

Your soul’s servant in every office of the gospel,

THOMAS BROOKS.

The Text Opened and the Point Proved

PRECIOUS REMEDIES AGAINST SATAN’S DEVICES.

2 Corinthians 2:11

So that Satan should not get an advantage over us; for we are not ignorant of his devices.

In the fifth verse the apostle shows that the incestuous man had by his incest saddened those precious souls whom God would not have saddened. Souls that walk sinfully are Hazaels to the godly, and draw many sighs and tears from them. Jeremiah weeps in secret for Judah’s sins, and Paul cannot speak of those belly-gods with dry eyes (Phil 3:18). And Lot’s righteous soul was burdened,33 vexed, and racked by the filthy Sodomites (2 Pet 2:7, 8). Every sinful Sodomite was a Hazael to his eyes, a Hadadrimmon to his heart. Gracious souls are accustomed to mourn for other men’s sins as well as their own, and for the souls34 and sins of those who make a mock of sin, and a jest of damning their own souls. Guilt or grief is all that gracious souls get by fellowship with worldly souls.

In the sixth verse he shows that the punishment inflicted on the incestuous man was sufficient, and therefore they should not refuse to receive him, since he had repented and sorrowed for his former faults and follies. It is not for the honor of Christ, the reputation of the gospel, nor the good of souls, for professing Christians to be like those35 bloody wretches who burned at the stake some who had recanted, saying that they would send them out of the world while they were in a good mind.

In verses 7, 8, 9, and 10 the apostle stirs up the church to forgive him, to comfort him, and to confirm their love toward him, so that he might not be swallowed up with excessive sorrow, for Satan was going about to mix the detestable tares of despair with the godly sorrow of a pure, penitent heart. It was a sweet saying of one: Let a man36 grieve for his sin, and then rejoice in his grief. That sorrow for sin which keeps the soul from looking toward the mercy-seat, and which keeps Christ and the soul apart, or which makes the soul unfit for the communion of saints, is a sinful sorrow.

In the eleventh verse he gives another reason to move them to show pity and mercy to the penitent sinner, who was mourning and groaning under his sin and misery, that is, “so that Satan should not get an advantage over us; for we are not ignorant of his devices.” Now a little to open the words.

So that Satan should not get an advantage over us,37 that is, so that Satan should not over-reach us. The Greek word signifies to have more than belongs to one. The comparison is taken from the greedy merchant, who seeks and takes every opportunity to cheat and deceive others. Satan is that wily merchant who devours not widows’ houses, but most men’s souls.

For we are not ignorant of Satan’s devices, or plots, or machinations, or stratagems.38 He is only a Christian in name who has no personal experience of Satan’s stratagems, his set and composed machinations, his artfully molded methods, his plots, darts, and depths, by which he outwitted our first parents, and by which he always fits each of us with a bargain to suit us, as he sees fit.

The main observation that I will draw from these words is this:

That Satan has his various devices to deceive, entangle, and ruin the souls of men.

I will first prove the point; secondly, show you+ his various devices; thirdly, the remedies against his devices; and fourthly, how it comes about that he has so many different devices to deceive, entangle, and ruin the souls of men. Fifthly, I will lay down some propositions concerning Satan and his devices. For the proof of the point, take these few Scriptures. Eph 6:11: “Put on the full armor of God, so that you+ can stand against the wiles of the devil.” The Greek word39 that is here rendered wiles is a notably emphatic word.

1. It signifies such snares as are laid behind one, such treacheries as come upon one’s back unawares. It denotes the methods, or ambushes, of that old subtle serpent, who, like Dan’s adder in the path, bites the heels of travelers, and so passes his venom to the head and heart. The word signifies an ambush, or a stratagem of war, by which the enemy sets upon a man ex insidiis, unawares.

2. It signifies such snares as are set to40 catch one on one’s road. A man walks along his road and does not think of it; suddenly he is caught by thieves, or falls into a pit, etc.

3. It signifies such snares as are purposely, artfully, and craftily set for taking the prey at the greatest possible advantage. The Greek μεθοδείας, being derived from μετά and ὁδός, properly signifies a waylaying, a circumvention, or a going about, as those do who seek after their prey. Julian by his craft drew more people from the faith than all his persecuting predecessors could by their cruelty. So Satan does more hurt in his sheepskin than by roaring like a lion.

Take one Scripture more for the proof of the point, and that is in the second letter to Timothy, the second chapter, and the last verse: “and that they may recover themselves out of the snare of the devil, who has taken them captive at his will.” The Greek word that is here rendered recover themselves signifies to awake41 themselves. The apostle alludes to one who is asleep or drunk, who is to be awakened and restored to his senses. And the Greek word that is here rendered taken captive signifies to be taken alive.42 The word is properly a word of war, and signifies to be taken alive, as soldiers are taken alive in war, or as birds are taken alive and ensnared in the fowler’s net. Satan has snares for the wise and snares for the simple, snares for hypocrites and snares for the upright, snares for bold souls and snares for timid souls, snares for the rich and snares for the poor, snares for the aged and snares for the young, etc. Happy are those souls that are not taken and held in the snares that he has laid. Take one proof more, and then I will proceed to the opening of the point, and that is in Rev 2:24: “But I say to the rest of you+ in Thyatira, as many as do not hold43 to this teaching and have not known the depths of Satan, as they call them: I will place no further burden upon you+; only hold fast until I come.” Those poor souls called their opinions the depths of God, when in fact they were the depths of Satan. You+ call your+ opinions depths, and so they are; but they are such depths as Satan has brought out of hell. They are the whisperings and hissings of that serpent, not the inspirations of God.

Part I. Devices to Draw the Soul into Sin

1. Presenting the Bait and Hiding the Hook

Now the second thing that I am to show you is his various devices. And here I will first show you the various devices that he has to draw the soul to sin. I will give these twelve as instances, which may call for our most serious consideration.

His first device to draw the soul to sin is to present the bait and hide the hook; to present the golden cup and hide the poison; to present the sweetness, the pleasure, and the profit that may flow in on the soul by yielding to sin, and to hide from the soul the wrath and misery that will certainly follow the committing of sin. By this device he took our first parents. Gen 3:4, 5: “And the serpent said to the woman, ‘You+ will not surely die. For God44 knows that in the day you+ eat of it, your+ eyes will be opened and you+ will be like God, knowing good and evil.’” Your+ eyes will be opened, and you+ will be like God: here is the bait, the sweetness, the pleasure, the profit. Oh, but he hides the hook, the shame, the wrath, and the loss that would certainly follow! There is an opening of the eyes of the mind to contemplation and joy, and there is an opening of the eyes of the body to shame and disgrace. He promises them the former, but intends the latter, and so cheats them, giving them an apple in exchange for Paradise, as he deals with thousands nowadays. Satan easily deceives us with fallacies, and then by his golden baits leads us on and leaves us in a fool’s paradise. He promises the soul honor, pleasure, and profit, etc., but pays the soul with the greatest contempt, shame, and loss that can be. By a golden bait he labored to catch Christ45 in Matt 4:8, 9. He shows him the beauty and the splendor of a bewitching world, which no doubt would have taken many a carnal heart; but here the devil’s fire fell on wet tinder, and so did not catch. These tempting objects did not win upon his affections at all, nor dazzle his eyes. Yet many have died eternally of the wound of the eye, and fallen forever by this vile strumpet the world, who by laying out her two fair breasts of profit and pleasure has wounded their souls and cast them down into utter perdition. By the glitter of her pomp and preferment she has slain millions, like the serpent Scytale, which, when she cannot overtake fleeing travelers, stuns and dazes them with her beautiful colors, so that they have no power to go on their way until she has stung them to death. Adversity has slain her thousand, but prosperity her ten thousand.

Now the remedies against this device of the devil are these.

First, keep at the greatest distance from sin, and from playing with the golden bait that Satan holds out to catch you. For this you have Rom 12:9: “Abhor what is evil; cling to what is good.” When we meet with anything extremely evil and contrary to us, nature abhors it, and draws back as far as it can46 from it. The Greek word that is there rendered abhor is very expressive: it signifies to hate it as hell itself, to hate it with horror. Anselm used to say that if he should see the shame of sin on the one hand and the pains of hell on the other, and must of necessity choose one, he would rather be thrust into hell without sin than go into heaven with sin; so great was his hatred and detestation of sin. It is our wisest and our safest47 course to stand at the furthest distance from sin; not to go near the house of the harlot, but to flee “from every appearance of evil.” The best way to avoid falling into the pit is to keep at the48 greatest distance from it. He who is so bold as to attempt to dance on the brink of the pit may find by woeful experience that it is a righteous thing with God that he should fall into the pit. Joseph keeps at a distance from sin, and from playing with Satan’s golden baits, and stands. David draws near and plays with the bait, and falls, and swallows bait and hook with a vengeance. David comes near the snare and is taken in it, to the breaking of his bones, the wounding of his conscience, and the loss of his God.

Sin is a plague, indeed the greatest and the most infectious plague in the world; and yet, ah, how few there are who tremble at it, who keep at a distance from it! 1 Cor 5:6: “Do you+ not know that a little leaven works through the whole batch of dough?” As soon as one sin had seized on Adam’s heart, all sin entered into his soul and overspread49 it. How Adam’s one sin has spread over all mankind! Rom 5:12: “Therefore, just as sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin, so also death was passed on to all men, because all sinned.” Ah, how the father’s sin infects the child, the husband’s the wife, the master’s the servant! The sin that is in one man’s heart is able to infect a whole world, it is of such a spreading and infectious nature. The story of the Italian who first made his enemy deny God and then stabbed him, and so murdered both body and soul at once, shows the utter malignity of sin. And oh, that what has been said on this head may prevail with you+ to stand at a distance from sin!

The second remedy is to consider50 that sin is only a bitter-sweet. The seeming sweetness that is in sin will quickly vanish, and lasting shame, sorrow, horror, and terror will come in its place. Job 20:12, 13, 14: “Though evil is sweet in his mouth and he conceals it under his tongue, though he cannot bear to let it go and keeps it in his mouth, yet in his stomach his food sours into the gall of asps within him.” Forbidden profits and pleasures are most pleasing to worldly men, who count madness mirth, etc. Many long to be meddling with the murdering morsels of sin, which do not nourish, but tear and consume the belly, the soul that receives them. Many eat on earth what they digest in hell; sin’s murdering morsels will deceive those who devour them. Adam’s51 apple was a bitter-sweet; Esau’s stew was a bitter-sweet; the Israelites’ quails a bitter-sweet, Jonathan’s honey a bitter-sweet, and Adonijah’s dainties a bitter-sweet. After the meal is ended comes the reckoning. Men must not think to dance and dine with the devil, and then to sit at supper with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven; to feed on the poison of asps, and yet think that the viper’s tongue will not slay them. When the asp stings a man, it first tickles him so that it makes him laugh, until the poison little by52 little gets to the heart, and then it pains him more than ever it delighted him. So does sin: it may please a little at first, but it will pain the soul with a vengeance at last. Indeed, if there were the least real delight in sin, there could be no perfect hell, where men will be most perfectly tormented with their sin.

The third remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that sin will usher in the greatest and the53 saddest losses that can befall our souls. It will usher in the loss of that divine favor which is better than life, and the loss of that joy which is inexpressible and full of glory, and the loss of that peace which surpasses understanding, and the loss of those divine influences by which the soul has been refreshed, enlivened,54 raised, strengthened, and gladdened, and the loss of many desirable outward blessings which the soul might otherwise have enjoyed. It was a sound and wholesome reply of an English captain at the loss of Calais. When a proud Frenchman scornfully asked, “When will you fetch Calais back?” he replied,55 “When your sins weigh down ours.” Ah, England! My constant prayer for you is that you may not sin away your mercies into the hands of those who cannot call mercy mercy, and who would rejoice in nothing more than to see your sorrow and misery, and to see the hand that has clothed you with much mercy and glory make you naked.

The fourth remedy against this device56 of Satan is to consider seriously that sin is of a very deceitful and bewitching nature. Sin comes from the greatest deceiver; it is a child of his own begetting, it is the ground of all the deceit in the world, and it is in its own nature exceedingly deceitful. Heb 3:13: “But exhort one another daily, as long as it is called today, so that none of you+ may be hardened by sin’s deceitfulness.” It will kiss the soul, and put on a fair show before the soul, and yet betray the soul forever. Like Delilah, it will smile on us so that it may betray us into the hands of the devil, as she betrayed Samson into the hands of the57 Philistines. Sin gives Satan a power over us, and an advantage to accuse us, and to lay claim to us as those who wear his badge. It is of a very bewitching nature: it so bewitches the soul where it is on the throne that the soul cannot leave it, though it perishes eternally by it. Sin so bewitches the soul that it makes58 the soul call evil good and good evil, bitter sweet and sweet bitter, light darkness and darkness light. And a soul thus bewitched with sin will hold out to the death, at sword’s point with God. Let God strike, and wound, and cut to the very bone, yet the bewitched soul does not care, does not fear, but will keep on in a course of wickedness, as you+ may see in Pharaoh, Balaam, and Judas. Tell the bewitched soul that sin is a viper that will certainly kill when it is not killed, that sin often kills secretly, unnoticed, eternally; yet the bewitched soul cannot and will not cease from sin. When the physicians told59 Theotimus that unless he abstained from drunkenness and uncleanness, etc., he would lose his eyes, his heart was so bewitched with his sins that he answered, “Then farewell, sweet light!” He would rather lose his eyes than leave his sins. So a man bewitched with sin would rather lose God, Christ, heaven, and his own soul than part with his sin. Oh, therefore, forever take heed of playing or nibbling at Satan’s golden baits!

44. So, to bring back Dr. Taylor the martyr, they promised him not only his pardon, but a bishopric. Foxe, Acts and Monuments, folio 1386. Inest peccatum cum delectaris: regnat si consenseris. [Sin is present when you delight in it; it reigns if you consent to it.] Augustine, on Ps 50.

45. This world shall at last be burned for a witch, says one. Multi amando res noxias sunt miseri, habendo miseriores. Augustine, on Ps 26. Many are miserable by loving hurtful things, but they are more miserable by having them. Men need to pray with Bernard, Da domine ut sic possideamus temporalia ut non perdamus aeterna. Grant us, Lord, that we may so share in temporal happiness that we may not lose eternal.

2. Painting Sin with Virtue’s Colors

The second device of Satan to draw the soul to sin is to paint sin with virtue’s colors. Satan knows that if he presented sin in its own nature and dress, the soul would rather flee from it than yield to it. Therefore he presents it to us, not in its own true colors, but painted and gilded over with the name and show of virtue, so that we may the more easily be overcome by it, and take the more pleasure in committing it. Pride he presents to the soul under the name and notion of neatness and cleanliness; covetousness (which the apostle condemns as idolatry) as nothing but good thrift; drunkenness as good fellowship; riotous living under the name and notion of generosity; and wantonness as a passing folly of youth, etc.

Now the remedies against this device of Satan are these.

First, consider that sin is not one bit less filthy, vile and abominable for being colored and painted with virtue’s colors. A poisonous pill is not one bit less poisonous because it is gilded over with gold. A wolf is not one bit less a wolf because he has put on a sheep’s skin. The devil is not one bit less a devil because he sometimes appears like an angel of light. So neither is sin any bit less filthy and abominable for being painted over with virtue’s colors.

The second remedy is this: the more sin is painted under the color60 of virtue, the more dangerous it is to the souls of men. We see this plainly in these days, in the very many souls who are turned out of the way that is holy (the way in which their souls have had sweet and glorious communion with God) into ways of the highest futility and folly, by Satan’s neat coloring over of sin and painting vice under the name and color of virtue. This is so notoriously known that I need only name it. The most dangerous vermin is too often found under the fairest and sweetest flowers; the fairest glove is often drawn on the foulest hand; and the richest robes are often put on the filthiest bodies. So too the fairest and sweetest names are put on the greatest and most horrible vices and errors in the world. Ah, if only we did not have so many sad proofs of this among us!

The third remedy against this device is to look on sin with the eye with61 which within a few hours we will see it. Ah, souls! When you+ lie on a dying bed and stand before a judgment seat, sin will be unmasked, and its dress and robes will then be taken off. Then it will appear more vile, filthy and terrible than hell itself. Then what once appeared most sweet will appear most bitter; what appeared most beautiful will appear most ugly; and what appeared most delightful will then appear most dreadful to the soul. Ah, the shame, the pain, the gall, the bitterness, the horror, the hell, that the sight of sin will raise in poor souls when its dress is taken off! Sin will surely prove evil and bitter to the soul when its robes are taken off. A man may have a kidney stone though he feels no attack of it. Conscience will work at last, though for the present one may feel no attack of accusation. Laban62 showed himself for what he was at parting. Sin will be bitterness in the end, when it appears to the soul in its own filthy nature. The devil deals with men as the panther does with beasts: he hides his ugly head until his sweet scent has drawn them into his power. Until we have sinned, Satan is a flatterer; when we have sinned, he is a tyrant. Ah, souls! The day is at hand when the devil will pull off the paint and decoration that he has put on sin, and present that monster sin to your+ souls in such a monstrous shape that it will cause your+ thoughts to be troubled, your+ face to change, the joints of your+ hips to be loosed, your+ knees to knock one against another, and your+ hearts to be so terrified that you+ will be ready, with Ahithophel and Judas, to strangle and hang your+ bodies on earth and your+ souls in hell, if the Lord does not have more mercy on you+ than he had on them. Oh, therefore, look on sin now as you+ must look on it to all eternity, and as God, conscience and Satan will present it to you+ another day.

The fourth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that even these very sins that Satan paints, and puts new names and colors63 on, cost the best blood, the noblest blood, the life-blood, the heart-blood of the Lord Jesus. Consider that Christ should come from the eternal bosom of his Father to a region of sorrow and death; that God should be manifested in the flesh, the Creator made a creature; that he who was clothed with glory should be wrapped in rags of flesh; that he who filled heaven and earth with his glory should be cradled in a manger; that the power of God should flee from weak man, the God of Israel into Egypt; that the God of the law should be subject to the law;64 the God of circumcision circumcised; the God who made the heavens working at Joseph’s humble trade; that he who binds the devils in chains should be tempted; that he whose is the world and all its fullness should hunger and thirst; that the God of strength should be weary, the Judge of all flesh condemned, the God of life put to death; that he who is one with his Father should cry out in misery, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”; that he who had the keys of hell and death at his belt should lie imprisoned in another man’s tomb, having nowhere in his lifetime to lay his head, nor after death to lay his body. Consider that that head, before which the angels cast down their crowns, should be crowned with thorns; that those eyes, purer than the sun, should be put out by the darkness of death; that those ears, which hear nothing but the hallelujahs of saints and angels, should hear the blasphemies of the multitude; that that face, which was fairer than the sons of men, should be spat on by those beastly, wretched Jews; that that mouth and tongue, which spoke as no man ever spoke, should be accused of blasphemy; that those hands that freely wielded the scepter of heaven should be nailed to the cross; that those feet, like fine brass, should be nailed to the cross for man’s sins; that each sense should be afflicted: his feeling or touch with a spear and nails;65 his smell with stench, being crucified at Golgotha, the place of skulls; his taste with vinegar and gall; his hearing with reproaches; and his sight with his mother and disciples mourning him; his soul comfortless and forsaken; and all this for those very sins that Satan paints and puts fine colors on. Oh, how the consideration of this should stir up the soul against sin, and move the soul to flee from it, and to use all holy means by which sin may be subdued and destroyed! After Julius Caesar was murdered, Antony brought out his coat, all bloody and cut, and laid it before the people, saying, “Look, here you+ have your+ emperor’s coat, bloody and torn like this.” At this the people were at once in an uproar, and cried out to kill those murderers. They took the tables and stools that were in the place and set them on fire, and ran to the houses of those who had killed Caesar and burned them. So when we consider that sin has killed our Lord Jesus, ah, how it should provoke our hearts to take revenge on sin, which has murdered the Lord of glory and66 has done a harm that all the devils in hell could never have done! It was good counsel that one gave: “Never let the thoughts of a crucified Christ go out of your+ minds. Let these be food and drink to you+; let them be your+ sweetness and consolation, your+ honey and your+ desire, your+ reading and your+ meditation, your+ life, death and resurrection.”

60. Turpiora sunt vitia quae virtutum specie celantur [Vices are the fouler for being hidden under the appearance of virtues], Jerome. So the Illuminates (as they called themselves), a pestilent sect in Aragon, professing and laying claim to a kind of angelic purity, fell suddenly to justifying bestiality, as many have done in these days.

61. Tacitus says of Tiberius that when his sins appeared in their own colors, they so terrified and tormented him that he declared to the Senate that he suffered death daily.

62. Satan, who now lures you to sin, will before long make you see that (Peccatum est deicidium) sin is a murdering of God. And this will make you murder two at once, your soul and your body, unless the Lord in mercy holds your hand.

63. Una guttula plus valet quam coelum & terra. Luther; that is, one little drop (speaking of the blood of Christ) is worth more than heaven and earth.

64. One of the rabbis, when he read what bitter torments the Messiah would suffer when he came into the world, cried out, Veniat Messias et ego non videam; that is, “Let the Messiah come, but let me not see him.” Dionysius, being in Egypt at the time of Christ’s suffering, and seeing an eclipse of the sun, and knowing it to be contrary to nature, cried out (aut Deus naturae patitur aut mundi machina dissolvitur), “Either the God of nature suffers, or the frame of the world will be dissolved.”

65. It is an excellent saying of Bernard (quanto pro nobis vilior tanto nobis charior): the more lowly Christ made himself for us, the more dear he ought to be to us.

66. Nolo vivere sine vulnere cum te video vulneratum. “O my God, as long as I see your wounds, I will never live without a wound,” says Bonaventure.

3. Lessening Sin

The third device that Satan has to draw the soul to sin is to extenuate and lessen sin. “Ah,” says Satan, “it is only a little pride, a little worldliness, a little uncleanness, a little drunkenness, etc.” As Lot said of Zoar,67 “it is only a little one, and my soul will live.” “Alas,” says Satan, “it is only a very little sin that you stick at so. You may commit it without any danger to your soul. It is only a little one; you may commit it, and yet your soul will live.”

Now the remedies against this device of Satan are these.

First, consider solemnly that those sins which we are apt to count small have brought on men the greatest wrath of God: such as the eating of an apple, gathering a few sticks on the Sabbath day, and touching the ark. Oh, the dreadful wrath that these sins brought down on the68 heads and hearts of men! The least sin is contrary to the law of God, the nature of God, the being of God and the glory of God, and therefore it is often punished severely by God. And do we not see daily the vengeance of the Almighty falling on the bodies, names, estates, families and souls of men for those sins that are only little ones in their eyes? Surely, if we are not utterly forsaken by God and blinded by Satan, we cannot fail to see it. Oh, therefore, when Satan says, “It is only a little one,” you must say, “Oh, but those sins that you call little are such as will cause God to rain hell out of heaven on sinners, as he did on the Sodomites.”

The second remedy against this device of Satan is to consider seriously that giving way to a lesser sin makes way for committing a greater. If a man yields to a lesser sin to avoid a greater, it is ten thousand to one that God in justice will leave that soul to fall into a greater. If we commit one sin to avoid another, it is just that we should avoid neither. For we have neither law nor power in our own hands to keep off sin as we please, and by yielding to the69 lesser, we tempt the tempter to tempt us to the greater. Sin is of an encroaching nature. It creeps on the soul by degrees, step by step, until it has brought the soul to the very height of sin. David gives way to his wandering eye, and this led him to those foul sins that caused God to break his bones, to turn his day into night, and to leave his soul in great darkness. Jacob and Peter and other saints have found this true by woeful experience: yielding to a lesser sin has been the ushering in of a greater. The little thief will open the door and make way for the greater, and the little wedge knocked in will make way for the greater. Satan will first draw you to sit with the drunkard, then to sip with the drunkard, and then at last to be drunk with the drunkard. He will first draw you to be unclean in your thoughts, then to be unclean in your looks, then to be unclean in your words, and at last to be unclean in your practices. He will first draw you to look on the golden wedge, then to like the golden wedge, then to handle the golden wedge, and then at last to gain the golden wedge by wicked ways, though you run the risk of losing God and your soul70 forever, as you may see in Gehazi, Achan and Judas, and in many in these days of ours. Sin never stands still. Ps 1:1: first ungodly, then sinners, then scorners. Here they go on from sin to sin until they come to the top of sin, namely, “to sit in the seat of scorners,” or as the Septuagint has it (τῶν λοιμῶν), to aspire to the honor of the chair of pestilence. Augustine, writing on John, tells the story of a certain man who held the opinion that the devil made the fly, and not God. Someone said to him, “If the devil made flies, then the devil made worms, and God did not make them, for they are living creatures as well as flies.” “True,” he said, “the devil did make worms.” “But,” said the other, “if the devil made worms, then he made birds, beasts and man.” He granted it all. So, says Augustine, by denying God in the fly he came to deny God in man, and to deny the whole creation. By all this we see that yielding to lesser sins draws the soul to commit greater ones. Ah, how many in these days have fallen first to having low thoughts of Scripture and ordinances, then to slighting Scripture and ordinances, then to making a nose of wax of Scripture and ordinances, then to casting off Scripture and ordinances, and then at last to advancing and lifting up themselves and their Christ-dishonoring and soul-damning opinions71 above Scripture and ordinances! Sin gains on men’s souls by imperceptible degrees. Eccl 10:13: “The beginning of his talk is folly, and the end of his speech is evil madness.” Corruption in the heart, when it breaks out, is like a breach in a sea wall, which begins as a narrow passage until it eats through and casts down everything before it. The debates of the soul are quick and soon ended, and something may be done in a moment that may undo a man forever. When a man has begun to sin, he does not know where or when or how he will put a stop to sin. Usually the soul goes on from evil to evil, from folly to folly, until it is ripe for eternal misery. Men usually grow from being wicked to being very wicked, and from very wicked to utterly wicked, and then God counts them as nothing forever.

The third remedy against this third device that Satan has to draw the soul to sin is to consider solemnly that it is sad to fall out with God over a trifle. The rich man would not give a crumb; therefore72 he was not to receive a drop. It is the greatest folly in the world to risk going to hell for a small matter. “I only tasted a little honey,” said Jonathan,73 “and now I must die.” It is a most unkind and unfaithful thing to break with God for a little. Little sins carry with them only little temptations to sin,74 and a man shows the most wickedness and unkindness when he sins on a little temptation. It is devilish to sin without a temptation; it is little less than devilish to sin on a little occasion. The less the temptation to sin is, the greater that sin is. Saul’s sin in not waiting for Samuel was not great in its matter, but it was great in its malice; for even if Samuel had not come at all, Saul should not have offered sacrifice. But this cost him dear: his soul and his kingdom. It is the greatest unkindness that can be shown to a friend to risk the complaining, bleeding and grieving of his soul on a light and slight occasion. So it is the greatest unkindness that can be shown to God, Christ and the Spirit for a soul to put God to complaining, Christ to bleeding and the Spirit to grieving by yielding to little sins. Therefore, when Satan says, “It is only a little one,” you must answer that often the greatest unkindness is shown to God’s glorious Majesty in acting the least folly, and therefore you will not displease your best and greatest friend by yielding to his least enemy.

The fourth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider seriously that there is great danger, indeed many times the most danger, in the smallest sins.75 “A little leaven works through the whole batch of dough.” If the serpent winds in his head, he will draw his whole body after it. Greater sins sooner startle the soul, and awaken and rouse the soul to repentance,76 than lesser sins do. Little sins often slide into the soul, and breed and work secretly and unnoticed77 in the soul, until they become so strong as to trample on the soul and cut the throat of the soul. There is often the greatest danger to our bodies in the least diseases that hang on us, because we are apt to make78 light of them, and to neglect the timely use of means for removing them, until they have grown so strong that they prove fatal to us. So there is often the most danger in the least sins. We are apt to take no notice of them, and to neglect those heavenly helps by which they should be weakened and destroyed, until they have grown to such strength that we are ready to cry out, “The medicine is79 too weak for the disease. I would pray, and I would hear the word, but I am afraid that sin has grown by degrees to such a head that I will never be able to prevail over it. As I have begun to fall,80 so I will utterly fall before it, and at last perish in it, unless the power and free grace of Christ act gloriously, beyond my present understanding and expectation.” The viper is killed by the little young ones that are nourished and cherished in her belly. So many men are eternally killed and betrayed by the little81 sins (as they call them) that are nourished in their own bosoms. “I do not know,” says one, “whether maintaining the least sin is not worse than committing the greatest; for the greatest may come from frailty, while maintaining the least shows obstinacy.” A little hole in the ship sinks it; a small breach in a sea wall carries away everything before it; a little stab at the heart kills a man; and a little sin, without a great deal of mercy, will damn a man.

The fifth remedy against this device82 of Satan is to consider solemnly that other saints have chosen to suffer the worst torments rather than commit the least sin, that is, the least as the world counts it. So you may see in Daniel and his companions, who would rather choose to burn and be cast to the lions than bow to the image that Nebuchadnezzar had set up. When this peccadillo (in the world’s account) and a hot, fiery furnace stood in competition, so that they must either fall into sin or be cast into the83 fiery furnace, such was their tender regard for the honor and glory of God, and their hatred of and indignation against sin, that they would rather burn than sin. They knew that it was far better to burn for not sinning than for God and conscience to raise a hell, a fire, in their bosoms for sin. I have read of that noble servant of God, Marcus Arethusius, minister of a church in the time of Constantine, who in Constantine’s time had been the cause of overthrowing an idol’s temple. Afterward, when Julian came to be emperor, he would force the people of that place to build it up again. They were ready to do it, but Arethusius refused. At this, those who were his own people, to whom he preached, took him and stripped him of all his clothes, and abused his naked body, and gave it up to the children to cut with their penknives. Then they had him put in a basket, and anointed his naked body with honey, and set him in the sun to be stung by wasps. And they showed all this cruelty because he would not do anything toward building up this idol-temple. Indeed, they came to this: if he would do even the least toward it, if he would give only a halfpenny to it, they would save him. But he refused it all, though giving a halfpenny might have saved his life. And in doing this he only lived up to the principle that most Christians talk of, and all profess, but few come up to, namely, that we must choose to suffer the worst torments that men and devils can invent and inflict, rather than commit the least sin by which God would be dishonored, our consciences wounded, religion reproached and our own souls endangered.

The sixth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider seriously that the soul is never able to stand under the guilt and weight of the least sin when God brings it home to the soul. The least sin will press down and sink the boldest sinner as low as hell, when God opens the eyes of a sinner and makes him see the horrid filthiness and abominable vileness that is in sin. What creatures are so little, base and vile as lice or gnats? And yet by these little, poor creatures God so plagued stubborn Pharaoh and all Egypt that, fainting under it, they were forced to cry out, “This is the finger of God.” When little84 creatures, indeed the least creatures, are armed with power from God, they will press down and sink the greatest, proudest and most stubborn tyrants that breathe. So when God puts a sword85 into the hand of a little sin and arms it against the soul, the soul will faint and fall under it. Some who have only planned adultery, without ever actually committing it; others who found a trifle and did not make it a matter of conscience to return it, knowing by the light of natural conscience that they did not do as they would be done by; and others who have had some unworthy thought of God, have been so frightened, dismayed86 and terrified by these sins, which are small (in men’s account), that they have wished they had never been born; that they could take no delight in any earthly comfort; that they have been put at their wits’ end, ready to take their own lives, wishing themselves annihilated.

Mr. Perkins mentions a good man, but very poor, who, being ready to starve, stole a lamb. When he was about to eat it with his poor children, and (as his custom was before meals) to ask a blessing, he dared not do it, but fell into a great perplexity of conscience, acknowledged his fault to the owner, and promised payment if ever he should be able.

The seventh remedy against this device is to consider solemnly that there is more evil in the least sin than in the greatest affliction. This appears as clear as the sun by the severe dealing of God the Father with his beloved Son, on whom he poured out all the vials of his fiercest wrath, and that for the least sin as well as for the greatest. “The wages87 of sin is death”: that is, of sin without distinction, whether great or small. Oh, how this should make us tremble at the least spark of lust as much as at hell itself, considering that God the Father would not spare the Son of his bosom, no, not for the least sin, but would make him drink the dregs of his wrath! And so much for the remedies that may fence and preserve our souls from being drawn to sin by this third device of Satan.

67. Gen 19:20.

68. Draco, the rigid lawgiver, being asked why he appointed death for all sins when sins were not equal, answered that he knew sins were not all equal, but he knew the least deserved death. So though the sins of men are not all equal, yet the least of them deserves eternal death.

69. Ps 137:9: “Blessed is he who seizes your little ones and dashes them against the stones.” Hugo’s gloss is devout, etc. (Sit nihil in te Babylonicum): let there be nothing of Babylon in you. Not only the grown men but the little ones must be dashed against the stones; not only great sins but little sins must be killed, or they will kill the soul forever.

87. Death is the pay of the least sin; the best wages that the least sin gives its soldiers is death of every kind. In a strict sense there is no little sin, because there is no little God to sin against.

4. The Best Men’s Sins

The fourth device that Satan has to draw the soul to sin is to present to the soul the best men’s sins and hide from the soul their virtues; to show the soul their sins and hide from the soul their sorrows and repentance: as by setting before the soul the adultery of David, the pride of Hezekiah, the impatience of Job, the drunkenness of Noah, the blasphemy of Peter, etc., and by hiding from the soul the tears, the sighs, the groans, the meltings, humblings and repentings of these precious souls.

Now the remedies against this device of the devil are as follows.

The first remedy against this device of Satan is to consider seriously that the Spirit of the Lord has been as careful to record the saints’ rising out of sin by repentance as he has to record their falling into sin. David falls fearfully, but by repentance he rises sweetly: “Blot out my transgressions. Wash me thoroughly of my iniquity and cleanse me from my sin. For I acknowledge my transgressions, and my sin is always before me. Purify me with hyssop, and I will be clean; wash me, and I will be whiter than snow. Deliver me from bloodguilt, O God, the God of my salvation.” It is true that Hezekiah’s heart was lifted up under the abundance of blessings that God had poured in on him; and it is as true that Hezekiah88 “humbled the pride of his heart—he and the people of Jerusalem—so that the wrath of the Lord did not come upon them during the days of Hezekiah.” It is true that Job curses the day of his birth; and it is as true that he rises by repentance. “Behold, I am vile,” he says. “How can I reply to You?89 I place my hand over my mouth. I have spoken once, but I have no answer—twice, but I have nothing to add.” “My ears had heard of You, but now my eyes have seen You. Therefore I abhor myself,90 and I repent in dust and ashes.” Peter falls dreadfully, but rises sweetly by repentance. A look of love from Christ melts him into tears; he knew that repentance was the key to the kingdom of grace. As once his faith was so great that he leaped, as it were, into a sea of waters to come to Christ, so now his repentance was so great that he leaped, as it were, into a sea of tears, because91 he had gone from Christ. Some say that after his sad fall he was weeping again and again, and that his face was even furrowed with continual tears. No sooner had he taken in poison than he vomited it up again, before it reached his vital parts. No sooner had he handled this serpent than he turned it into a rod to scourge his soul with remorse for sinning against such clear light, such strong love, and such sweet revelations of the heart of Christ to him. Clement notes that Peter so repented that all his life afterward, every night when he heard the rooster crow, he would fall on his knees and, weeping bitterly, beg pardon for this sin. Ah, souls! You+ can easily sin like the saints, but can you+ repent with the saints? Many can sin with David and Peter who cannot repent with David and Peter, and so must perish forever. The emperor Theodosius, pressing to receive the Lord’s Supper, excused92 his own foul deed by David’s having done the like. To this Ambrose replied, “You have followed David transgressing; follow David repenting, and then think of the table of the Lord.”

The second remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that these saints did not make a trade of sin. They fell once or twice (and rose by repentance) so that they might93 keep the closer to Christ forever. They fell incidentally, on some occasion, and with much reluctance; but you sin presumptuously, obstinately, readily, delightfully and habitually. By making a trade of sin you have brought on your soul a kind of cursed necessity of sinning, so that you could as well cease to be, or cease to live, as cease to sin. Sin has become by custom like a second nature to you, which you cannot, which you will not, lay aside, though you know that if you do not lay sin aside, God will lay your soul aside forever; though you know that if sin and your soul do not part, Christ and your soul can never meet. Will you make a trade of sin, and cry out, “Did not David sin like this, and Noah94 sin like this, and Peter sin like this, etc.?” No! Their hearts turned aside to folly one day, but your heart turns aside to folly every day. And when they had fallen, they rose by repentance, and by the actings of faith on a crucified Christ; but you fall, and have neither strength nor will to rise, but wallow in sin, and will eternally die in your sins, unless the Lord is the more merciful to your soul. Do you think, O soul, that this is good reasoning: “Such a one tasted poison only once, and yet narrowly escaped; but I drink poison daily, and yet I will escape”? Yet such is the mad reasoning of worldly souls: “David and Peter, etc., sinned once, foully and fearfully; they tasted poison only once, and were sick to death; but I taste it daily, and yet I will not taste eternal death.” Remember, O souls, that the day is at hand when self-flatterers will be found self-deceivers, indeed, self-murderers.

The third remedy against this device of Satan is to consider seriously that though God does not (and never will) disinherit his people for their sins, yet he has severely punished his people for their sins. David sins, and God breaks his bones for his sin: “Let me95 hear joy and gladness; let the bones You have broken rejoice.” “And because you have done this, the sword will not depart from your house to the day of your death.” Though God will not utterly take his loving devotion from them, nor allow his faithfulness to fail, nor break his covenant, nor alter what has gone out of his mouth, yet he will punish their transgressions with the rod, and their iniquity with stripes (Ps 89:30, 35). Scripture abounds with instances of this kind. This is so well-known a truth, among all who know anything of truth, that to cite more Scriptures to prove it would be to light a candle to see the sun at noon. The Jews have a proverb that “There is no punishment that comes on Israel in which there is not an ounce of the golden calf”; meaning that it was so great a sin that God remembered it in every plague, and that it had an influence on every trouble that befell them. Every man’s heart may say to him in his sufferings, as the heart of Apollodorus96 in the cauldron said, “I have been the cause of this.” God is most angry when he shows no anger. God keep me from this mercy! This kind of mercy is worse than97 all other misery. One, writing to a sick friend, has this expression: “I count it a part of unhappiness not to know adversity. I judge you to be miserable, because you have not been miserable.” It is mercy that our affliction is not an execution but a correction. He who has deserved hanging may be glad if he escapes with a whipping. God’s corrections are our instructions, his lashes our lessons, his98 scourges our schoolmasters, his chastisements our warnings. And to note this, both the Hebrews and the Greeks express chastening and teaching99 by one and the same word (musar, paideia), because the latter is the true100 end of the former, according to the proverb, “Smarting makes wise, and vexation gives understanding.” That is why Luther fitly calls affliction “the Christian man’s theology.”101 So says Job 33:14–18: “For God speaks in one way and in another, yet no one notices. In a dream, in a vision in the night, when deep sleep falls upon men as they slumber on their beds, He opens102 the ears of men and seals their instruction, to turn a man from wrongdoing and keep him from pride, to preserve his soul from the Pit and his life from perishing by the sword.” When Satan tells you of other men’s sins to draw you to sin, then think of the same men’s sufferings to keep you from sin. Lay your hand on your heart and say, “O my soul, if you sin with David, you must suffer with David, etc.”

The fourth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that there are only two main ends of God’s recording the falls of his saints. The one is to keep from fainting,103 sinking and despair, under the burden of their sins, those who fall through weakness and infirmity. The other is that their falls may be like landmarks, to warn others who stand to take heed lest they fall. It never entered into the heart of God to record his children’s sins so that others might be encouraged to sin, but so that others might be warned to look to their standing, to cling the more tightly to the hem of Christ’s robe, and to avoid all occasions and temptations that may lead the soul to fall as others have fallen. When they have been left by Christ, the Lord has made their sins like landmarks, to warn his people to take heed how they come near those sands and rocks, those snares and baits, that have been fatal to the choicest treasures, namely, the joy, peace, comfort and glorious enjoyments, of the finest spirits and noblest souls that ever sailed through the ocean of this sinful, troublesome world, as you may see in David, Job, Peter, etc. There is nothing in the world that can so notoriously thwart the grand end of God’s recording the sins of his saints as for anyone to take encouragement from it to sin. And wherever you find such a soul, you may write him down as Christless, graceless, a soul cast off by God, a soul that Satan has by the hand; and the eternal God knows where he will lead him.

103. “I have known a good man,” said Bernard, “who, when he heard of anyone who had committed some notorious sin, used to say to himself (ille hodie & ego cras), ‘He fell today; so may I tomorrow.’”

5. God as All Mercy

The fifth device that Satan has to draw the soul to sin is to present God to the soul as one made up all of mercy. “Oh,” says Satan, “you need not make such a matter of sin. You need not be so fearful of sin, nor so unwilling to sin. For God is a God of mercy, a God full of mercy, a God who delights in mercy, a God who is ready to show mercy, a God who is never weary of showing mercy, a God more inclined to pardon his people than to punish his people. And therefore he will not seize on the soul’s sins to punish it. Why then,” says Satan, “should you make such a matter of sin?”

Now the remedies against this device of Satan are these.

The first remedy is to consider seriously that it is the sorest judgment in this world to be left to sin on any pretense whatever. Oh, unhappy man, when God leaves you to yourself104 and does not resist you in your sins! Woe, woe to him at whose sins God winks! When God lets the way to hell be a smooth and pleasant way, that is hell on this side of hell, and a dreadful sign of God’s indignation against a man, a token of his rejection, and a sign that God does not intend good to him. That is a sad word: “Ephraim is joined to idols; leave him alone!” He will not be counseled or corrected; he has made a match with wickedness; he shall have his bellyful of it; he falls with his eyes open; let him fall at his own peril. And that is a terrible saying: “So I gave them up to the lusts of their own hearts,105 to follow their own counsels.” A soul given up to sin is a soul ripe for hell, a soul hurrying to destruction. Ah,106 Lord! This mercy I humbly beg: that whatever you give me up to, you will not give me up to the ways of my own heart. If you will give me up to be afflicted, or tempted, or reproached, etc., I will patiently sit down and say, “It is the Lord; let him do with me what seems good in his own eyes.” Do anything with me, lay what burden you will upon me, so long as you do not give me up to the ways of my own heart, etc.

The second remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that God is as just as he is merciful. As the Scriptures speak of him as a very merciful God, so they speak of him107 as a very just God. Witness his casting the angels out of heaven and binding them in chains of darkness until the judgment of the great day. Witness his turning Adam out of paradise, his drowning of the old world, and his raining hell out of heaven upon Sodom. Witness all the crosses, losses, sicknesses, and diseases that are in the world. Witness Tophet, which was prepared of old; witness his “storing up wrath for the day of wrath, when God’s righteous judgment will be revealed.” But above all, witness the pouring out of all his wrath upon his bosom Son, when he bore the sins of his people and cried out, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”108

The third remedy against this device of Satan is to consider seriously that sins against mercy will bring the greatest and the sorest judgments upon men’s heads and hearts. Mercy is Alpha; justice is Omega. David, speaking of these attributes, places mercy in the vanguard and justice in the rearguard, saying, “I will sing of Your mercy and justice.”109 When mercy is despised, then justice takes the throne. God is like a110 prince who does not send his army against rebels before he has sent his pardon and proclaimed it by a herald. He first hangs out the white flag of mercy. If this wins men in, they are happy forever; but if they hold out, then God will put out his red flag of justice and judgment. If the one is despised, the other will be felt with a vengeance. See this in the Israelites.111 He loved them and chose them when they were in their blood and most unlovely. He multiplied them, not by means but by miracle; for from seventy souls they grew in a few years to six hundred thousand. The more they were oppressed, the more they prospered: like chamomile, the more you tread it, the more you spread it; or like a palm tree, the more it is pressed down, the further it spreads; or like fire, the more it is raked, the more it burns. Their mercies came in upon them like Job’s messengers, one on the heels of another.112 “He took off their sackcloth and clothed them with gladness, and surrounded them with songs of deliverance; he carried them on eagles’ wings; he kept them as the apple of his eye,” etc. But they, abusing his mercy, became the greatest objects of his wrath. As I know of no man who can reckon up their mercies, so I know of no man who can sum up the miseries that have come upon them for their sins. For as our Savior prophesied concerning Jerusalem, “that not one stone113 would be left on another,” so it was fulfilled forty years after his ascension by Vespasian the emperor and his son Titus. They besieged Jerusalem, and the Jews were oppressed with a grievous famine, in which their food was old shoes, old leather, old hay, and the dung of beasts. There died, partly by the sword and partly by the famine, eleven hundred thousand of the poorer sort. Two thousand in one night were disemboweled; six thousand were burned in a porch of the temple; the whole city was sacked and burned and leveled to the ground; and ninety-seven thousand were taken captive and put to base and miserable service, as Eusebius and Josephus say. And to this day, in all parts of the world, are they not the refuse of the world? None are less loved, and none more abhorred, than they. And so Capernaum, which was lifted up to heaven, was threatened to be114 thrown down to hell. No souls fall so low into hell (if they fall) as those souls who by a hand of mercy are lifted up nearest to heaven. You+ careless souls who are so apt to abuse mercy, consider this: in the days of the gospel, the plagues that God inflicts on the despisers and abusers of mercy are usually spiritual plagues, such as blindness of mind, hardness of heart, and numbness of conscience. These are ten thousand times worse than the worst of outward plagues that can befall you+. And therefore, though you+ may escape temporal judgments, yet you+ will not escape spiritual judgments: “How shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation?” says the apostle. Oh, therefore, whenever Satan presents God to the soul as one made up all of mercy, so that he may draw you to do wickedly, tell him that sins against mercy will bring the greatest misery upon the soul, and that therefore, whatever becomes of you, you will not sin against mercy, etc.

The fourth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider seriously that though God’s general mercy is over all his works, yet his special mercy115 is confined to those who are divinely qualified. So in Exodus 34:6, 7: “And the Lord passed in front of him and proclaimed: ‘The Lord, the Lord God, merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in goodness and faithfulness, maintaining mercy to thousands, forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin. Yet He will by no means leave the guilty unpunished.’” Exod 20:6: “and showing mercy to thousands of those who love Me and keep My commandments.” Ps 25:10: “All the Lord’s ways are mercy and faithfulness to those who keep His covenant and His decrees.” Ps 32:10: “Many are the sorrows of the wicked, but mercy surrounds him who trusts in the Lord.” Ps 33:18: “Surely the eyes of the Lord are on those who fear Him, on those whose hope is in His mercy.” Ps 103:11: “For as high as the heavens are above the earth, so great is His mercy toward those who fear Him.” Verse 17: “But from everlasting to everlasting the mercy of the Lord is upon those who fear Him.” When Satan attempts to draw you to sin by presenting God as a God all made up of mercy, oh, then reply that though God’s general mercy extends to all the works of his hand, yet his special mercy is confined to those who are divinely qualified: to those who love him and keep his commandments, to those who trust in him, who by hope hang upon him, and who fear him. Reply that you must be such a one here, or else you can never be happy hereafter; you must partake of his special mercy, or else perish eternally in everlasting misery, notwithstanding God’s general mercy.

The fifth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that those who were once glorious on earth, and are now triumphing in heaven, looked upon the mercy of God as the most powerful reason to preserve them from sin and to fence their souls against sin, and not as an encouragement116 to sin. Ps 26:3, 4, 5, 6: “For Your loving kindness is before my eyes, and I have walked in Your truth. I do not sit with deceitful men, nor keep company with hypocrites. I hate the mob of evildoers, and refuse to sit with the wicked.” So Joseph strengthens himself against sin by remembering mercy. “How then could I,” he says, “do such a great117 evil and sin against God?” He had fixed his eye on mercy, and therefore sin could not enter, though the irons entered into his soul. His soul, being taken with mercy, was not moved by the shamelessness of his master’s wife. Satan knocked often at the door, but the sight of mercy would not allow Joseph to answer or open. Joseph, like a pearl in a puddle, keeps his virtue still. So Paul: “Shall we continue in sin so that grace may increase? Certainly not!118 How can we who died to sin live in it any longer?” There is nothing in the world that makes a man more unlike a saint, and more like Satan, than to argue from mercy to sinful liberty, from divine goodness to licentiousness. This is the devil’s logic, and in whomever you find it, you may write, “This soul is lost.” A man may as truly say that the sea burns or that fire cools, as that free grace and mercy should make a truly gracious soul do wickedly. So the same apostle: “Therefore I urge you+, brothers, by the mercies of God, to offer your+ bodies as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God, which is your+ spiritual service of worship.” So John: “I am writing these things to you+ so that you+ will not sin.” What was it that he wrote? He wrote that we might have “fellowship … with the Father and with His Son,”119 and that “the blood of Jesus His Son cleanses us from all sin,” and that “if we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins,” and that if we do sin, “we have an advocate before the Father—Jesus Christ, the Righteous One.” These choice favors and mercies the apostle holds out as the choicest means to preserve the soul from sin and to keep it at the greatest distance from sin; and if this will not do it, you may write the man down as void of Christ and grace, and undone forever.
