6. Repentance Made Easy

The sixth device that Satan has to draw the soul to sin is persuading the soul that the work of repentance is an easy work, and that therefore the soul need not make such a matter of sin. “Why, suppose you do sin,” says Satan; “it is no such difficult thing to return, and confess, and be sorrowful, and beg pardon, and cry, ‘Lord, have mercy upon me.’ And if you do but this, God will cancel the debt, and pardon your sins, and save your souls,” etc. By this device Satan draws many a soul to sin, and makes many millions of souls servants, or rather slaves, to sin, etc.

Now the remedies against this device of Satan are as follows.

The first remedy is to consider seriously120 that repentance is a mighty work, a difficult work, a work that is above our power. There is no power below the power that raised Christ from the dead and made the world that can break the heart of a sinner or turn the heart of a sinner. You are as able to melt adamant as to melt your own heart, to turn a flint into flesh as to turn your own heart to the Lord, to raise the dead and to make a world as to repent. Repentance is a flower that does not grow in nature’s garden. “Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? Neither are you+ able to do good—you+ who are accustomed to doing evil” (Jer 13:23). Repentance is a gift that comes down from above; men are not born with repentance in their hearts as they are born with tongues in their mouths.121 Acts 5:31: “God exalted Him to His right hand as Prince and Savior, in order to grant repentance and forgiveness of sins to Israel.” So in 2 Tim 2:25: “gently reproving those who oppose him, in the hope that God may grant them repentance leading to a knowledge of the truth.” It is not in the power of any mortal to repent at pleasure. Some ignorant, deluded souls vainly imagine that these five words, “Lord, have mercy upon me,” are efficacious to send them to heaven. But as many are ruined by buying a counterfeit jewel, so many are in hell by mistaking their repentance. Many rest in their repentance, though it is but the shadow of repentance, which caused one to say, “Repentance damns more than sin.”

The second remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly the nature of true repentance. Repentance is something other than what worldly men imagine. Repentance is sometimes taken in a more strict and narrow122 sense, for godly sorrow; sometimes repentance is taken in a broad sense, for amendment of life. Repentance has three things in it, namely, the act, the subject, and the terms.

1. The formal act of repentance is a changing and converting. It is often set forth in Scripture by turning: “Turn me, and I will be turned,” says Ephraim; “after I was turned, I repented,” he says. It is a turning from darkness to light.

2. The subject changed and converted is the whole man: both the sinner’s heart and his life; first his heart, then his life; first his person, then his practice and conduct. “Wash and cleanse yourselves+”: there is the change of their persons. “Remove your+ evil deeds from My sight. Stop doing evil! Learn to do right”: there is the change of their practices. So “Cast away from yourselves+” (says Ezekiel) “all the transgressions you+ have committed”: there is the change of the life; “and fashion for yourselves+ a new heart and a new spirit”: there is the change of the heart.

3. The terms of this change and conversion, from which and to which both heart and life must be changed, are these: from all sin, to God. The heart must be changed from the state and power of sin, the life from the acts of sin, but both to God: the heart to be under his power in a state of grace, the life to be under his rule in all new obedience. As the apostle speaks: “to open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God.” So the prophet Isaiah says, “Let the wicked man forsake his own way and the unrighteous man his own thoughts; let him return to the Lord.” Thus much for the nature of evangelical repentance. Now, souls, tell me whether it is such an easy thing to repent as Satan suggests. Besides what has been said, I desire that you+ take notice that repentance includes a turning from the most darling sin: Ephraim shall say, “What have I to do anymore with idols?” Indeed, it is a turning from all sin to God. Ezek 18:30: “Therefore, O house of Israel, I will judge you+, each according to his ways, declares the Lord God. Repent and turn from all your+ transgressions, so that iniquity will not be your+ ruin.” Herod turned from many sins, but did not turn from his Herodias, which was his ruin. Judas turned from all visible wickedness, yet he would not cast out that golden devil, covetousness, and therefore was cast into the hottest place in hell. He who does not turn from every sin does not turn aright from any one sin. Every sin strikes at the honor of God, the being of God, the glory of God, the heart of Christ, the joy of the Spirit, and the peace of a man’s conscience. And therefore a soul truly penitent strikes at all, hates all, fights against all, and will labor to draw strength from a crucified Christ to crucify all. A true penitent knows neither father nor mother, neither right eye nor right hand, but will pluck out the one and cut off the other. Saul spared but one Agag, and that cost him his soul and his kingdom. Besides, repentance is not only a turning from all sin, but also a turning to all good: to a love of all good, to a prizing of all good, and to a following after all good. Ezek 18:21: “But if the wicked man turns from all the sins he has committed, keeps all My statutes, and does what is just and right, he will surely live; he will not die.” That is, a righteousness and holiness that is only negative is no righteousness or holiness. David fulfilled all the will of God and had regard for all his commandments, and so had Zechariah and Elizabeth. It is not enough that the tree does not bear bad fruit; it must bear good fruit, or else it must be cut down and thrown into the fire. So it is not enough that you+ are not wicked in this way and that; you+ must be gracious and good in this way and that, or else divine justice will put the axe of divine vengeance to the root of your+ souls and cut you+ off forever. “Every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.” Besides, repentance includes a sense of sin’s sinfulness, how opposite and contrary it is to the blessed God. God is light, sin is darkness; God is life, sin is death; God is heaven, sin is hell; God is beauty, sin is deformity. True repentance also includes a sense of sin’s harmfulness: how it cast angels out of heaven and Adam out of paradise; how it laid the first cornerstone in hell, and brought in all the curses, crosses, and miseries that are in the world; how it makes men liable to all temporal, spiritual, and eternal wrath; how it has made men godless, Christless, hopeless, and heavenless in this world. Further, true repentance includes sorrow for sin, contrition of heart. It breaks the heart with sighs and sobs and groans, because a loving God and Father is offended by sin, a blessed Savior crucified afresh, and the sweet Comforter, the Spirit,123 grieved and vexed. Again, repentance includes not only a loathing of sin, but also a loathing of ourselves for sin. As a man not only loathes poison, but loathes the very dish or vessel that has the smell of the poison, so a true penitent not only loathes his sin, but loathes himself, the vessel that still smells of sin. So Ezek 20:43: “And there you+ will remember your+ ways and all the deeds with which you+ have defiled yourselves+, and you+ will loathe yourselves+ for all the evils you+ have done.” True repentance will bring your+ hearts not only to loathe your+ sins, but also to loathe yourselves+. Again, true repentance not only brings a man to loathe himself for his sins, but also makes him ashamed of his sin. “What fruit did you+ reap at that time from the things of which you+ are (now) ashamed?” says the apostle. So Ezekiel: “And you will be ashamed and never again open your mouth because of your disgrace, when I am pacified toward you for all you have done, declares the Lord God.” When a penitent soul sees his sins pardoned, the anger of God pacified, and divine justice satisfied, then he sits down (and blushes, as the Hebrew has it) as one ashamed. Indeed, true repentance124 brings a man to thwart his sinful self and to walk contrary to his sinful self, to take a holy revenge upon sin, as you+ may see in Paul, the jailer, Mary Magdalene, and Manasseh. This the apostle shows in 2 Cor 7:10, 11: “For godly sorrow brings repentance never to be regretted, but worldly sorrow brings death. Consider what this godly sorrow has produced in you+: what earnestness, what eagerness to clear yourselves+, what indignation, what alarm, what longing, what zeal, what revenge!” Now, souls, add all these things together, and tell me whether it is such an easy thing to repent as Satan would make the soul believe; and I am confident your+ hearts will answer that it is as hard a thing to repent as it is to make a world or to raise the dead. I will conclude this second remedy with a worthy saying of a precious holy man: “Repentance,” he says, “strips us stark naked of all the garments of the old Adam, and does not leave so much as the shirt behind. In this rotten building it does not leave one stone upon another.” As the flood drowned Noah’s own friends and servants, so the flood of repenting tears must drown our sweetest and most profitable sins.

The third remedy against this device of Satan is to consider seriously that repentance is a continued act; the word “repent” implies its continuing. True repentance inclines a man’s125 heart to perform God’s statutes always, even to the end. A true penitent must go on from faith to faith, from strength to strength; he must never stand still nor turn back. Repentance is a grace, and must have its daily operation as well as other graces. True repentance is a continual spring, where the waters of godly sorrow are always flowing: “My sin is always before me.” A true penitent is often casting his eyes back to the days of his former folly, and this makes him drench his couch with his tears morning and evening. “Remember not the sins of my youth,” says one blessed penitent; and “I was a blasphemer, a persecutor, and a violent man,” says another penitent. Repentance is a continued act of turning, a repentance never to be regretted, a turning never to turn again to folly. A true penitent always has something within him to turn from. He can never get near enough to God, no, not so near to him as he once was; and therefore he is continually turning and turning, so that he may get nearer and nearer to him, who is his chief good and his only happiness (optimum126 maximum), the best and the greatest. They are every day crying out, “What wretched men we are! Who will rescue us from this body of death?” They are continually aware of sin, and continually fighting against sin, and continually sorrowing for sin, and continually loathing themselves for sin. Repentance is no passing act, but a continued act of the soul. And tell me, oh tempted soul, whether it is such an easy thing as Satan would make you believe, to be every day turning more and more from sin, and turning nearer and nearer to God, your choicest blessedness. A true penitent can as easily content himself with one act of faith or one act of love as he can content himself with one act of repentance. A Jewish rabbi, pressing the practice of repentance upon his disciples, exhorted them to be sure to repent the day before they died. One of them replied that the day of any man’s death was very uncertain. “Repent every day, then,” said the rabbi, “and then you+ will be sure to repent the day before you+ die.” You+ are wise, and know how to apply it to your+ own advantage.

The fourth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that if the work of repentance were such an easy work as Satan would127 make it, then surely so many would not lie roaring and crying out (of wrath and eternal ruin) under the horrors and terrors of conscience for not repenting. Indeed, no doubt so many millions would not go to hell for not repenting, if it were such an easy thing to repent. Ah, do not poor souls under horrors of conscience cry out and say, “Were all this world a lump of gold, and in our hand to dispose of, we would give it for the least dram of true repentance”? And will you say it is an easy thing to repent? When a poor sinner whose conscience is awakened judges the exchange of all the world for the least dram of repentance to be the happiest exchange that ever sinner made, tell me, oh soul, is it128 good going to hell? Is it good dwelling with the devouring fire, with everlasting burnings? Is it good to be forever separated from the blessed and glorious presence of God, angels, and saints, and to be forever shut out from those good things of eternal life, which are so many that they exceed number, so great that they exceed measure, so precious that they exceed all estimation? We know it is the greatest misery that can befall the sons of men; and would they not prevent it by repentance, if it were such an easy thing to repent as Satan would make it? Well then, do not run the risk of losing God, Christ, heaven, and your soul forever by listening to this device of Satan, namely, that it is an easy thing to repent, etc. If it is so easy, why then do wicked men’s hearts rise so against those who press the doctrine of repentance in the sweetest way, and by the strongest and choicest arguments that the Scripture affords? And why do they kill two at once, the faithful laborer’s name and their own souls, by their wicked words and actions, because they are urged to repent, which Satan tells them is so easy a thing? Surely, were repentance so easy, wicked men would not be so much enraged when that doctrine is pressed upon them by evangelical considerations.

The fifth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider seriously that to repent of sin is as great a work of grace as not to sin. By our sinful falls the powers of the soul are weakened, the129 strength of grace is decayed, our evidences for heaven are blotted, fears and doubts are raised in the soul (Will God pardon this scarlet sin once more, and show mercy to this wretched soul?), corruptions in the heart gain more ground and are confirmed, and the conscience of a man after his falls is the more enraged or the more numbed. Now for a soul, notwithstanding all this, to repent of his falls shows that it is as great a work of grace to repent of sin as it is not to sin. Repentance is the vomit of the soul, and of all medicine none is so difficult and hard as to vomit. The same means that tend to preserve the soul from sin work the soul to rise by repentance when it has fallen into sin. We know that the mercy and loving kindness of God is one special means to keep the soul from sin, as David said: “For Your loving kindness is before my eyes, and I have130 walked in Your truth. I do not sit with deceitful men, nor keep company with hypocrites. I hate the mob of evildoers, and refuse to sit with the wicked.” So by the same means the soul is raised by repentance out of sin, as you+ may see in Mary Magdalene, who loved much and131 wept much because much was forgiven her; so those in Hosea: “Come, let us return to the Lord. For He has torn us to pieces, but He will heal us; He has wounded us, but He will bind up our wounds. After two days He will revive us; on the third day He will raise us up, that we may live in His sight,” or before his face, as the Hebrew has it, that is, in his132 favor. Confidence in God’s mercy and love, that he would heal them, bind up their wounds, revive their dejected spirits, and cause them to live in his favor, was what moved their hearts to repent and return to him. I might show you+ this truth further in many other particulars, but this may suffice. Only remember this in general: there is as much of the power of God, and the love of God, and faith in God, and fear of God, and care to please God, and zeal for the glory of God required to bring a man to repent133 of sin as there is to keep a man from sin. By this you+ may easily judge that to repent of sin is as great a work as not to sin. And now tell me, oh soul, is it an easy thing not to sin? Then we know for certain that it is not an easy thing to repent of sin.

The sixth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider seriously that he who now tempts you to sin on the ground that repentance is easy will before long, to drive you to despair134 and to break the neck of your soul forever, present repentance as the most difficult and hardest work in the world. And to this end he will set your sins in order before you and make them say, “We are yours, and we must follow you.” Now Satan will help to bring the soul to look up and see God angry, to look inward and see conscience accusing and condemning, and to look downward and see hell’s mouth open to receive the impenitent soul; and all this to make the work of repentance impossible to the soul. “What,” says Satan, “do you think that is easy which the whole power of grace cannot conquer while we are in this world? Is it easy,” says Satan, “to turn from some outward act of sin to which you have been addicted? Do you not remember that you have often complained against such and such particular sins, and resolved to leave them, and yet to this hour you have not, you cannot? What will it be, then, to turn from every sin? Indeed, to mortify and cut off those sins, those darling lusts, that are like joints and members, that are like right hands and right eyes? Have you not loved your sins above your Savior? Have you not preferred earth to heaven? Have you not all along neglected the means of grace, and despised the offers of grace, and vexed the Spirit of grace? There would be no end if I should set before you the infinite evils that you have committed, and the innumerable good services that you have omitted,135 and the frequent checks of your own conscience that you have scorned. And therefore you may well conclude that you can never repent, that you will never repent.” “Now,” says Satan, “only consider a little your numberless sins, and the greatness of your sins, the foulness of your sins, the heinousness of your sins, the circumstances of your sins, and you will easily see that those sins you thought to be but specks are indeed mountains. And is it not now in vain to repent of them? Surely,” says Satan, “if you should seek repentance and grace with tears, as Esau did, you will not find it. Your hourglass has run out, your sun is set, the door of mercy is shut, the golden scepter is taken in, and now you who have despised mercy will be destroyed forever by justice. For such a wretch as you are to attempt repentance is to attempt a thing impossible. It is impossible that you, who in all your life could never conquer one sin, should master such a numberless number of sins, which are so near, so dear, so necessary, and so profitable to you, which have so long shared your bed and your table, which have been your old acquaintances and companions. Have you not often purposed, promised, vowed, and resolved to enter upon the136 practice of repentance, and yet to this day could never attain it? Surely it is in vain to strive against the stream where it is so impossible to overcome. You are lost, and cast forever to hell; you must go to hell; you shall.” Ah, souls! He who now tempts you+ to sin by suggesting to you+ the easiness of repentance will at last, to drive you+ to despair, present repentance as the hardest work in all the world, a work as far above man as heaven is above hell, as light is above darkness. Oh, that you+ were wise, to break off your+ sins by timely repentance!

120. Fallen man has lost (imperium suum, and imperium sui) the command of himself and the command of created things; and certainly he who cannot command himself cannot repent by himself. Da poenitentiam & postea indulgentiam [Give repentance, and afterward pardon], said the dying Fulgentius.

121. It was a vain boast of King Cyrus that caused it to be written upon his tombstone (πάντα ποιεῖν ἐδυνάμην), I could do all things. So could Paul too, but it was through Christ who strengthened him.

122. The Hebrew word for repentance is תשובה, from שוב, which signifies to return. It implies a going back from what a man had done; it denotes a returning or converting from one thing to another, from sin to God. The Greeks have two words by which they express the nature of repentance. One is μεταμελεῖν, which signifies to be full of care, anxious, troubled after a thing is done. The other word, μετάνοια, is resipiscentia, after-wit or after-wisdom, the mind’s recovering of wisdom, or growing wiser after our folly; Ab ἄνοια dementia & μετά post [from ἄνοια, madness, and μετά, after], it being the correction of men’s folly, and a returning ad sanam mentem [to a sound mind]. True repentance is a thorough change both of the mind and of the conduct. Optima & aptissima poenitentia est nova vita [The best and fittest repentance is a new life], says Luther, and the saying is an excellent saying. Repentance for sin is worth nothing without repentance from sin. “If you repent with a contradiction,” says Tertullian, “God will pardon you with a contradiction. You repent, and yet continue in your sin; God will pardon you, and yet send you to hell. There is a pardon with a contradiction.” Negative goodness serves no man to save him from the axe. It is said of Ithacus that the hatred of the Priscillian heresy was all the virtue he had. The evil servant did not waste his talent in riotous living. Those reprobates in Matt 25 did not rob the saints, but they did not relieve them; for this they must eternally perish.

123. True repentance is a sorrowing for sin as it is offensivum Dei, aversivum à Deo [offensive to God, turning away from God]. This both comes from God and drives a man to God, as it did the church in the Song of Songs, and the prodigal. Ezek 20:22, 23.

124. Quantum displicet Deo immunditia peccati, in tantum placet Deo erubescentia poenitentis. Bernard, that is: The more God has been displeased with the blackness of sin, the more he will be pleased with the blushing of the sinner. Those who do not burn now in zeal against sin must before long burn in hell for sin.

125. Anselm in his Meditations confesses that all his life was either damnable for sin committed or unprofitable for good omitted, and at last concludes (Quid restat o peccator nisi ut in tota vita tua deplores totam vitam tuam): Oh, what then remains, but in our whole life to lament the sins of our whole life!

126. It is truly said of God that he is omnia super omnia [all things above all things].

127. If you are reluctant in thoughts of repentance, be eager in thoughts of hell, whose flames only the streams of the penitent eye can quench. Tertullian.

128. Oh, how you will tear and rend yourself! How you will lament fruitless repenting! What will you say? “Woe is me, that I have not cast off the burden of sin! Woe is me, that I have not washed away my spots, but am now pierced with my iniquities! Now I have lost the surpassing joy of angels.” Basil.

129. Yet it is better to be kept from sin than to be cured of sin by repentance, as it is better for a man to be preserved from a disease than to be cured of the disease.

130. Ps 26:3, 4, 5.

131. Luke 7:37, 38, 39, etc. Hos 6:1, 2.

132. לפניו

133. 2 Cor 7:11.

134. Bede tells of a certain great man who was admonished in his sickness to repent. He answered that he would not repent yet, for if he should recover, his companions would laugh at him. But as he grew sicker and sicker, his friends pressed him again to repent; but then he told them it was too late (Quia jam judicatus sum & condemnatus): “For now,” he said, “I am judged and condemned.”

135. As one Lamachus, a commander, said to one of his soldiers who was brought before him for misbehavior and pleaded that he would do so no more (Non licet in bello bis peccare): no man may offend twice in war. So God will not allow men to neglect the day of grace often.

136. Repentance is a work that must be done in time, or men are utterly undone forever. Aut poenitendum aut pereundum [Either repent or perish].

7. The Occasions of Sin

Now the seventh device that Satan has to draw the soul to sin is by making the soul bold to venture on the occasions of sin. Satan says, “You may walk by the harlot’s door, though you will not go into the harlot’s bed. You may sit and dine with the drunkard, though you will not get drunk with the drunkard. You may look on Jezebel’s beauty, and you may play and toy with Delilah, though you do not commit wickedness with the one or the other. You may handle the golden wedge with Achan, though you do not steal the golden wedge,” etc.

Now the remedies against this device are as follows.

The first remedy is to dwell solemnly on those Scriptures that expressly command us to avoid the occasions of sin and the least appearance of evil. 1 Thess 5:22: “Abstain from all137 appearance of evil.” Whatever is heterodox, unsound and unsavory, shun it as you would shun a serpent in your way, or poison in your food. Theodosius tore up the Arians’ arguments, presented to him in writing, because he found them contrary to the Scriptures. And Augustine retracted even mere ironies, because they had the appearance of lying. When God had commanded the Jews to abstain from swine’s flesh, they would not so much as name it, but in their common talk would call a sow by another name. To abstain from all appearance of evil is to do nothing in which sin appears, or which has a shadow of sin. Bernard glosses it finely:138 abstain from “whatever has an evil look, or an evil report,” so that a man may wound neither his conscience nor his good name. We must shun, and be wary of, the very show and shadow of sin, if we care at all for our good name among others or our comfort at home. It was good counsel that Livia gave her husband139 Augustus: “You must not only not do wrong, but not even seem to do so,” etc. So Jude 23: “And save others with fear, snatching them out of the fire, hating even the garment spotted by the flesh.” It is a phrase taken from ceremonial uncleanness, which was contracted by touching the houses, the vessels and the garments of unclean persons. Under the law men might not touch a menstrual cloth, nor would God accept a spotted peace offering. So we must hate and avoid not only gross sins, but everything that may carry a savor or suspicion of sin. We must abhor the very signs and tokens of sin. So in Prov 5:8: “Keep your path far from her; do not go near the door of her house.” He who would not be burned must dread the fire; he who would not hear the bell must not meddle with the rope. To venture on the occasion of sin and then to pray, “Lead us not into140 temptation,” is the same as thrusting your finger into the fire and then praying that it may not be burned. So in Prov 4:14, 15 you have another command: “Do not set foot on the path of the wicked or walk in the way of evildoers. Avoid it; do not travel on it. Turn from it and pass on by.” This threefold progression of Solomon’s shows with great emphasis how necessary it is for men to flee from all appearance of sin, as the seaman shuns sandbanks and shoals, and as men shun those who have plague sores running on them. As weeds endanger the grain, as infection endangers the blood, or as an infected house endangers the neighborhood, so the company of the bad endangers those who are good. Close intimacy with wicked companions is one of the strongest chains of hell, and binds us to a share both in sin and in punishment.

The second remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that ordinarily there is no conquest over sin unless the soul turns from the occasion of sin. It is impossible for the man who plays and sports with the occasions of sin to get the conquest of sin. God will not remove the temptation unless141 we turn from the occasion. It is a just and righteous thing with God that the man who will venture to dance on the brink of the pit should fall into the pit, and that the man who will not flee from the occasions of sin should be a slave to sin. As long as there is fuel in our hearts for a temptation, we cannot be secure. He who has gunpowder about him had better keep far enough away from sparks. To rush on the occasions of sin is both to tempt ourselves and to tempt Satan to tempt our souls. It is very rare for any soul to play with the occasions of sin and not be ensnared by sin. It is seldom that God keeps from the acts of sin the soul that will not keep away from the occasions of sin. He who ventures on the occasions of sin is like the man who would quench the fire with oil, which is a fuel to maintain it and increase it. Ah, souls! Remember often how frequently you+ have been overcome by sin when you+ have boldly gone on the occasions of sin. Look back, souls, to the days of your+ folly, when you+ were conquered as easily as you+ were tempted, and vanquished as easily as you+ were assaulted, when you+ played with the occasions of sin. And therefore, as you+ would be kept in the future from committing sin, and be made victorious over sin, oh, flee from the occasions of sin!

The third remedy against this device of Satan is to consider seriously that other precious saints, who were once glorious on earth and are now triumphing in heaven, have turned from the occasions of sin as from hell itself. You+ may see this in Joseph: Gen 39:10: “And although she spoke to Joseph day after day, he refused to go to bed with her or even be with her.” Joseph was famous for all four cardinal virtues, if ever anyone was. In this one temptation you+ may see his fortitude, justice, temperance142 and prudence, in that he shuns the occasion (for he would not so much as be with her). And what a man is in temptation, that he is indeed; for temptation is only a tap to let corruption run out. The Nazirite was not only forbidden to drink wine; he might not even taste a grape, or the skin of a grape. The leper was to shave his hair and pare his nails. The devil counts a fit occasion half a conquest. For he knows that corrupt nature has143 a seedbed of all sin, which, once drawn out and watered by some sinful occasion, is soon set to work producing death and destruction. God will not remove the temptation until we remove the occasion. A bird is safe while she is aloft, but she never comes near the snare without danger. Shunning the occasions of sin makes a man most like the best of men. A soul eminently gracious dares not come near the powder train, though he is far from the blast. So Job 31:1: “I have made a covenant with my eyes.144 How then could I gaze with desire at a virgin?” I set a watch at the entrance of my senses, so that my soul might not be infected and endangered through them. The eye is the window of the soul, and if it were always open, the soul might smart for it. A man must not look intently at what he must not love entirely. The disciples were carried away by gazing at the beauty of the temple. It is best and safest to have the eye always fixed on the highest and noblest objects, as the mariner’s eye is fixed on the star while his hand is on the helm. So David, when he was himself, shuns the occasion of sin: Ps 26:4, 5: “I do not sit with deceitful men, nor keep company with hypocrites. I hate the mob of evildoers, and refuse to sit with the wicked.” Stories speak of some who could not sleep when they thought of the trophies of other worthies who went before them. The highest and choicest examples are to some, and should be to all, very enlivening and stirring. And oh, that the examples of those worthy saints, David, Joseph and Job, might prevail with all your+ souls to shun and avoid the occasions of sin! Everyone should strive to be like them in grace whom they desire to equal in glory. He who shoots at the sun, though he falls far short, will shoot higher than he who aims at a shrub. It is best (and it shows much of Christ within) to eye the highest and worthiest examples.

The fourth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that avoiding the occasions of sin is an evidence of grace, and something that lifts a man above most other men in the world. What a man is in temptation, that he is indeed. And when sinful occasions present themselves before the soul, avoiding them shows both the truth145 and the strength of grace. So it is when, with Lot, a man can be chaste in Sodom; and with Timothy can live temperately in Asia, among the luxurious Ephesians; and with Job can walk uprightly in the land of Uz, where the people were profane in their lives and superstitious in their worship; and with Daniel can be holy in Babylon; and with Abraham righteous in Chaldea; and with Nehemiah zealous in Damascus, etc. Many a wicked man is swollen and full of sinful corruption, but does not show it for lack of occasion. But that man is surely good who will not be bad in his course, though tempted by occasions. A Christless soul is so far from refusing occasions when they come his way that he looks and longs for them. And rather than go without them, he will buy them, not only with love or money, but also with the loss of his soul. Nothing but grace can fence a man against the occasions of sin when he is strongly tempted to them. Therefore, as you+ would cherish in your+ own bosoms a precious evidence of the truth and strength of your+ graces, shun all sinful occasions.

137. Epiphanius says that under the old law, when any dead body was carried past a house, they were required to shut their doors and windows.

138. Quicquid est male coloratum.

139. Socrates speaks of two young men who flung away their belts when, being in an idol’s temple, the purifying water fell on them, detesting, says the historian, the garment spotted by the flesh.

140. One said, “As often as I have been among worldly men, I have come home less a man than I was before.”

141. The fable says that the butterfly asked the owl how she should deal with the fire, which had singed her wings, and the owl counseled her not to look so much as at its smoke.

142. There are stories of heathens who would not look on women of excellent beauty, for fear of being ensnared.

143. Democritus plucked out his own eyes to avoid the danger of uncleanness.

144. ברית כרתי, I cut a covenant. In making covenants it was a custom among the Jews to cut some beast or other in pieces and to walk between the pieces, to signify that they desired God to destroy those who should break the covenant.

145. Plutarch says of Demosthenes that he was excellent at praising the worthy acts of his ancestors, but not so at imitating them. Oh, that this did not apply to many professing Christians in our times!

8. The Outward Mercies of Worldly Men

The eighth device that Satan has to draw the soul to sin is by presenting146 to the soul the outward mercies that worldly men enjoy, and the outward miseries they are free from, while they have walked in the ways of sin. Satan says, “Do you not see, O soul, the many mercies that such and such people enjoy, who walk in the very ways your soul startles to think of? And do you not see the many crosses they are delivered from, crosses that make other men (who say they dare not walk in such ways) spend their days in sighing, weeping, groaning and mourning? And therefore,” says Satan, “if ever you would be freed from the dark night of adversity and enjoy the sunshine of prosperity, you must walk in their ways.” By this stratagem the devil took those in Jer 44:16-18: “As for the word you have spoken to us in the name of the Lord, we will not listen to you! Instead, we will do everything we vowed to do: We will burn incense to the Queen of Heaven and offer147 drink offerings to her, just as we, our fathers, our kings and our officials did in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem. At that time we had plenty of food and good things, and we saw no disaster. But from the time we stopped burning incense to the Queen of Heaven and pouring out drink offerings to her, we have lacked everything and have been perishing by sword and famine.” This is just the language of a world of ignorant, profane and superstitious souls in London and England, who would have made themselves a captain148 to return to bondage, yes, to a bondage worse than the one the Israelites groaned under. “Oh,” they say, “since such and such persons have been put down and set aside, we have had nothing but plundering and taxing and butchering of men,” etc. “And therefore we will do as we and our kings and nobles and fathers have done before; for then we had plenty at home and peace abroad,” etc., “and there was no one to make us afraid.”

Now the remedies against this device of Satan are as follows.

The first remedy is to consider solemnly that no man knows how the heart of God stands by his hand. God’s hand of mercy may be toward a man when his heart may be set against that man, as you may see in Saul and149 others. And the hand of God may be set against a man when the heart of God is dearly set on that man, as you may see in Job and Ephraim. The hand of God was sorely set against them, and yet the heart and compassion of God were strongly working toward them. No man knows either love or hatred by outward mercy or misery. For all things come alike to all: to the righteous and to the unrighteous, to the good and to the bad, to the clean and to the unclean, etc. The sun of prosperity shines as well on the brambles of the wilderness as on the fruit trees of the orchard. The snow and hail of adversity fall on the best gardens as well as on the stinking dunghills or the wild waste. Ahab’s and Josiah’s ends agree in their very circumstances. Saul and Jonathan, though different in their natures, merits and conduct, yet in their deaths were not divided. Health, wealth, honors, etc., crosses, sicknesses, losses, etc., are cast on good men and bad men without distinction. The whole Turkish empire is150 nothing but a crust thrown by heaven’s great householder to his dogs. Moses dies in the wilderness, as well as those who grumbled; Nabal is rich, as well as Abraham; Ahithophel is wise, as well as Solomon; and Doeg is honored by Saul, as well as Joseph was by Pharaoh. Usually the worst of men have most of these outward things, and the best of men have least of earth, though most of heaven.

The second remedy against this device of Satan is to consider seriously that there is nothing in the world that so provokes God to wrath and anger as men taking encouragement from God’s goodness and mercy to do wickedly. You+ may see this by the wrath that fell on the old world, and by God’s raining hell out of heaven on151 Sodom and Gomorrah. This is clear in Jer 44:20-28. The words are worthy of your+ best meditation. Oh, that they were engraved in all your+ hearts, and constantly in all your+ thoughts! Though they are too long for me to copy them out, yet they are not too long for you+ to remember them. To argue from mercy to sinful liberty is the devil’s logic, and such logicians always walk as on a mine of gunpowder, ready to be blown up. No such souls can ever turn aside or avoid the wrath of God. This is wickedness at its height: for a man to be very bad because God is very good. A worse spirit than this is not in hell. Ah, Lord! Does not wrath, yes, the greatest wrath, lie at this man’s door? Are not the strongest chains of darkness prepared for such a soul? To sin against mercy is to sin against humanity. It is bestial; no, it is worse. To render good for evil is divine; to render good for good is human; to render evil for evil is brutish; but to render evil for good is devilish. And from this evil deliver my soul, O God.

The third remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that there is no greater misery in this life than not to be in misery, no greater152 affliction than not to be afflicted. Woe, woe to that soul on whom God will not spend a rod! This is the saddest stroke of all, when God refuses to strike at all: “Ephraim is joined to idols; leave him alone!” “Why should you+ be struck any more? You+ will rebel more and more.” When the physician gives up on the patient, you say, “Ring out his knell; the man is dead.” So when God gives a soul up to sin without restraint, you may truly say, “This soul is lost.” You may ring out his knell, for he is twice dead and plucked up by the roots. Freedom from punishment is the mother of false security, the stepmother of virtue, the poison of religion, the moth of holiness, and the bringer-in of wickedness. “Nothing,” said one, “seems more unhappy to me than he to whom no adversity has happened.” Outward mercies often prove a snare to our souls. Ezek 3:20: “I put a stumbling block before him.” Vatablus’s note there is:153 I will prosper him in all things, and not restrain him from sin by affliction. Prosperity has been a stumbling block at which millions have stumbled and fallen, and broken the neck of their souls forever.

The fourth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider seriously that what wicked men lack, under all their outward mercy and freedom from adversity, is far greater than all their outward enjoyments. They have many mercies, yet they lack more than they enjoy; the mercies they enjoy are nothing to the mercies they lack. It is true, they have honors and riches and pleasures and friends, and are mighty in power. Their descendants are established in their sight with them, and their offspring before their eyes. Their homes are safe from fear, and the rod of God is not on them. “They send forth their little ones like a flock; their children skip about, singing to the tambourine and lyre and making merry at the154 sound of the flute. They spend their days in prosperity. Their eyes bulge with fatness; they have more than heart could wish. They have no struggle in their death; their bodies are well-fed. They are not afflicted like other men,” as David and Job speak. Yet all this is nothing to what they lack. They lack a share in God, Christ, the Spirit, the promises, the covenant of grace and everlasting glory. They lack acceptance with God and reconciliation with God. They lack righteousness, justification, sanctification, adoption and redemption. They lack the pardon of sin, and power against sin, and freedom from the dominion of sin. They lack the favor that is better than life, and the joy that is inexpressible and full of glory, and the peace that surpasses understanding, and the155 grace whose least spark is worth more than heaven and earth. They lack a house that has foundations, whose builder and maker is God. They lack the riches that do not perish, the glory that does not fade, the kingdom that does not shake. Wicked men are the neediest men in the world. Yes, they lack the two things that should make their mercies sweet, namely, the blessing of God and contentment with their condition; and without these their heaven is only a hell this side of hell. When their hearts are lifted up and grown big with the thought of their abundance, if conscience only puts156 in a word and says, “It is true, here is this and that outward mercy; oh, but where is a share in Christ? Where is the favor of God? Where are the comforts of the Holy Spirit? Where are your evidences for heaven?” etc., this word from conscience makes the man’s face change, his thoughts be troubled, his heart be dismayed, and all his mercies on the right hand and the left be as dead and withered. Ah, if only the eyes of wicked men were open to see what they lack under their abundance! They would cry out and say, as Absalom did, “What are all these to me, so long as I cannot see the king’s face?” What are honor and riches and the favor of men, so long as I lack the favor of God, the pardon of my sins, a share in Christ and the hope of glory? O God, give me these, or I die; give me these, or else I will die eternally.

The fifth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that outward things are not what they seem and are thought to be. They have indeed a glorious outside, but if you view their insides, you will easily find that they fill the head full of cares and the heart full of fears. What if the fire should consume one part of my estate, and the sea should be a grave to swallow up another part of my estate? What if my servants should be unfaithful away from home, and my children deceitful at home? Ah, the secret fretting, vexing and gnawing that daily, yes, hourly, attend the souls of those men whose hands are full of worldly goods! It was a good speech of an emperor: “You gaze on my purple robe and golden crown,” he said, “but if you knew what cares are under it, you would not pick it up from the ground to have it.” It was a true saying of Augustine on Psalm 26: “Many are157 miserable by loving hurtful things, but they are more miserable by having them.” It is not what men enjoy, but the principle it comes from, that makes men happy. An abundance of these outward things usually brings great distraction, great vexation, and great condemnation at last to those who possess them. If God gives them in his wrath, and does not sanctify them in his love, they will at last be witnesses against a man, and racks to torture and torment a man, and millstones to sink a man forever, in that day when God will call men to account, not for the use but for the abuse of mercy.

The sixth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider seriously the end and design of God in heaping mercy on the heads of the wicked, and in giving them (a quietus est [a discharge]) rest158 and quiet from the sorrows and sufferings that others sigh under. David in Ps 73:17-20 shows the end and design of God in this. He says, “When I entered God’s sanctuary, then I discerned their end. Surely You set them on slick ground; You cast them down into ruin. How suddenly they are laid waste, completely swept away by terrors! Like one waking from a dream, so You, O Lord, awaken and despise their form.” So in Ps 92:7: “When the wicked sprout like grass, and all evildoers flourish, it is that they may be forever destroyed.” God’s setting them up is only in order to his casting them down; his raising them high is only in order to his bringing them low. Exod 9:16: “But I have raised you up for this very purpose, that I might display My power in you, and that My name might be159 proclaimed in all the earth.” I have appointed you and set you up as a target, so that I may let fly at you, and follow you close with plague upon plague, till I have beaten the very breath out of your body, and gained a name for myself by setting my feet on the neck of all your pride, power, pomp and glory. Ah, souls! What man in his right mind would be lifted up only to be cast down, would be set higher than others when it is only in order to his being brought lower than others? There is not a wicked man in the world who is set up with Lucifer as high as heaven but will with Lucifer be brought down as low as hell. Can you think seriously of this, O soul, and not say, “O Lord, I humbly ask that you will let me be little in this world, so that I may be great in another world; and low here, so that I may be high forever hereafter. Let me be low, and feed low, and live low, so long as I may live with you forever. Let me now be clothed with rags, so long as you will clothe me at last with your robes. Let me now be set on a dunghill, so long as I may at last be raised to sit with you on your throne. Lord, make me gracious rather than great, inwardly holy rather than outwardly happy. And rather turn me back into my first nothing, yes, make me worse than nothing, than set me up for a time so that you may bring me low forever”?

The seventh remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that God often most plagues and punishes those whom others think he most spares and loves. That is, God plagues and punishes them most with spiritual judgments (which are the greatest, the sorest and the heaviest) whom he least punishes with temporal punishments. There are no men on earth160 so inwardly plagued as those who meet with the fewest outward plagues. Oh, the blindness of mind, the hardness of heart, the searing of conscience, that those souls are given up to who, in the eye of the world, are reputed the happiest men because they are not outwardly afflicted and plagued like other men! Ah, souls! It would be better for all the temporal plagues that ever came on the children of men since the fall of Adam to meet at once on your+ souls, than for you+ to be given up to the least spiritual plague, to the least measure of spiritual blindness or spiritual hardness of heart, etc. Nothing will make that man better, nor move him, who is given up to spiritual judgments. Let God smile or frown, stroke or strike, cut or kill, he does not mind161 it, he does not heed it. Let life or death, heaven or hell, be set before him, it does not stir him. He is mad for his sin, and God is fully set on doing justice on his soul. This man’s preservation is only a reservation for a greater condemnation. This man can set no bounds to himself; he has become a child of fathomless perdition. He has guilt in his bosom and vengeance at his back wherever he goes. Neither ministry nor misery, neither miracle nor mercy, can soften his heart. And if this soul is not in hell this side of hell, who is? Who is?

The eighth remedy against this device of Satan is to dwell more on the strict account that worldly men must give for all the good they enjoy162 than on the outward good they enjoy. Ah, if men dwelt more on the account they must give before long for all the mercies they have enjoyed, and for all the favors they have abused, and for all the sins they have committed, it would make their hearts tremble and their lips quiver, and rottenness enter their bones. It would cause their souls to cry out and say, “Oh, that our mercies had been fewer and smaller, so that our account might have been easier, and our torment and misery (for our abuse of so great mercy) not greater than we are able to bear! Oh, cursed be the day when the crown of honor was set on our heads, and the treasures of this world were cast into our laps! Oh, cursed be the day when the sun of prosperity shone so strongly on us, and this flattering world smiled so much on us, as to lead us to forget God, to slight Jesus Christ, to neglect our souls, and to put far from us the day of our account!” Philip the Third of Spain, whose life was free from gross evils, professed that he would rather lose all his kingdom than offend God willingly. Yet in the agony of death, considering more thoroughly the163 account he was to give to God, fear struck into him, and these words burst from him: “Oh, would to God I had never reigned! Oh, that in those years I have spent in my kingdom I had lived a life in the wilderness! Oh, that I had lived a solitary life with God! How much more securely I would now die! How much more confidently I would go to the throne of God! What does all my glory profit me, except that I have so much the more torment in my death?” God keeps an exact account of every penny that is laid out on him and his, and that is laid out against him and his. And men will know and feel this in the day of account, though now they shut their eyes and164 will not understand. The sleeping of vengeance causes the overflowing of sin, and the overflow of sin causes the awakening of vengeance. Abused mercy will certainly turn into fury. God’s forbearance is no acquittal. The day is at hand when he will pay wicked men for the abuse of new and old mercies. If he seems to be slow, yet he is sure: he has leaden heels but iron hands. The farther back he swings his blow, or draws his arrow, the deeper he will wound in the day of vengeance. Men’s actions are all in print in heaven, and God will, in the day of account, read them aloud in the ears of all the world, so that they may all say amen to the righteous sentence he will pass on all the despisers and abusers of mercy.

146. It was a weighty saying of Seneca (Nihil est infelicius eo, cui nil unquam contigit adversi): there is nothing more unhappy than he who never felt adversity.

147. Some of the heathens would be wicked as their gods were, counting it a dishonor to their god to be unlike him. Lactantius.

148. It is said of one of the emperors that Rome had no war in his days, because it was plague enough to have such an emperor. You+ are wise, and know how to apply it.

149. Tully judged the Jews’ religion to be worthless, because they were so often overcome and impoverished and afflicted; and the religion of Rome to be right, because the Romans prospered and became lords of the world. And yet, though the Romans had God’s hand, the Jews had his heart; for they were dearly beloved, though sorely afflicted.

150. Nihil est nisi mica panis. Luther.

151. Such souls make God a God of rags, one who will not do as he says. But they will find God to be as severe in punishing as he is gracious to others in pardoning. Good turns add weight to unkindness, and our guilt is increased by our obligations.

152. Religio peperit divitias & filia devoravit matrem. Religion brought forth riches, and the daughter soon devoured the mother, says Augustine.

153. Faciam, ut omnia habeat prospera; calamitatibus eum à peccato non revocabo.

154. Men who enjoy all worldly comforts may truly say, Omnes humanae consolationes sunt desolationes [All human consolations are desolations].

155. Nec Christus nec coelum patitur hyperbolen. Neither Christ nor heaven can be overstated.

156. A crown of gold cannot cure the headache, nor can a velvet slipper ease the gout; no more can honor or riches, etc., quiet and still the conscience. The heart of man is a three-cornered triangle, which the whole round circle of the world cannot fill (as mathematicians say), but all the corners will complain of emptiness and hunger for something else.

157. Multi amando res noxias sunt miseri, habendo miseriores. Augustine.

158. Valerian the Roman emperor fell from being an emperor to be a footstool to Sapor, king of Persia. Dionysius, king of Sicily, fell from his kingly glory to be a schoolmaster. The splendid Queen Zenobia was brought to Rome in golden chains.

159. Valens an emperor, Belisarius a famous general, Henry the Fourth, Bajazet, Pythias, Pompey the Great and William the Conqueror: these, from being very high, were brought very low. They all fell from great glory and majesty to great poverty and misery. Da Domine ut sic possideamus temporalia ut non perdamus aeterna. Bernard. Grant us, Lord, that we may so partake of temporal happiness that we may not lose eternal.

160. Ps 81:12. Ps 78:26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31. Ps 106:15: “He granted their request, but sent leanness into their soul.” It is a heavy plague to have a fat body and a lean soul, a house full of gold and a heart full of sin.

161. It is better to have a sore conscience than a seared one. It is better to have no heart than a hard heart; no mind than a blind mind.

162. In that day men will give an account (De bonis commissis, de bonis dimissis, de malis commissis, de malis permissis) of good things committed to them, of good things neglected by them, of evils committed by them, and of evils allowed by them.

163. In die judicii plus valebit conscientia pura, quam marsupia plena. Bernard. Then a good conscience will be worth more than all the world’s goods.

164. Jerome always thought that that voice was in his ears (Surgite mortui & venite ad judicium): “Arise, you+ dead, and come to judgment.” As often as I think of that day, how my whole body quakes, and my heart within me trembles!

9. The Crosses of the Saints

The ninth device that Satan has to draw the soul to sin is by presenting to the soul the crosses, losses, reproaches, sorrows and sufferings that daily attend those who walk in the ways of holiness. Satan says, “Do you not see that there are none in the world so vexed, afflicted and tossed about as those who walk more carefully and more holily than their neighbors? They are a byword at home and a reproach in the world. Their miseries come in upon them like Job’s messengers, one on the heels of another, and there is no end to their sorrows and troubles. Therefore,” says Satan, “you had better walk in ways that are less troublesome and less afflicted, though they are more sinful. For who but a madman would spend his days in sorrow, vexation and affliction, when it may be avoided by walking in the ways that I set before him?”

Now the remedies against this device of Satan are as follows.

The first remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that all the afflictions that attend the people of God are such as will turn to their profit and glorious advantage. They will reveal a filthiness and vileness in sin that the soul has never yet seen. A German divine said in his sickness, “In this disease165 I have learned how great God is, and what the evil of sin is. I never truly knew what God was before, nor what sin meant, till now.” Afflictions are a crystal mirror in which the soul has the clearest sight of the ugly face of sin. In this mirror the soul comes to see that sin is only a bitter-sweet. Indeed, in this mirror the soul comes to see sin not only as an evil, but as the greatest evil in the world, an evil far worse than hell.

Again, afflictions will help in the166 mortifying and purging away of the saints’ sins. Afflictions are God’s furnace, by which he cleanses his people from their dross. Affliction is a fire to purge out167 our dross and to make virtue shine. It is a potion to carry away infection, better than all the Benedicta Medicamenta [blessed medicines], as physicians call them. Aloes kills worms, and colds and frosts kill vermin; so afflictions kill the corruptions that are in our hearts. The Jews kept their idols under all the thundering of the prophets; but after their captivity in Babylon, it is observed, no idols have been found among them.

Again, afflictions are sweet preservatives to keep the saints from sin, which is a greater evil than hell itself. As Job said, “Surely it is fitting to say to God,168 ‘I have borne chastisement; I will offend no more. Teach me what I cannot see; if I have done wrong, I will not do it again.’ Once I have spoken foolishly, indeed169 twice, but I will do so no more,” says Job. The burnt child dreads the fire. “Ah,” says the soul under the rod, “sin is only a bitter-sweet, and for the future I intend, by the strength of Christ, not to buy repentance at so dear a price.” The rabbis, to scare their students away from sin, used to tell them that sin made God’s head ache; and saints under the rod have found by woeful experience that sin makes not only their heads but their hearts ache too. Augustine, by wandering out of his way, escaped a man who lay in wait to harm him. If afflictions did not put us out of our way, we would many times meet with some sin or other that would harm our precious souls.

Again, afflictions will work the saints to be more fruitful in holiness. Heb 12:10, 11: “But He afflicts us for our profit, so that170 we may share in His holiness.” The flowers smell sweetest after a shower. Vines bear better for bleeding. The walnut tree is most fruitful when it is most beaten. Saints spring up and thrive most inwardly when they are most outwardly afflicted. Afflictions are called by some the mother of virtue. Manasseh’s chain was more profitable to him than his crown. Luther could not understand some Scriptures till he was in affliction. The cross at the head of the child’s alphabet is no letter, and yet it taught him more than all the letters in the row. God’s house of171 correction is his school of instruction. All the stones that came about Stephen’s ears only knocked him closer to Christ the cornerstone. The waves only lifted Noah’s ark nearer to heaven, and the higher the waters rose, the nearer the ark was lifted up to heaven. Afflictions lift up the soul to richer, clearer and fuller enjoyments of God. Hos 2:14: “Behold, I will allure her and lead her to the wilderness, and speak to her tenderly,” or rather, as the Hebrew has it, I172 will earnestly or vehemently speak to her heart. God makes afflictions only inlets to the soul’s sweeter and fuller enjoyment of his blessed self. When was it that Stephen saw the heavens open, and Christ standing at the right hand of God? It was when the stones were flying about173 his ears, and there was only a short step between him and eternity. And when did God appear in his glory to Jacob? It was in the day of his troubles, when the stones were his pillows, the ground his bed, the hedges his curtains, and the heavens his canopy. Then he saw the angels of God ascending and descending in their shining robes. The plant in Nazianzen grows by cutting: being cut, it flourishes; it contends with the axe; it lives by dying, and by cutting it grows. So do saints by the afflictions that befall them. They gain more experience of the power of God supporting them, of the wisdom of God directing them, of the grace of God refreshing and cheering them, and of the goodness of God quieting them and enlivening them to a greater love for holiness, a greater delight in holiness, and a more vehement pursuit of holiness. I have read of a fountain that is cold at noonday and grows warm at midnight. So many a precious saint who is cold Godward, heavenward and holiness-ward in the day of prosperity grows warm Godward, heavenward and holiness-ward in the midnight of adversity.

Again, afflictions serve to keep the hearts of the saints humble and tender. Lam 3:19, 20: “I remember my affliction and wandering, the wormwood and the gall. My soul still remembers them174 and is humbled within me,” or bowed down within me, as the original has it. So David, when he was under the rod, could say, “I have become mute; I do not open my mouth because of what You have done.” I have read of one who, whenever anything turned out prosperously, would read over the Lamentations of Jeremiah,175 and that kept his heart tender, humble and low. Prosperity does no more to puff up the soul than adversity does to bow it down. The saints find this by experience, and therefore they can kiss and embrace the cross as others do the world’s crown.

Again, afflictions serve to bring the saints nearer to God, and to make them more importunate and earnest in prayer with God. “Before I was afflicted, I went astray;176 but now I keep Your word. It was good for me to be afflicted, that I might learn Your statutes.” “For I am like a lion to Ephraim and like a young lion to the house of177 Judah. I, even I, will tear them to pieces and then go away. I will carry them off where no one can rescue them. Then I will return to My place until they admit their guilt and seek My face; in their affliction they will earnestly seek Me.” And so they did: “Come,” they say, “let us return to the Lord. For He has torn us to pieces, but He will heal us; He has wounded us, but He will bind up our wounds. After two days He will revive us; on the third day He will raise us up, that we may live in His presence.” So when God had hedged up their way with thorns, then they say, “I will return178 to my first husband, for then I was better off than now.” Ah, the joy, the peace, the comfort, the delight and contentment that attended us when we kept close communion with God call for our return to God. We will return to our first husband, for then we were better off than now.

When Tiribazus, a Persian nobleman, was arrested, he drew his sword and defended himself; but when they told179 him that they had come to take him to the king, he yielded willingly. So, though a saint may at first hold out a little, yet when he remembers that afflictions are to carry him nearer to God, he yields and kisses the rod. Afflictions are like the thorn at the nightingale’s breast, which wakes her and sets her to her sweet and delightful singing.

Again, afflictions serve to revive and recover decayed graces. They inflame the love that has grown cold, and they enliven the faith that is decaying, and they put life into the hopes that are withering, and spirit into the joys and comforts that are languishing. Musk, says one, when it has lost its sweetness, recovers it if it is put into the sewer among filth; so afflictions recover and revive decayed graces. The more the saints are beaten with the hammer of afflictions, the more they are made the trumpets of God’s praises, and the more their graces are revived and enlivened. Adversity abases the loveliness of the world that might entice us; it abates the vigor of the flesh within that might incite us to folly and futility; and it aids the spirit in its quarrel with those two, which does much to revive and recover decayed graces. Now suppose afflictions and troubles do attend the ways of holiness; yet seeing that they all work for the great profit and singular advantage of the saints, let no soul be so mad as to leave an afflicted way of holiness to walk in a smooth path of wickedness.

The second remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that all the afflictions that befall180 the saints reach only their worse part. They do not reach, they do not hurt, their noble part, their best part. All the arrows stick in the shield; they do not reach the conscience. “Who can harm you+ if you+ are zealous for what is good?” says the apostle; that is, no one will harm you+. They may afflict you+ in this way and that, but they shall never harm you+.

It was the speech of a heathen whom the tyrant commanded to be put into a mortar and beaten to pieces with an iron pestle. He cried out to his persecutors, “You+ beat only the vessel, the case, the husk of Anaxarchus; you+ do not beat me.” His body was to him only a case, a husk; he counted his soul himself, and that they could not reach. You+ are wise and know how to apply it. Socrates said of his enemies, “They may kill me, but they cannot hurt me.” So afflictions may kill us, but they cannot hurt us. They may take away my life, but they cannot take away my God, my Christ, my crown.

The third remedy against this device of Satan is to consider seriously that the afflictions that attend the saints in the ways of holiness are only short and momentary. “Sorrow may stay the night, but joy comes in the morning.”181 This short storm will end in an everlasting calm; this short night will end in a glorious day that will never end. It is only a very short time between grace and glory, between our title to the crown and our wearing the crown, between our right to the heavenly inheritance and our possessing the heavenly inheritance. Fourteen thousand years to the Lord are only as one day. What is our life but a shadow, a bubble, a flower, a running messenger, a span, a dream, etc.? Indeed, the hand of the Lord rests on us for so small a while that Luther cannot find diminutives enough to make it small; for he calls it a very little little cross that we bear. The prophet in Isa 26:20 (to pikron mikron [the bitter is small]) says the indignation does not (transire) pass, but (pertransire) passes over. Its sharpness, shortness and suddenness are set forth by the labor of a woman, John 16:21. And that is a182 sweet Scripture: “You+ need to persevere, so that after you+ have done the will of God, you+ will receive what He has promised. For, ‘In just a little while, He who is coming will come and will not delay.’” (Tantillum, tantillum183 adhuc pusillum): a little, little, little while. When Athanasius’s friends came to lament over him because of his misery and banishment, he said, “It is only a little cloud, and it will soon be gone.” It will be only as a day before God gives his184 afflicted ones beauty for ashes, the oil of gladness for the spirit of heaviness; before he turns all your+ sighing into singing, all your+ lamentations into consolations, your+ sackcloth into silks, ashes into ointments, and your+ fasts into everlasting feasts, etc.

The fourth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider seriously that the afflictions that befall the saints are such as proceed from God’s dearest love. “Those I love, I rebuke185 and discipline. Therefore be earnest and repent.” “Saints,” says God, “do not think that I hate you+ because I rebuke you+ in this way.” He who escapes rebuke may suspect his adoption. God had one Son without corruption, but no son without correction. A gracious soul may look through the darkest cloud and see a God smiling on him. We must look through the anger of his correction to the sweetness of his face, as in a rainbow we see the beautiful image of the sun’s light in the midst of a dark and watery cloud. When Munster lay sick, and his friends asked him how he was and how he felt, he pointed to his sores and ulcers (of which he was full) and said, “These are God’s gems and jewels, with which he adorns his best friends, and to me they are more precious than all the gold and silver in the world.” A soul at its first conversion is only rough-cast; but God by afflictions squares it and fits it and fashions it for that glory above. This shows that afflictions flow from precious love. Therefore the afflictions that attend the people of God should be no bar to holiness, and no motive to draw the soul to ways of wickedness.

The fifth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that it is our duty and glory to measure afflictions not by the smart, but by the end. When Israel was sent out of186 Egypt, it was with gold and earrings. So the Jews were sent out of Babylon with gifts, jewels and all necessary utensils. Look more at the latter end of a187 Christian than at the beginning of his affliction. Consider the patience of Job, and what end the Lord made with him. Do not look at Lazarus lying at the rich man’s188 door, but lying in Abraham’s bosom. Do not look at the beginning of Joseph, who was so far from his dream that the sun and moon would bow to him, that for two years he was cast where he could see neither sun, moon, nor stars; but behold him at last made ruler over Egypt. Do not look at David when there was only a step between him and189 death, nor as he was envied by some and slighted and despised by others; but behold him seated on his royal throne, and dying in his bed of honor, with his son Solomon and all his glittering nobles about him. Afflictions are only a dark entry into your+ Father’s house; they are only a dirty lane to a royal palace. Now tell me, souls, is it not very great madness to shun the ways of holiness and to walk in the ways of wickedness because of the afflictions that attend the ways of holiness?

The sixth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider seriously that God’s design in all the afflictions that befall the saints is only to test them, not to wrong them or ruin them, as ignorant souls are apt to think. “He knows the way I have taken; when He has tested me, I will come forth as gold,” says patient Job. So in Deut 8:2: “Remember that these forty years the Lord your God led you all the way in the wilderness, so that He might humble you and test you in order to know what was in your heart, whether or not190 you would keep His commandments.” God afflicted them in this way so that he might make known to themselves and to others what was in their hearts. When fire is put to green wood, a great deal of watery stuff comes out that did not appear before. When the pond is empty, the mud, filth and toads come to light. The snow covers many a dunghill; so prosperity covers many a rotten heart. It is easy to wade in a warm bath, and every bird can sing on a sunny day, etc. Hard weather tests what health we have; afflictions test what sap we have, what grace we have. Withered leaves soon fall off in windy weather; rotten boughs quickly break under heavy weights, etc. You+ are wise and know how to apply it.

Afflictions are like pinching frosts191 that will search us out. Where we are most unsound, we will complain soonest, and where most corruptions lie, we will shrink most. We test metal by knocking; if it rings well, then we like it. So God tests his own by knocking, and if under the knocks they give a pleasant sound, God will turn their night into day, and their bitter into sweet, and their cross into a crown. And they will hear that voice: “Arise, shine, for … the glory of the Lord rises upon you, and the favors of the Lord are flowing in on you.”

The seventh and last remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that the afflictions, wrath and misery that attend the ways of wickedness are far greater and heavier than those that attend the ways of holiness. Oh, the galling, cutting, lashing and gnawing of conscience that attend souls in a way of wickedness! “The wicked” (says Isaiah) “are like the storm-tossed sea, for it cannot be still, and its waves192 churn up mire and muck. ‘There is no peace,’ says my God, ‘for the wicked.’” There are snares in all their mercies, and curses and crosses attend all their comforts, both at home and away. What is a fine suit of clothes with the plague in it? And what is a golden cup with poison at the bottom? Or what is a silk stocking with a broken leg in it? The curse of God, the wrath of God, the hatred of God and the fierce indignation of God always attend sinners walking in a way of wickedness. Turn to Deuteronomy 28 and read from verse 15 to the end of that chapter; and turn to Leviticus 26 and read from verse 14 to the end of that chapter. Then you will see how the curse of God haunts the wicked man (like a Fury) in all his ways. In the city it attends him;193 in the country it hovers over him; coming in, it accompanies him; going out, it follows him; and in travel it is his companion. It fills his storehouse with strife, and mingles the wrath of God with his sweetest morsel. It is a moth in his wardrobe, a plague among his cattle, mildew in his field, rot among his sheep, and often makes the fruit of his body his greatest vexation and shame. No solid joy, no lasting peace, no194 pure comfort attends sinners in their sinful ways. There is a sword of vengeance that every moment hangs over their heads by a thin thread; and what joy and contentment can attend such souls, if the eye of conscience is open just far enough to see the sword? Ah, the horrors and terrors, the tremblings and shakings, that attend their souls!
