10. Comparing Ourselves with Worse Men

The tenth device that Satan has to draw the souls of men to sin is by working on them to be frequent in195 comparing themselves and their ways with those who are reputed or reported to be worse than themselves. By this device the devil drew the proud Pharisee to bless himself in a cursed condition: “God, I thank You that I am not like the other men—swindlers, evildoers, adulterers—or even like this tax collector,” etc. “Why,” says Satan, “you swear only petty oaths, such as by your faith and truth, etc., but such and such people swear by wounds and blood. You are now and then a little wanton, but such and such people daily defile and pollute themselves by actual uncleanness and filthiness. You cheat and take advantage of your neighbors in things that are only toys and trifles, but such and such people cheat and take advantage of others in things of the greatest concern, even to their ruin and undoing. You only sit and chat and sip with the drunkard, but such and such people sit and drink themselves drunk with the drunkard. You are only a little proud in heart and dress, in looks and words,” etc.

Now the remedies against this device of Satan are as follows.

The first remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly this: there is no greater or clearer argument to prove a man a196 hypocrite than to be sharp-sighted toward others and blind at home; than to see a speck in another man’s eye, and not a beam in his own eye; than to use spectacles to look at other men’s sins, rather than mirrors to look at his own; than to be always holding his finger on other men’s sores; than to be amplifying and exaggerating other men’s sins, and lessening his own, etc.

The second remedy against this device of Satan is to spend more time197 comparing your+ inward and outward actions with the rule, with that word by which you+ must be judged at last, than comparing yourselves+ with those who are worse than yourselves+. The man who, comparing himself with others who are worse than himself, may seem (to himself and others) to be an angel, may yet, comparing himself with the word, see himself to be like the devil, yes, a very devil: “Have I not chosen you+, the Twelve? Yet one of you+ is a devil!” Such men are as like him as if they were spit out of his mouth. Satan is called the god of this world because, as God at first only spoke the word and it was done, so if the devil only holds up his finger, or gives the least hint, they will do his will, though they ruin their souls forever. Ah, what monsters these men would appear to be, if only they compared themselves with a righteous rule, and not with the most unrighteous men! They would appear to be as black as hell itself.

The third remedy against this device of Satan is to consider seriously that though your sins are not as great as others’, yet without sound repentance on your side and pardoning mercy on God’s, you will be as certainly damned198 as others, though not equally tormented with others. Though hell will not be so hot for you as for others, yet you will go to hell as certainly as others, unless the glorious grace of God shines on you in the face of Christ. God will suit men’s punishments to their sins. The greatest sins will be attended with the greatest punishments, and lesser sins with lesser punishments. Alas, what a poor comfort this will be to you when you come to die: to consider that you will not be equally tormented with others, and yet must be forever shut out from the glorious presence of God, Christ, angels and saints, and from those good things of eternal life that are so many that they exceed number,199 so great that they exceed measure, so precious that they exceed all valuing! It is certain that the tears of hell are not enough to bewail the loss of heaven. The worm of grief gnaws as painfully as the fire burns. If those souls in Acts 20:37, 38 wept because they would see Paul’s face no more, how deplorable is the eternal loss of the beatific vision! But this is not all. You will not only be shut out of heaven, but shut up in hell forever; not only shut out from the presence of God and angels, etc., but shut up with devils and damned spirits forever; not only shut out from200 those sweet, surpassing, inexpressible and everlasting pleasures that are at God’s right hand, but shut up forever under torments that are easeless, remediless and endless. Ah, souls! Would it not be ten thousand times better for you+ to break off your+ sins by repentance than to go on in your+ sins until you+ feel the truth of what you+ now hear? The God of Israel is very merciful. Ah, that you+ would repent and return, so that your+ souls might live forever! Remember this: grievous is the torment of the damned for the bitterness of the punishments, but most grievous for the eternity of the punishments. For to be tormented without end, this is201 what goes beyond all the bounds of despair. Ah, how the thought of this makes the damned roar and cry out in anguish of heart, and tear their hair, and gnash their teeth, and rage in madness, that they must dwell in everlasting burnings forever!

11. Error in the Judgment

The eleventh device that Satan has to draw the soul to sin is by polluting and defiling the souls and judgments of men with dangerous errors, errors whose own tendency is to carry the souls of men to all looseness and wickedness, as woeful experience abundantly shows. Ah, how many are filled with these and similar Christ-dishonoring and soul-ruining opinions! Namely: That ordinances are poor, low, carnal things, and are not only to be lived above, but lived without also. That the Scriptures are full of fallacies and uncertainties, and are to be heeded no further than they agree with the spirit that is in men. That it is a poor, low thing, if not idolatry too, to worship God in a Mediator. That the resurrection is already past. That there was never any such man or person as Jesus Christ, but that it is all an allegory, and signifies nothing but light and love and such good frames born in men. That there is no God, nor devil, heaven, nor hell, except what is within us. That there is no sin in the saints, and they are under no law but that of the spirit, which is all freedom. That sin and grace are equally from God and agree with his will. With a hundred other horrid opinions, which have made wickedness break in like a flood among us, etc.

Now the general remedies against this device of Satan are as follows.

The first remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that an erroneous, vain mind is as hateful202 to God as a life of vice. He who had the leprosy in his head was to be pronounced utterly unclean. Gross errors make the heart foolish, and render the life loose and the soul of little weight in the eye of God. Error spreads and eats away203 like gangrene, and makes the soul a leper in the sight of God. It was God’s heavy and dreadful plague on the Gentiles to be given up to a mind void of judgment, or an undiscerning mind, or a mind rejected, disallowed and abhorred by God, or a mind that no one has cause to glory in, but rather to be ashamed204 of. I think that in these days God punishes many men’s former wickedness by giving them up to soul-ruining errors. Ah Lord! This mercy I humbly beg: that you would rather take me into your own hand and do anything with me than give me up to those sad errors to which thousands have married their souls, and so are in the way of perishing forever.

The second remedy against this device of Satan is to receive the truth affectionately, and let it dwell in your+ souls richly. When men stand out against the truth, when truth would enter205 and men bar the door of their souls against it, God in justice gives up such souls to be deluded and deceived by error, to their eternal ruin. 2 Thess 2:10, 11, 12: “Because they did not receive the love of the truth that would have saved them, … God will send them a powerful delusion”206 (or as the Greek has it, the efficacy of error) “so that they believe a lie, in order that all may be damned who have disbelieved the truth and delighted in wickedness.” Ah, sirs! As you+ love your+ souls, do not tempt God; do not provoke God, by your+ withstanding truth and outfacing truth, to give you+ up to believe a lie, that you+ may be damned. There are no men on earth so fenced against error as those who receive the truth in the love of it. Such souls207 are not easily “tossed about … and carried around by every wind of teaching, by the sleight of men and the cunning craftiness of their deceitful scheming.” It is not he who receives most of the truth into his head, but he who receives most of the truth affectionately into his heart, who will enjoy the happiness of having his judgment sound and clear when others are deluded and deceived by those who make it their business to infect the judgments and ruin the souls of men.

Ah, souls! If you+ do not want your+ judgments polluted and defiled208 with error, let the word of the Lord, which is more precious than gold, indeed than fine gold, dwell richly in you+. It is not the hearing of truth, nor the knowing of truth, nor the commending of truth, nor the talking of truth, but the indwelling of truth in your+ souls that will keep your+ judgments chaste and sound in the midst of all those glittering errors. Those errors betray many souls into the hands of him who can easily “masquerade as an angel of light,” so that he may draw others to lie in chains of darkness with him forever. Oh, do not let the word be a stranger, but make it your+ choicest companion! Then you+ will be able to stand in the day when many fall on your+ right hand and on your+ left by the cunning of those who say, “Look, here is Christ,” and “Look, there is Christ.” There was more cleverness than grace in the saying of the man who advised his friend not to come too near to truth, lest its heels kick out his teeth. Ah, souls! If truth dwells richly in209 you+, you+ are happy; if not, you+ are unhappy in all your+ greatest good fortune. “It is with truth,” says Melanchthon, “as it is with holy water. Everyone praises it and thinks it has some rare power in it; but offer to sprinkle them with it, and they will shut their eyes and turn their faces away from it.”

The third remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that error makes its owner suffer loss. All the pains and labor that men take to defend and maintain their errors, to spread them abroad and infect the world with them, will bring them no profit and no comfort in that day when “each man’s210 work will be made evident, and the fire will test its quality,” as the apostle shows in that remarkable Scripture, 1 Cor 3:11, 12, 13, 14, 15. Ah, that all those who rise early and go to bed late, who spend their time, their strength, their spirits, their all, to advance and spread abroad God-dishonoring and soul-ruining opinions, would seriously consider this: that they will lose all the pains, cost and expense that they have spent or will spend for the propagating of error; and if they are ever saved, it will be by fire, as the apostle shows there. Ah, sirs! Is it nothing to lay out your+ money for that which is not bread, and your+ strength for that which will not, which cannot, profit you+ in the day when you+ must settle your+ accounts and all your+ works must be tested by fire? Ah, that such souls would now at last buy the truth and not sell it! Remember, you+ can never pay too much for it, whatever you+ give for it; you+ can never sell it at its worth, even if you+ had all the world in exchange for it. It is said of Caesar211 that he took greater care of his books than of his royal robes; for when he swam through the waters to escape his enemies, he carried his books in his hand above the water, but lost his robes. Ah, what are Caesar’s books to God’s books? Well, remember this: one day, indeed one hour, spent in the pursuit of truth or the spreading abroad of truth will yield the soul more comfort and profit than many thousand years spent in the pursuit and spreading abroad of corrupt and vain opinions that have their rise from hell and not from heaven, from the god of this world and not from that God who will at last judge this world and all the corrupt opinions of men.

The fourth remedy against this device of Satan is to hate, reject and abhor all those doctrines and opinions that are contrary to godliness and that open a door to profaneness;212 and all such doctrines and opinions as require men to hold out a strictness beyond what the Scripture requires; and all such doctrines and opinions as advance and lift up corrupted nature to the doing of supernatural things, which none can do except by that supernatural power that raised Christ from the grave; and all such opinions as lift up our own righteousness in the place of Christ’s righteousness, that put good works on the throne of Christ and make them co-partners with Christ, etc.; and all those opinions and doctrines that so set up and cry up Christ and his righteousness as to cry down all duties of holiness and righteousness; and all those doctrines and opinions that make the glorious and blessed privileges of believers in the days of the gospel less, fewer and weaker than they were in the time of the law. Ah, if your+ souls rose up with a holy hatred and a strong indignation against such doctrines and opinions, you+ would stand when others fall, and you+ would shine like the sun in her glory, when many who were once like shining stars may go out like stinking candle-ends.

The fifth remedy against this device of Satan is to hold fast the truth. As men take no hold on the arm of flesh till they have let go their hold on213 the arm of God, so men take no hold on error till they have let go their hold on truth. Therefore hold fast the truth. Truth is your crown; hold fast your crown, and let no man take your crown from you. Has not God made214 truth sweet to your soul, indeed “sweeter than honey, than the honeycomb”? And will you not go on to heaven feeding on truth, that heavenly honeycomb, as Samson fed on his honeycomb? Ah, souls! Have you+ not found truth sweetening your+ spirits, and cheering your+ spirits, and warming your+ spirits, and raising your+ spirits, and strengthening your+ spirits? Have you+ not found truth a guide to lead you+, a staff to uphold you+, a heart-medicine to strengthen you+, and a plaster to heal you+? And will you+ not hold fast the truth? Has not truth been your+ best friend in your+ worst days? Has not truth stood by you+ when friends have forsaken you+? Has not truth done more for you+ than all the world could do against you+, and will you+ not hold fast the truth? Is not truth your+ right eye, without which you+ cannot see for Christ? And your+ right hand, without which you+ cannot do anything for Christ? And your+ right foot, without which you+ cannot walk with Christ? And will you+ not hold fast truth? Oh, hold fast the truth in your+ judgments and understandings, in your+ wills and affections, in your+ profession of faith215 and conduct! Truth is more precious than gold or rubies, and all the things you can desire are not to be compared with her. Truth is that heavenly mirror in which we may see the luster and glory of divine wisdom, power, greatness, love and mercifulness. In this mirror you+ may see the face of Christ, the favor of Christ, the riches of Christ, and the heart of Christ beating and working sweetly toward your+ souls. Oh, let your+ souls cling to truth as Ruth216 did to Naomi, and say, “I will not leave truth or turn back from following after truth. Wherever truth goes, I will go, and wherever truth lodges, I will lodge, and nothing but death shall part truth and my soul.” What John said to the church of Philadelphia I may say to you+: “Hold fast to what you have, so that no one will take your crown.” The crown is the top of royalties; such a thing is truth. Let217 no man take your crown. “Hold fast to the faithful word,” as Titus speaks. You+ had better let go anything than truth. You+ had better let go your+218 honors and riches, your+ friends and pleasures, and the world’s favors, indeed your+ nearest and dearest relations, yes, your+ very lives, than let go truth. Oh, keep the truth, and truth will keep you+ safe and happy for219 ever! Blessed are those souls that are kept by truth.

The sixth remedy against this device of Satan is to keep humble. Humility will keep the soul free from many darts of Satan’s casting and erroneous snares of his spreading. As low trees and shrubs are free from many violent gusts and blasts of wind that shake and tear the taller trees, so humble souls are free from those gusts and blasts of error that tear and rend proud, lofty souls. Satan and the world have least power to fasten errors on humble souls. The God of light and truth delights to dwell with the humble; and the more light and truth dwell in the soul, the further off darkness and error will stand from the soul. The God of grace pours grace into humble souls as men pour liquid into empty vessels; and the more grace is poured into the soul, the less error will be able to overpower the soul or to infect it. That is a sweet word in220 Ps 25:9: “He guides the meek” (or the humble) “in judgment and teaches the meek His way.” And certainly souls guided by God and taught by God are not easily drawn aside into ways of error. Oh, beware of spiritual pride! Pride fills our fancies, and weakens our graces, and makes room in our hearts for error. There are no men on earth so soon entangled and so easily conquered by error as proud souls. Oh, it is dangerous to love to be wise above what is written; to be overcurious and unsober in your+ desire for knowledge; to221 trust to your+ own capacities and abilities; to undertake to pry into all secrets; and to be puffed up by a carnal mind! Souls that are soaring up in this way above the bounds and limits of humility usually fall into the very worst of errors, as experience daily shows.

The seventh remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly the great evils that errors have produced. Error is a fruitful mother, and has brought forth such monstrous222 children as have set towns, cities and nations on fire. Error is that whorish woman who has cast down many, wounded many, indeed slain many strong men, and many great men, and many learned men, and many professing men, in former times and in our own time, as is all too evident to all who are not much forsaken by God, destitute of the truth, and blinded by Satan. Oh, the graces that error has weakened, and the sweet joys and comforts that error has clouded, if not buried! Oh, the hands that error has weakened, the eyes that error has blinded, the judgments of men that error has perverted, the minds that error has darkened, the hearts that error has hardened, the affections that error has cooled, the consciences that error has seared, and the lives of men that error has polluted! Ah, souls! Can you+ solemnly consider this and not tremble more at error than at hell itself? etc.

218. Hold it fast as with tooth and nail, against those who would snatch it from us.

219. I have read of one who, seeing in a vision many snares of the devil spread on the earth, sat down mourning and said within himself (Quis pertransiet ista), “Who shall pass through these?” And he heard a voice answering (humilitas pertransiet), “Humility shall pass through them.”

220. Ps 25:9. ענוים Gnanavim, from ענה gnanah, which signifies the humble, or afflicted. The high tide quickly ebbs, and the highest sun is soon declining; you+ know how to apply it.

221. The proud soul is like the man who gazed at the moon but fell into the pit.

222. Errors in conscience produce many great evils, not only (ad intra) within men’s own souls, but also (ad extra) in human affairs.

12. Wicked Company

The twelfth device that Satan has to draw the soul to sin is to make it fond of wicked company and keep wicked society. And oh, the horrid impieties and wickedness that Satan has drawn men to sin by working on them to sit and associate themselves with worldly people!

Now the remedies against this device of Satan are as follows.

The first remedy against this device of Satan is to dwell (till your+ hearts are moved) on those commands of God that expressly require us to shun the society of the wicked. Eph 5:11: “Have no fellowship223 with the fruitless deeds of darkness, but rather expose them.” Prov 4:14, 15, 16: “Do not set foot on the path of the wicked or walk in the way of evildoers. Avoid it; do not travel on it. Turn from it and pass on by.” 1 Cor 5:9, 10, 11. 2 Thess 3:6. Prov 1:10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15. Turn to these Scriptures, and let your+ souls dwell on them till a holy indignation is raised in your+ souls against fellowship with worldly men. “God will not take the wicked by the hand,” as Job speaks; why then should you+? God’s commands are not like those that are easily reversed; they are like those of the Medes, which cannot be changed. If these commands are not kept by you now, they will at last be witnesses against you, and millstones to sink you, in the day when Christ judges you.

The second remedy against this device of Satan is to consider seriously that their company is very infectious224 and dangerous, as is clear from the Scriptures mentioned above. Ah, how many have lost their names, and lost their estates, and strength, and God, and heaven, and souls, by society with wicked men! As you+ shun a stinking carcass, as the seaman shuns sands and rocks and shoals, as you+ shun those who have the plague-sore running on them, so you+ should shun the society of wicked men. As weeds endanger the grain, as infection endangers the blood, or as an infected house endangers the neighborhood, so does wicked company endanger the soul. Bias, a heathen, was at sea in a great storm, and saw many wicked men with him in the ship calling on the gods. “Oh,” he said, “stop praying, hold your+ tongues! I would not have the gods take notice that you+ are here; they will surely drown us all if they do.” Ah, sirs! Could a heathen225 see so much danger in the society of wicked men, and can you+ see none?

The third remedy against this device226 of Satan is always to look on wicked men under the names and descriptions by which the Scripture sets them out. The Scripture calls them lions for their fierceness, and bears for their cruelty, and dragons for their hideousness, and dogs for their filthiness, and wolves for their cunning. The Scripture calls them scorpions, vipers, thorns, briers, thistles, brambles, stubble, dirt, chaff, dust, dross, smoke, scum, as you may see in the note. It is not safe to look on wicked men under the names and descriptions they give themselves, or that flatterers give them; this may delude the soul. But looking on them under the names and descriptions the Scripture gives them may keep the soul from frequenting their company and delighting in their society. Do not tell me what this man calls them, or how such and such a person regards them; tell me what the Scripture calls them. How does the Scripture regard them? As Nabal’s name was, so was his nature; and as wicked men’s names are, so are their natures. You may know well enough what is within them by the fitting names the Holy Spirit has given them.

The fourth and last remedy against227 this device of Satan is to consider that the society and company of wicked men have been a great grief and burden to those precious souls who were once glorious on earth and are now triumphing in heaven. Ps 120:5, 6: “Woe to me that I dwell in Meshech, that I live among the tents of Kedar! Too long have I dwelt among those who hate peace.” So Jeremiah: “If only I had a traveler’s lodge in the wilderness, I would abandon my people and depart from them, for they are all adulterers, a crowd of faithless people” (Jer 9:2). So they tormented Lot’s228 “righteous soul” by their “depraved conduct.” They made his life a burden; they made death more desirable to him than life; indeed, they made his life a lingering death. Guilt or grief is all the good that gracious souls get by keeping company with wicked men.

223. Non parentum aut majorum authoritas sed Dei docentis imperium [Not the authority of parents or forefathers, but the command of God who teaches], Jerome. The commands of God must outweigh all the authority and example of men.

224. Eusebius reports of John the Evangelist that he would not allow Cerinthus the heretic in the same bath with him, lest some judgment should fall on them both. Eusebius, book 3, chapter 25. A man who keeps bad company is like one who walks in the sun: he is tanned without noticing it.

225. Prov 13:20.

226. 2 Tim 4:17. Isa 11:7. Ezek 29:3. Matt 10:16. Rev 9:3, 5, 10. Matt 3:7. Isa 10:17; 27:4; 55:13. Ezek 2:6. Judg 9:14. Job 21:18. Ps 18:42. Ps 1:4. Ps 18:42. Ezek 22:18, 19. Isa 65:5. Ezek 24:6. Lactantius says of Lucian (nec diis, nec hominibus pepercit) that he spared neither God nor man. Such monsters are wicked men, which should make their company a burden and not a delight to all who have tasted the sweetness of divine love.

227. “O Lord, do not let me go to hell, where the wicked are, for, Lord, you know I never loved their company here,” said a gracious gentlewoman when she was about to die, being in much trouble of conscience.

228. 2 Pet 2:7, 8. See Beza.

Part II. Devices to Keep Souls from Holy Duties

1. The World in Its Best Dress

The second thing to be shown is the various devices that Satan has (as to draw souls to sin, so also) to keep souls from holy duties, to hinder souls in holy services, and to keep them away from religious performances.

Then the angel showed me Joshua the high priest standing before the angel of the Lord, with Satan standing at his right hand to resist him. Zech 3:1.

I will show you the truth of this in the following particulars.

The first device that Satan has to draw souls from holy duties, and to keep them away from religious services, is,

By presenting the world to the soul in such a dress and in such a garb as to ensnare the soul and to win over the affections of the soul.229 He represents the world to them in its beauty and splendor, which proves a bewitching sight to a world of men. It is true that this did not take hold of Christ, because Satan could find nothing in him for his temptation to work on. But Satan finds something in us for this temptation to work on, so that he no sooner casts out his golden bait than we are ready to play with it and to nibble at it; he no sooner throws out his golden ball than men are apt to run after it, though they lose God and their souls in the pursuit. Ah! how many professing Christians in these days have for a time followed hard after God, Christ, and230 ordinances, until the devil set before them the world in all its beauty and splendor. This has so bewitched their souls that they have come to have low thoughts of holy things, and then to be cold in their affections toward holy things, and then to slight them, and at last, like the young man in the gospel, to turn their backs on them. Ah, the time, the thoughts, the spirits, the hearts, the souls, the duties, the services that the inordinate love of this wicked world eats up and destroys, and has eaten up and destroyed! Where one thousand are destroyed231 by the world’s frowns, ten thousand are destroyed by the world’s smiles. The world, like a Siren, sings to us and sinks us; it kisses us and betrays us, like Judas; it kisses us and strikes us under the fifth rib, like Joab. The honors, splendor, and all the glory of this world are only sweet poisons, which will greatly endanger us, if they do not eternally destroy us. Ah, the multitude of souls who have gorged themselves on these sweet baits and died forever!

Now the remedies against this device of Satan are as follows.

The first remedy against this device232 of Satan is to dwell on the impotence and weakness of all these things below. They are not able to secure you+ from the least evil. They are not able to obtain for you+ the least desirable good. The crown of gold cannot cure the headache, nor the velvet slipper ease the gout, nor the jewel about the neck take away the toothache. The frogs of Egypt entered the houses of the rich men of Egypt as well as of the poor. Our daily experience shows233 this: all the honors and riches, etc., that men enjoy cannot free them from the colic, the fever, or lesser diseases. Indeed, what may seem strangest of all is that a great deal of wealth cannot keep men from falling into extreme poverty. In Judg 1:6, 7 you+ will find seventy kings with their fingers and toes cut off, glad, like puppies, to lick up crumbs under another king’s table; and shortly after, the same king who brought them to this penury is reduced to the same poverty and misery. Why then should that be a bar to keep you out of heaven which cannot give you the least ease on earth?

The second remedy against this device of Satan is to dwell on the vanity of all worldly good, as well as on its impotence. This is the sum of Solomon’s sermon: “Vanity of vanities! Everything is vanity.” This234 our first parents found, and therefore they named their second son Abel, that is, vanity. Solomon, who had tried these things and could best tell their vanity, preaches this sermon over again and again: “Vanity of vanities! Everything is vanity.” It is sad to think how many thousands there are who can say with the Preacher, “Vanity of vanities! Everything is vanity,”235 indeed, can swear it, and yet follow after these things as if there were no other glory or happiness but what is to be found in the very things they call vanity. Such men will sell Christ, heaven, and their souls for a trifle; they call these things vanity, but do not heartily believe them to be vanity, and set their hearts on them as if they were their crown, the height of all their royalty and glory. Oh, let your+ souls dwell on the vanity of all things here below, until your+ hearts are so thoroughly convinced and persuaded of their vanity as to trample on them, and make them a footstool for Christ to mount up and ride in holy triumph in your+ hearts.236 Chrysostom once said that if he were the fittest man in the world to preach a sermon to the whole world gathered together in one congregation, and had some high mountain for his pulpit, from which he might have all the world in view, and were furnished with a voice of brass, a voice as loud as the trumpet of the archangel, so that all the world might hear him, he would choose to preach on no other text than that in the Psalms: “O mortal men, how long will you+ love vanity and seek after lies?”237 Tell me, you+ who say that all things under the sun are vanity: if you+ really believe what you+ say, why do you+ spend more thoughts and time on the world than you+ do on Christ, heaven, and your+ immortal souls? Why then do you+ neglect your+ duty toward God to get the world? Why then do you+ pursue the world so eagerly, and are so cold in pursuing God, Christ, and holiness? Why then are your+ hearts so exceedingly lifted up when the world comes in and smiles on you+, and so much dejected and cast down when the world frowns on you+ and, like Jonah’s gourd, withers before you+?

The third remedy against this device of Satan is to dwell much on the uncertainty, the changeableness, and the inconstancy of all things under the sun.238 Man himself is only the dream of a dream, the offspring of a fancy, an empty vanity, the elaborate picture of nothing, a poor, feeble, dying flash. All temporal things are as passing as a hasty, headlong torrent, a shadow, a ship, a bird, an arrow, a messenger that runs by. “Why should you set your eyes on that which is not?” says Solomon. And the apostle says, “The present form of this world is passing away.” Heaven239 alone has a foundation; the earth has none, but is hung “upon nothing,” as Job speaks. The apostle told Timothy to “instruct those who are rich … not to be conceited and not to put their hope in the uncertainty of wealth.” Riches are like bad servants whose shoes are made of running leather, who will never stay long with one master. As a bird hops from tree to tree, so the honors and riches of this world pass from man to man. Let Job and Nebuchadnezzar testify to this truth, who fell240 from great wealth to great need. No man can promise himself that he will be wealthy until night. One storm at sea, one coal of fire, one false friend, one unadvised word, one false witness may make you a beggar and a prisoner all at once. All the riches and glory of this world are only like smoke and chaff that vanish, “like a dream, like a vision in the night” that does not last; as when a hungry man dreams and thinks that he is eating, and when he awakes his soul is empty; and like a thirsty man who thinks he is drinking, and behold, when he awakes his soul is faint, as the prophet Isaiah says. Where is the glory of Solomon? The splendid buildings of Nebuchadnezzar? The nine hundred chariots of Sisera? The power of Alexander? The authority of Augustus, who commanded the whole world to be taxed? Those who have been most glorious in what men generally count glorious and excellent have had inglorious ends: Samson for strength, Absalom for beauty, Ahithophel for shrewd counsel, Haman for favor, Asahel for swiftness, Alexander for great conquest, and yet poisoned after twelve years. You may see the same in the four mighty kingdoms, the Chaldean, Persian, Greek, and Roman:241 how soon they were gone and forgotten! Now rich, now poor; now full, now empty; now in favor, soon out of favor; now honorable, now despised; now health, now sickness; now strength, now weakness. Oh, do not let these uncertain things keep you from those holy services and heavenly employments that may make you happy forever, and make your soul eternally blessed and at ease, when all these passing things bid your soul an everlasting farewell.

The fourth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider that the great things of this world are very hurtful and dangerous to the outward and the inward man, through the242 corruptions that are in the hearts of men. Oh, the rest, the peace, the comfort, the contentment that the things of this world strip many men of! Oh, the fears, the cares, the envy, the malice, the dangers, the harms that they subject men to! They often make men carnally confident: “A rich man’s wealth is his fortified city; it is like a high wall in his imagination.” “In prosperity I said, ‘I will never be shaken.’” They often swell the heart with pride, and make men forget God, and neglect God, and despise the Rock of their salvation: “When Jeshurun grew fat, becoming fat, bloated, and gorged, then he forgot God, and abandoned the God who made him, and scorned the Rock of his salvation,” as Moses spoke. Ah, the time, the thoughts, the spirits that the things of the world consume and spend! Oh, how they hinder the actings of faith on God! How they interrupt our sweet communion with God! How they abate our love to the people of God, and cool our love to the things of God, and bring us to act like those who are most unlike God! Oh, the deadness, the dullness, the barrenness that attends men under great outward blessings! Oh, the riches of the world choke243 the word, so that men live under the most soul-searching and soul-enriching means with lean souls! Though they have full purses, though their chests are full of silver, yet their hearts are empty of grace. In Gen 13:2 it is said that Abraham “was very rich in livestock, in silver and in gold.” In the Hebrew (Chabbedh) it reads, Abraham was very heavy, to show that riches are a heavy burden, and many times a hindrance to heaven and happiness. King Henry the Fourth asked the Duke of Alva if he had observed the great eclipse of the sun which had lately happened. “No,” said the duke, “I have so much to do on earth that I have no leisure to look up to heaven.” Ah, if only this were not true of most professing Christians in these days! It is very sad to think how their hearts and time are so much taken up with earthly things that they scarcely have any leisure to look up to heaven, or to look after Christ and the things that belong to their everlasting peace.

Riches, though well gotten, are still only like manna: those who gathered less had no lack, and to those who gathered more it was only a trouble and an annoyance. The world is troublesome, and yet it is loved; what would it be if it were peaceable? You+ embrace it, though it is filthy; what would you+ do if it were beautiful? You+ cannot keep your+ hands from the thorns; how eager would you+ then be in gathering the flowers? The world may fitly be likened to the serpent Scytale, of which it is reported that244 when she cannot overtake fleeing travelers, she so stuns and dazes them with her beautiful colors that they have no power to pass on until she has stung them. Ah! how many thousands are there now on earth who have found this true by experience, who have spun a fine thread to strangle themselves, both temporally and eternally, by being bewitched by the beauty and splendor of this enticing world!

The fifth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider that all the happiness of this world is mixed. Our light is mixed with darkness, our joy with sorrow, our pleasures with pain, our honor with dishonor, our riches with need. If our sight is spiritual, clear, and sharp, we may see in the happiness of this world our wine mixed with water, our honey with gall, our sugar with wormwood, and our roses with thorns. Sorrow attends worldly joy,245 danger attends worldly safety, loss attends worldly labors, tears attend worldly purposes. As to these things, men’s hopes are vain, their sorrow certain, and their joy feigned. The apostle calls this world a sea of glass: a sea for its troubles, and glass for its brittleness and bitterness. The honors, profits, pleasures, and delights of this world are true gardens of Adonis, where we can gather nothing but trivial flowers surrounded by many briers.

The sixth remedy against this device of Satan is to get better acquaintance with, and better assurance of, more blessed and glorious things. What246 raised up their spirits, in the tenth and eleventh chapters of Hebrews, to trample on all the beauty, splendor, and glory of the world was their acquaintance with and assurance of better and more lasting things. “They joyfully accepted the confiscation of their property, knowing that they had in heaven a better and more lasting possession. They247 were looking forward to the city with foundations, whose architect and builder is God. And they were longing for a better country, a heavenly one. They saw Him who is invisible, and were looking ahead to their reward.” And this made them count all the glory and splendor of this world too poor and contemptible for them to set their hearts on. The main reason why men dote on the world, and damn their souls to get the world, is that they are not acquainted with a greater glory. Men ate acorns until they became acquainted with the use of wheat. Ah, if men were better acquainted with what union and communion with God means, what it is to “have a new name, and a new stone, that no one knows except the one who has it”; if they only tasted more of heaven, and lived more in heaven, and had more glorious hopes of going to heaven, ah! how easily would they have the moon under their feet! It was an excellent saying of Louis of Bavaria, emperor of Germany,248 that such goods are worth getting and owning as will not sink or wash away if a shipwreck happens, but will wade and swim out with us. It is recorded of Lazarus that after his resurrection from the dead he was never seen to laugh; his thoughts and affections were so fixed in heaven, though his body was on earth. And therefore he could not help but slight temporal things,249 his heart being so bent and set on eternal things. There are goods of the throne of grace, such as God, Christ, the Spirit, adoption, justification, remission of sin, peace with God, and peace with conscience; and there are goods of the footstool, such as honors, riches, the favor of men, and the other comforts and conveniences of this life. Now he who has acquaintance with and assurance of the goods of the throne will easily trample on the goods of the footstool. Ah, that you+ would make it your+ business, your+ work, to attend more to, and to make more sure to your+ own souls, the great250 things of eternity, which will yield you+ joy in life, and peace in death, and a crown of righteousness in the day of Christ’s appearing; and which will lift up your+ souls above all the beauty and splendor of this bewitching world, and raise your+ feet above other men’s heads! When a man comes to be assured of a crown, a scepter, the royal robes, etc., he then begins to have low, paltry, and contemptible thoughts of those things that he highly prized before. So assurance of greater and more glorious things will breed in the soul a holy scorn and contempt of all these poor, paltry things, which the soul once valued above God, Christ, and heaven, etc.

The seventh remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that true happiness and satisfaction are not to be had in the enjoyment of any worldly good. True happiness is too big and too glorious a thing to be251 found in anything below that God who is a Christian’s (summum bonum) chief good. The blessed angels, those glittering courtiers, have all happiness and blessedness, and yet they have neither gold nor silver nor jewels, nor any of the beauty and splendor of this world. Certainly, if happiness were to be found in these things, the Lord Jesus, who is the rightful and royal heir of all things, would have exchanged his cradle for a crown, his birth-chamber (a stable) for a royal palace, his poverty for plenty, his despised followers for shining courtiers, and his lowly provisions for the choicest delicacies, etc. Certainly, happiness does not lie in those things that a man252 may enjoy and yet be miserable forever. Now a man may be great and godless, like Pharaoh; honorable and damnable, like Saul; rich and miserable, like the rich man, etc. Therefore happiness does not lie in these things. Certainly happiness does not lie in those things that cannot comfort a man on his deathbed. Is it honors, riches, or friends, etc., that can comfort you when you come to die? Or is it not rather faith in the blood of Christ, the witness of the253 Spirit of Christ, the sense and feeling of the love and favor of Christ, and the hope of reigning eternally with Christ? Can happiness lie in those things that cannot give us health, or strength, or ease, or a good night’s rest, or an hour’s sleep, or a good appetite? Why, all the honors, riches, and delights of this world cannot give these poor things to us; therefore certainly happiness does not lie in the enjoyment of them, etc. And surely happiness is not to be found in those things that cannot satisfy the souls of men; and none of these things can satisfy the soul of man. “He who loves money is never satisfied by money, and he who loves wealth254 is never satisfied by income. This too is vanity,” says the wise man. The barren womb, the leech’s daughter, the grave, and hell will be satisfied as soon as the soul of man will be by the enjoyment of any worldly good. Some one thing or another will always be lacking to the soul that has nothing but outward good to live on. You may as soon fill a bag with wisdom, a chest with virtue, or a circle with a triangle, as the heart of man with anything here below. A man may have enough of the world to sink him, but he can never have enough to satisfy him, etc.

The eighth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly the dignity of the soul. Oh, the soul of man is worth more than a thousand worlds! It is the greatest abasing of it255 that can be, to let it dote on a little shining earth, on a little painted beauty and fading glory, when it is capable of union with Christ, of communion with God, and of enjoying the eternal vision of God. Seneca could say, “I am too great, and born to greater things, than to be a slave to my body.” Oh, say for your+ part, “My soul is too great, and born to greater things, than that I should confine it to a heap of white and yellow clay.” I have dwelt the longer on the remedies that may help us against this dangerous device of Satan, because he usually does more hurt to the souls of men by this device than he does by all other devices. To close, I wish, as Chrysostom once did, that this sentence, Eccl 2:11 (“Yet when I considered all the works that my hands had accomplished and what I had toiled to achieve, I found everything to be vanity, a pursuit of the wind; there was nothing to be gained under the sun”), were engraved on the doorposts through which you+ enter; on the tables where you+ sit; on the dishes out of which you+ eat; on the cups out of which you+ drink; on the bedsteads where you+ lie; on the walls of the houses where you+ dwell; on the garments which you+ wear; on the heads of the horses on which you+ ride; and on the foreheads of all whom you+ meet; so that your+ souls may not be kept away by the beauty and splendor of the world from those holy and heavenly services that may make you+ blessed while you+ live and happy when you+ die; and so that you+ may breathe out your+ last into his bosom who lives forever, and who will make those happy forever who prefer Christ’s spiritual and eternal things above all temporal, passing things.

229. The beauty of the world overthrows a Christian more than its strength; the flattering sunshine more than the blustering storm. In storms we keep our garments close about us.

230. The people who live by the Nile are made deaf by the noise of the waters; so the world makes such a noise in men’s ears that they cannot hear the things of heaven. The world is like the swallows’ dung that put out Tobias’s eyes.

231. The champions could not wring an apple out of Milo’s hand by strength, but a fair maid got it at once by fair means.

232. The prior whom Melanchthon tells of rolled his hands up and down in a basin full of gold coins, thinking by this to charm away his gout, but it would not work.

233. Nugas the Scythian, despising the rich presents and ornaments that were sent to him by the emperor of Constantinople, asked whether those things could drive away calamities, diseases, or death.

234. Gelimer, king of the Vandals, led in triumph by Belisarius, cried out, “Vanity of vanities! Everything is vanity.”

235. The fancy of Lucian, who places Charon on the top of a high hill, viewing all the affairs of living men and looking on their greatest cities as little birds’ nests, is very pleasant.

236. Oh, the imperfection, the ingratitude, the fickleness, the inconstancy, the treachery of those created things we most slavishly love!

237. Ah! if we would only weigh man’s pains against his payment, his afflictions against his blessings, his miseries against his pleasures, we would then see that there is nothing gained by the bargain, and conclude, “Vanity of vanities! Everything is vanity.”

238. Riches were never true to anyone who trusted in them; they have deceived men as Job’s brook did the poor traveler in the summer season.

239. 1 Cor 7:31: σχῆμα implies that there is nothing of any firmness or solid substance in created things.

240. The most renowned Frederick lost everything, and begged to be made merely the sexton of the church that he himself had built. I have read of a poor fisherman who, while his nets were drying, slept on the rock and dreamed that he was made a king. He started up all of a sudden and, leaping for joy, fell down from the rock, and in place of his imaginary happiness lost his little portion of pleasures.

241. John compares the pomp of this world to the moon, which (crescit & decrescit) increases and decreases. Rev 12:1.

242. 243. That four good mothers beget four bad daughters (great familiarity begets contempt; truth, hatred; virtue, envy; riches, ignorance) is a French proverb. Gen 13:2. כבד. 247. Luther, being once in some need, happened to be sent a good sum of money unexpectedly by a nobleman of Germany. Being somewhat dismayed at this, he said, “I fear that God will give me my reward here; but I protest, I will not be so satisfied.”

252. Philosophers could say that he was never a happy man who might afterward become miserable.
