255. Plutarch tells of Themistocles that he did not count it fitting for his rank to stoop down to take up the spoils the enemies had scattered in flight, but said to one of his followers (Ἀνελοῦ σαυτῷ σὺ γὰρ οὐκ εἶ Θεμιστοκλῆς), “You may, for you are not Themistocles.” Oh, what a sad thing it is that a heathen should set his feet on the very things on which most professing Christians set their hearts, and for the gain of which many, like Balaam, run the risk of losing their immortal souls forever!

2. The Dangers of Duty

The second device that Satan has to draw souls from holy duties, and to keep them away from religious services, is,

By presenting to them the danger, the losses, and the sufferings that attend the performance of such and such religious services. By this device Satan kept those who believed in Christ quiet, and kept them from confessing Christ, in John 12:42: “Nevertheless, many of the leaders believed in Him; but because of the Pharisees they did not confess Him, for fear that they would be put out of the synagogue.” “I would walk in all the ways of God; I would give myself up to the strictest ways of holiness; but I am afraid that dangers will attend me on the one hand, and losses, and perhaps such and such sufferings, on the other,” says many a man. Oh, how should we help ourselves against this temptation and device of Satan?

Now the remedies against this device of Satan are as follows.

The first remedy against this device of Satan is to consider that all the troubles and afflictions that you+ meet with in a way of righteousness will never hurt you+; they will never harm you+. “Who can harm256 you+ if you+ are zealous for what is good?” says the apostle; that is, no one will harm you+. Natural conscience cannot help paying homage to the image of God stamped on the natures, words, works, and lives of the godly, as we may see in the conduct of Nebuchadnezzar and257 Darius toward Daniel. All the afflictions and troubles that attend men in a way of righteousness can never rob them of their treasure, of their jewels. They may rob them of some light, slight things, such as the sword that is by their side, or the stick that is in their hand, or the flowers or ribbons that are in their hats. The treasure of a saint is the presence of God, the favor of God, union and communion with God, the pardon of sin, the joy of the Spirit, the peace of conscience; and these are jewels that no one can give but Christ, and no one can take away but Christ. Now, why should a gracious soul keep away from a way of holiness because of afflictions, etc., when no afflictions can strip a man of his heavenly jewels, which are his ornaments and his safety here, and will be his happiness and glory hereafter? Why should that man be afraid or troubled about258 storms at sea whose treasures are secure in a friend’s hand on land? Why, a believer’s treasure is always safe in the hands of Christ: his life is safe, his soul is safe, his grace is safe, his comfort is safe, and his crown is safe in the hand of Christ. “I know whom259 I have believed, and I am convinced that He is able to guard what I have entrusted to Him for that day,” says the apostle. The child’s most precious things are most secure in his father’s hands; so are our souls, our graces, and our comforts in the hand of Christ.

The second remedy against this device of Satan is to consider that other precious saints, who were shining260 lights on earth and are now triumphing in heaven, have held on in religious services, despite all the troubles and dangers that surrounded them. Nehemiah and Ezra were surrounded with dangers on the left hand and on the right, and yet in the face of them all they held on building the temple and the wall of Jerusalem. So did Daniel, and those precious worthies in Ps 44, under a lack of outward encouragements, and in the face of a world of very great discouragements, their souls clung to God and his ways. Though they were crushed in the lair of jackals and covered with the shadow of death; indeed, though they were counted all day long as sheep to be slaughtered, yet their hearts did not turn back, nor did their steps stray from his ways. Though bonds and imprisonment awaited Paul and the rest of the apostles in every place, yet they held on in the work and service of the Lord. Why then should you+ fall away from their worthy examples, which it is your+ duty and your+ glory to follow?

The third remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that all the troubles and dangers that attend the performance of holy duties and heavenly services are only temporal and momentary, but the neglect of them may lay you open to all temporal, spiritual, and eternal dangers. “How shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation?” He does not say, if we reject or renounce such a great salvation, but if we neglect, or shift off (as the word is), “such261 a great salvation.” He does not say, how shall we escape if we oppose or persecute such a great salvation? No, but if we let slip or neglect such a great salvation, how shall we escape? That is, we cannot escape by any way, or means, or device in the world; divine justice will be above us, in spite of our very souls. Doing such and such heavenly services may lay you+ open to the frowns of men, but neglecting them will lay you+ open to the frowns of God. Doing them may make you+ contemptible in the eyes of men,262 but neglecting them may make you+ contemptible in the eyes of God. Doing them may be the loss of your estate, but neglecting them may be the loss of God, Christ, heaven, and your soul forever. Doing them may shut you out from some outward, temporal contentments; neglecting them may shut you out from that excellent, matchless glory which “no eye has seen, no ear has heard, no heart has imagined.” Remember this: there is no man who breathes who will not suffer more by neglecting those holy and heavenly services that God commands, commends, and rewards than he can possibly suffer by doing them, etc.

The fourth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider that God knows how to deliver from troubles by troubles, from afflictions by afflictions, from dangers by dangers. By lesser troubles and afflictions God often delivers his people from greater ones, so that they will say, “We would have perished if we had not perished; we would have been undone if we had not been263 undone; we would have been in danger if we had not been in danger.” God will so order all the afflictions that befall you+ in the way of righteousness that your+264 souls will say, “We would not for all the world have missed meeting with such and such troubles and afflictions; for surely, if these had not befallen us, it would have gone worse and worse with us.” Oh, the carnal complacency, pride, formality, dead-heartedness, lukewarmness, censoriousness, and earthliness that God has cured us of by the troubles and dangers that we have met with in the ways and services of the Lord! I remember a story of a godly man who, as he was going to take ship for France, broke his leg; and it pleased providence so to order it that the ship he should have gone in was cast away at that very time, and not a man saved. So by breaking a bone his life was saved. So the Lord many times breaks our bones, but it is in order to save our lives and our souls forever. He gives us a potion that makes us heart-sick, but it is in order to make us perfectly well, and to purge us of those infections that have made our heads ache, and God’s heart ache, and our souls sick and heavy to the death, etc. Oh, therefore, do not let any danger or misery hinder you from your duty.

The fifth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that you+ will gain more in the service of God, and by walking in righteous and holy ways, though troubles and afflictions should attend you+, than you+ can possibly suffer or lose by being found in the service of God. “Godliness … is great gain.” Oh, the joy, the peace,265 the comfort, the rest that saints meet with in the ways and service of God! They find that religious services are not empty things, but things in which God is pleased to reveal his beauty and glory to their souls. “My soul thirsts for God” (says David), “that I might see Your beauty and Your glory, as I have seen You in the sanctuary.” Oh, the sweet looks, the sweet words, the sweet hints, the sweet nudges, the sweet influences, the sweet love letters that gracious souls have from heaven when they wait on God in holy and heavenly services! The least of these will eclipse and outweigh all the splendor and glory of this world, and richly repay the soul for all the troubles, afflictions, and dangers that have attended it in the service of God. Oh, the saints can say under all their troubles and afflictions that they have food to eat and drink to266 drink that the world does not know of; that they have such inflowings, such refreshments, such warmings, etc., as they would not exchange for all the honors, riches, and delicacies of this world. Ah! let a Christian only compare his external losses with his spiritual, internal, and eternal gain, and he will find that for every penny he loses in the service of God he gains a pound; for every pound he loses he gains a hundred; for every hundred lost he gains a thousand. We lose pins in his service and find pearls. We lose the favor of men, and peace with men, and perhaps the comforts and contentments of created things; and we gain the favor of God, peace with conscience, and the comforts and contentments of a better life. Ah! if the men of this world knew the sweetness that saints enjoy in afflictions, they would rather choose Manasseh’s iron chain than his golden crown; they would rather be Paul a prisoner than Paul caught up to the third heaven. For light afflictions they will have a267 weight of glory; for a few afflictions they will have those joys, pleasures, and contentments that are like the stars of heaven or the sands of the sea, which cannot be numbered; for momentary afflictions they will have an eternal crown of glory. “It is only shutting your eyes, and you will be in heaven at once,” said the martyr. Oh, therefore, do not let any afflictions or troubles bring you to shun the ways of God, or to quit that service which should be dearer to you than a world, indeed, than your very life, etc.

256. Nemo proprie laeditur nisi a seipso. Nobody is truly hurt except by himself and his own fault.

257. Gordius, that blessed martyr, counted it a loss to him not to suffer many kinds of tortures. He says tortures are only tradings with God for glory. The greater the combat, the greater the reward that follows.

258. That was a notable saying of Luther: “Let him who died for my soul see to its salvation.”

259. 2 Tim 1:12.

260. William Flower, martyr, said, “Heaven shall as soon fall as I will forsake my profession of faith, or budge in the least degree from it.” So Sanctus, under as great torment as you+ have read of, cried out (Christianus sum), “I am a Christian”; no torment could bring him to turn from the service of his God. I might produce a cloud of witnesses; but if these do not move you+ to be noble and brave, I am afraid more will not.

261. ἀμελήσαντες. Disregard; not care for it.

262. Francis Xavier counseled John the Third, king of Portugal, to meditate every day for a quarter of an hour on that text, “What will it profit a man if he gains the whole world, yet forfeits his soul?”

263. Periissem nisi periissem.

264. Non essem ego salvus nisi istae periissent. Anaxagoras: had these things not perished, I could not have been safe, said this philosopher when he saw great possessions that he had lost.

265. Tertullian, in his book to the martyrs, has an apt saying (Negotiatio est aliquid amittere ut majora lucreris), that is, it is right and good trading when something is parted with to gain more. He applies it to their sufferings, in which, though the flesh lost something, yet the spirit gained much more.

266. When the noble general Zelislaus had lost his hand in the wars of the king of Poland, the king sent him a golden hand in its place. What we lose in Christ’s service, he will make up by giving us some golden blessings.

267. Though the cross is bitter, yet it is only short: a little storm, as one said of Julian’s persecution, and an eternal calm follows.

3. The Difficulty of Duty

The third device that Satan has to hinder souls from holy and heavenly services, from gracious and religious performances, is,

By presenting to the soul the difficulty of performing them. Satan says, “It is so hard and difficult a thing to pray as you should, and to wait on God as you should, and to walk with God as you should, and to be lively, warm and active in the communion of saints as you should, that you would be ten thousand times better off neglecting them than meddling with them.” No doubt by this device Satan has kept, and still keeps, thousands from waiting on God, and from giving him the service that is due to his name, etc.

Now the remedies against this device are as follows.

The first remedy against this device of Satan is to dwell more on the necessity of the service and duty than on the difficulty that attends the duty. You+ should reason with your+ souls like this: “Oh, our souls! Though such and such duties and services are hard and difficult, are they not exceedingly necessary for the honor of God and the keeping up of his name in268 the world? Are they not necessary for keeping sin under, for strengthening weak graces, for reviving languishing comforts, for keeping your+ blessed evidences clear and bright, for scattering your+ fears, for raising your+ hopes, for gladdening the hearts of the righteous, and for stopping the mouths of unrighteous souls, who are ready to take every advantage to blaspheme the name of God and to throw dirt and contempt on his people and ways?” Oh, never stop thinking on the necessity of this and that duty, till your+ souls are lifted up far above all the difficulties that attend religious duties.

The second remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that the Lord Jesus will make his services easy to you+ by the sweet revealing of himself to your+ souls while you+ are in his service. “You meet those who gladly do right, who remember You in Your ways,” as the prophet Isaiah says. If meeting with269 God, who is goodness itself, sweetness itself, beauty itself, strength itself, glory itself, will not sweeten his service to your soul, nothing in heaven or earth will. Jacob’s meeting with Rachel, and enjoying Rachel, made his hard service easy and delightful to him. And will not the soul’s enjoying God and meeting with God make his service much more easy and delightful? No doubt it will. The Lord will give such sweet help by his Spirit and grace as will make his service joyous and not burdensome, a delight and not a burden, a heaven and not a hell, to believing souls. The confidence of this divine help raised Nehemiah’s spirit far above all the difficulties and discouragements that attended him in the work and service of the Lord, as you+ may see in Neh 2:19, 20: “But when Sanballat270 the Horonite, Tobiah the Ammonite official, and Geshem the Arab heard about this, they mocked us and ridiculed us, saying, ‘What is this you+ are doing? Are you+ rebelling against the king?’ So I answered them and said, ‘The God of heaven will prosper us; therefore we, His servants, will arise and build. But you+ have no portion, right, or claim in Jerusalem.’ ” Ah souls! While you+ are in the very service of the Lord, you+ will find by experience that the God of heaven will prosper you+, support you+, encourage and strengthen you+, and carry you+ through the hardest service with the greatest sweetness and cheerfulness possible. Remember this: God will suit your+ strength to your+ work, and in the hardest service you+ will have the choicest help.

The third remedy against this device of Satan is to dwell on the hard and difficult things that the Lord Jesus Christ has gone through for your+ temporal, spiritual and eternal good. Ah, what a sea of blood, a sea of wrath, of sin, of sorrow and misery the Lord Jesus waded through for your+ internal and eternal good! Christ did not plead, “This cross is too heavy for me to bear, this wrath is too great for me to lie under, this cup (which has in it all the ingredients of divine displeasure) is too bitter for me to sip, let alone to drink its very dregs.” No, Christ does not insist on this. He does not plead the difficulty of the service, but resolutely and bravely wades through all, as the prophet Isaiah shows: “The Lord God has opened My ears, and I have not been rebellious, nor have I turned back. I offered My back to those who struck Me, and My cheeks to those who tore out My beard. I did not hide My face from scorn and spittle.” Christ makes nothing of his Father’s wrath, the burden of your+ sins, the malice271 of Satan and the rage of the world, but sweetly and triumphantly passes through all. Ah souls! If this consideration will not raise your+ spirits above all the discouragements you+ meet with, to acknowledge Christ and his service, and to stick and cleave to Christ and his service, I am afraid nothing will. A soul not stirred by this, not raised and lifted up by this to be resolute and brave in the service of God in spite of all dangers and difficulties, is a soul left by God to much blindness and hardness.

The fourth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider that religious duties, holy and heavenly exercises, are difficult only to the worse, the ignoble part of a saint. They are not difficult to the noble and better part of a saint. To the noble part, the soul and the renewed affections of a saint, holy exercises are a heavenly pleasure and recreation, as the apostle says: “In my inner272 being I delight in God’s law. With my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin.” To the noble part of a saint, Christ’s “yoke is easy” and his “burden is light.” All the commands and ways of Christ (even those that call for plucking out right eyes and cutting off right hands) are joyous and not burdensome to the noble part of a saint. All the ways and services of Christ are pleasantness itself (in the abstract) to the better part of a saint. A saint, so far as he is renewed, is always at his best when he sees most of God, when he tastes most of God, when he is highest in his enjoyment of God, and most warm and lively in the service of God. “Oh,” says the noble part of a saint, “that it might always be like this! Oh, that my strength were the strength of stones, and my flesh bronze, so that my worse part might serve my noble part better, and that I might act with an untiring power in that service which is a pleasure, a paradise to me!”

The fifth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly the great reward and glorious recompense that attend those who cleave to the service of the Lord in the273 face of all difficulties and discouragements. Though the work is hard, yet the wages are great. Heaven will make amends for all; indeed, one hour in heaven will abundantly repay you for cleaving to the Lord and his ways in the face of all difficulties. This carried the apostle through the greatest difficulties: he had an eye to the recompense of the reward; he looked for a house that had foundations, whose builder and maker was God, and for a heavenly country. Indeed, this bore up the spirit of Christ in the face of all difficulties and discouragements: “Looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy set before Him endured the cross, scorning its shame, and sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.”

Christians who would hold on in the service of the Lord must look more on the crown than on the cross, more on their future glory than on their present misery, more on their encouragements than on their discouragements. God’s very service is wages. His ways are strewn with roses, and paved with joy that is unspeakable274 and full of glory, and with peace that passes understanding. Some degree of comfort follows every good action, as heat accompanies fire, as beams and influences issue from the sun. “By them indeed Your servant is warned; in keeping them is great reward.” Not only for keeping them, but in keeping them, there is great reward. The joy, the rest, the refreshing, the comforts, the contentments, the smiles, the inflowings that saints now enjoy in the ways of God are so precious and glorious in their eyes that they would not exchange them for ten thousand worlds. Ah, if the tips are this sweet and glorious before payday comes, what will that glory be with which Christ will crown his saints for cleaving to his service in the face of all difficulties, when he says to his Father, “Here am I, and the children You have given Me”? If there is so much to be had in a wilderness, what then will be had in paradise? etc.

268. The necessity of doing your+ duty appears from this: you+ are his servants by a threefold right. You+ are his servants (jure creationis, jure sustentationis, jure redemptionis) by right of creation, by right of sustaining, and by right of redemption.

269. Isa 64:5. פגעת Paganta is taken in various ways, but most take the word here to mean meeting a soul with that deep compassion and tenderness with which the father of the prodigal met the prodigal. God is pater miserationum [the Father of mercies]; he is all compassion; he is as swift to show mercy as he is slow to anger.

270. Luther spoke excellently to Melanchthon, who was apt to be discouraged by doubts and difficulties and fears of enemies, and so to give up the work they had undertaken: “If the work is not good, why did we ever take it up? If it is good, why should we ever turn from it? Why,” he says, “should we fear the conquered world, when we have Christ the Conqueror on our side?” Isa 40:31. “Since the head was crowned with thorns, it is not fitting that the members should be crowned with rosebuds,” says Zanchius.

271. Godfrey of Bouillon, first king of Jerusalem, refused to be crowned with a crown of gold, saying that it did not become a Christian to wear a crown of gold there, where Christ had once worn a crown of thorns for our salvation.

272. As every flower has its sweet scent, so every good duty carries food in its mouth, that is, comfort in the doing of it. χρηστός, that is, my yoke is a kindly, a gracious, a pleasant, a good and a profitable yoke, the opposite of πονηρός, painful, tedious.

273. Basil speaks of some martyrs who were thrown out naked all night in a cold, frosty season, and were to be burned the next day, and of how they comforted themselves like this: “The winter is sharp, but paradise is sweet; here we shiver with cold, but the bosom of Abraham will make amends for all.”

274. This is praemium ante praemium [a reward before the reward], a sure reward of well-doing: in doing it (not only for doing it) there is great reward, Ps 19:11.

4. False Inferences from Christ’s Work

The fourth device that Satan has to keep souls from holy exercises, from religious services, is,

By leading them to draw false inferences from the blessed and glorious things that Christ has done: that Jesus Christ has done all for us, and therefore there is nothing for us to do but to joy and rejoice. He has perfectly justified us, fulfilled the law, satisfied divine justice, pacified his Father’s wrath, and gone to heaven to prepare a place for us, and in the meantime to intercede for us; and therefore away with praying and mourning and hearing, etc. Ah, what a world of professing Christians Satan has drawn from religious services in these days, by leading them to draw such sad, wild and strange inferences from the sweet and excellent things that the Lord Jesus has done for his beloved ones!

Now the remedies against this device of Satan are as follows.

The first remedy against this device of Satan is to dwell as much on the Scriptures that show you+ the duties and services Christ requires of you+ as on the Scriptures that declare275 to you+ the precious and glorious things that Christ has done for you+. It is a sad and dangerous thing to have two eyes to behold our dignity and privileges, and not one eye to see our duties and services. I should look with one eye on the choice and excellent things that Christ has done for me, to raise my heart to love Christ with the purest love, to joy in Christ with the strongest joy, and to lift up Christ above all, who has made himself my all. And I should look with the other eye on the services and duties that the Scriptures require of those for whom Christ has done such blessed things, as in that word of the apostle: “Do you+ not know that your+ body276 is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you+, whom you+ have received from God? You+ are not your+ own; you+ were bought at a price. Therefore glorify God with your+ body, and in your+ spirit, which are God’s.” And that one277: “Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast and immovable. Always excel in the work of the Lord, because you+ know that your+ labor in the Lord is not in vain.” And that one: “Let us not grow weary in well-doing, for in due278 time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up.” And that of the apostle: “Rejoice at all times; pray without ceasing.” And that in Philippians: “Work out your+ salvation with279 fear and trembling.” And that one: “Do this until I come.” And that one: “Let us consider how to spur one another on to love and good deeds. Let us not neglect meeting together, as some have made a habit,280 but let us encourage one another, and all the more as you+ see the Day approaching.” Now a soul that would not be drawn away by this device of Satan must not look with a squint eye on these blessed Scriptures, and many more of the same kind. He must dwell on them; he must make these Scriptures his chief and choicest companions. This will be a happy means to keep him close to Christ and his service in these times, when many turn their backs on Christ on the pretense of having a great share in the great and glorious things that Christ has done, etc.

The second remedy against this device of Satan is to consider that the great and glorious things Jesus Christ has done, and is doing, for us should be so far from taking us away from religious services and godly performances that they should be the greatest possible motives and encouragements to perform them, as the Scriptures abundantly show. I281 will give only some instances, such as this: “that we, being delivered from the hands of our enemies, may serve Him without fear, in holiness and righteousness before Him all the days of our lives.” Christ has freed you+ from all your+ enemies: from the curse of the law, the reigning, damning power of sin, the wrath of God, the sting of death and the torments of hell. But what is Christ’s end and design in doing these great and marvelous things for his people? It is not that they should throw off duties of righteousness and holiness, but that their hearts may be all the more free and sweet in all holy duties and heavenly services. So the apostle: “I will be their God, and they will be My people. I will be a Father to you+, and you+ will be My sons and daughters, says the Lord Almighty.” (Mark what follows.) “Therefore, beloved, since we have these promises, let us cleanse ourselves from everything that defiles body and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God.” And again: “The grace of God has appeared,282 bringing salvation to everyone. It instructs us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live sensible, upright, and godly lives in the present age, as we await the blessed hope and glorious283 appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ. He gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for Himself a people for His own possession, zealous for good deeds.” Ah souls! I know no arguments that so work you+ to a lively and constant performance of all heavenly services as those drawn from considering the great and glorious things that Christ has done for you+. If such arguments will not take hold of you+ and win you+ over, I do think that throwing hellfire in your+ faces will never do it.

The third remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that those precious souls for whom Jesus Christ284 has done and suffered as much as he has for you+ have been exceedingly active and lively in all religious services and heavenly performances. He did as much and suffered as much for David285 as for you+, and yet who was more in praying and praising God than David? “Seven times a day I praise You.” Who was more in studying and meditating on the word than David? “Your law is my meditation day and night.” You+ may read the same truth as you+ run in Jacob, Moses, Job, Daniel, and in the rest of the holy prophets and apostles, for whom Christ has done as much as for you+. Ah, how all those worthies have abounded in works of righteousness and holiness, to the praise of free grace! Certainly Satan has got the upper hand of those souls who argue like this:286 “Christ has done such and such glorious things for us; therefore we need not make it any matter of care or conscience to do such and such religious services, as men say the word calls for.” If this logic is not from hell, what is? Ah, if the holy prophets and apostles were alive to hear such logic come out of the mouths of those who profess to have a share in the great and glorious things that Jesus Christ has done for his chosen ones, how they would blush to look on such souls! And how their hearts would grieve and break within them to hear the language and observe the actions of such souls!

The fourth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider seriously this: those who do not walk in ways of righteousness and holiness (who do not wait on God in the various duties and services that he commands) cannot have such evidence in their own souls of their righteousness before God, of their fellowship and communion287 with God, of their blessedness here and their happiness hereafter, as those souls have who love and delight in the ways of the Lord, who are always at their best when they are most in the works and service of the Lord. “Little children,” says the apostle, “let no one deceive you+: The one who practices righteousness is righteous, just as Christ is righteous.” “By this,” says the same apostle, “the children of God are distinguished from the children of the devil: Anyone who does not practice righteousness is not of God, nor is anyone288 who does not love his brother.” “If you+ know that He is righteous,” says the same apostle, “you+ also know that everyone who practices righteousness has been born of Him. If anyone says, ‘I know Him,’ but does not keep His commandments, he is a liar, and the truth is not in him. But if anyone keeps His word, the love of God has been truly perfected in him. By this we know that we are in Him: Whoever claims to abide in Him must walk as Jesus289 walked. If we say we have fellowship with Him yet walk in the darkness, we lie and do not practice the truth. But if we walk in the light as He is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus His Son cleanses us from all sin,” says the same apostle. So James in his second chapter: “What good is it, my brothers, if someone claims to have faith, but has no works? Can such faith save him?” That is, it cannot; for as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead. To look after holy and heavenly works is the best way to keep the soul from being deceived and deluded by Satan’s delusions and by sudden flashes of joy and comfort; for holy works are a more tangible and constant pledge of the precious Spirit, begetting and maintaining in the soul a more solid, pure, clear, strong and lasting joy. Ah souls! If you+ would have in yourselves+ a constant and blessed evidence of your+ fellowship with the Father and the Son, and of the truth of grace, and of your+ future happiness, see that you+ cleave close to holy services, and that you+ do not turn your+ backs on religious duties.

The fifth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that290 there are other choice and glorious ends for the saints’ performance of religious duties than the justifying of their persons before God, or the satisfying of the law or justice of God, or the purchasing of the pardon of sin, etc. Namely: to testify to their justification (“a good tree cannot help bearing good fruit”); to testify to their love to God and their sincere obedience to the commands of God; to testify to their deliverance from spiritual bondage; to give evidence of the indwelling291 of the Spirit; to stop the mouths of the worst of men; and to gladden those righteous souls whom God would not have saddened. These, and many other choice ends, are why those who have a share in the glorious works of Christ should, in spite of that, keep close to the holy duties and religious services commanded292 by Christ. And if these considerations will not prevail with you+ to wait on God in holy and heavenly duties, I am afraid that if one rose from the dead, his arguments would not win you+ over, but you+ would hold on in your+ sins and neglect his service, though you+ lost your+ souls forever, etc.

275. Tertullian has this expression of the fullness of the Scriptures (Adoro plenitudinem Scripturarum): “I adore the fullness of the Scripture.” Gregory calls the Scripture (cor & animam Dei) the heart and soul of God. Who then will not dwell on it?

277. 1 Cor 15:58.

278. Gal 6:9.

279. Phil 2:12, 13. 1 Cor 11:26. Heb 10:24, 25.

280. The Jews were much given to turning over the leaves of the Scripture, but they did not weigh their matter, John 5:39. “You+ search the Scriptures”: in the Greek it seems to be indicative rather than imperative.

281. 1 Pet 2:9. Luke 1:74, 75. This I am sure of: all man’s happiness here is his holiness, and his holiness will hereafter be his happiness. Christ has broken the devil’s yoke off our necks for this very reason, that his Father might have better service from our hearts. Compare 2 Cor 6:16, 17, 18 with 7:1.

5. The Fewness and Poverty of the Godly

The fifth device that Satan has to draw souls away from religious services, and to keep souls from holy duties and heavenly performances, is,

By presenting to them the fewness and poverty of those who walk in the ways of God, who hold on in religious practices. Satan says, “Do you+ not see that those who walk in such and such religious ways are the poorest, the293 lowliest and the most despised persons in the world?” This worked on them in John 7: “Then the Pharisees replied, ‘Have you+ also been deceived? Have any of the rulers or Pharisees believed in Him? But this crowd that does not know the law, they are under a curse.’ ”

Now the remedies against this device of Satan are as follows.

The first remedy against this device294 of Satan is to consider that though they are outwardly poor, yet they are inwardly rich; though they are poor in temporal things, yet they are rich in spiritual things. The worth and riches of the saints are inward: “The king’s daughter is all glorious within.” “Listen, my beloved brothers: Has not God chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith and to inherit the kingdom He promised those who love Him?” says James. “I know your poverty, though you are rich!” says John to the church of Smyrna. What if they have little in possession? Yet they have a glorious kingdom in store for them. “Do not be afraid, little flock, for your+ Father is pleased to give you+ the kingdom.” Though saints have little in hand, yet they have much in hope. You+ count those happy, in a worldly sense, who have much coming to them, though they have only a little in possession. And will you+ count the saints miserable because they have little in hand, little in possession, though they have a glorious kingdom coming to them after this? I am sure the poorest saint who breathes would not exchange (were it in his power) what he has in hope and in store for the possession of as many worlds as there are stars in heaven or sands in the sea, etc.

The second remedy against this device of Satan is to consider that in all ages God has had some who were great, rich, wise and honorable, who have chosen his ways and cleaved to his service in the face of all difficulties.295 Though not many wise men have, yet some wise men have; though not many mighty, yet some mighty have; and though not many noble, yet some noble have. Witness Abraham, Jacob, Job, and various kings and others that the Scriptures speak of. And ah, how many we have among ourselves whose souls have cleaved to the Lord, who have swum to his service through the blood of the slain, and who have not counted their lives dear to them, so that they and others might enjoy the holy things of Christ according to the mind and heart of Christ, etc.

The third remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that the spiritual riches of the poorest saints infinitely surpass the temporal riches of all the wicked men in the296 world. Their spiritual riches satisfy them; they can sit down satisfied with the riches of grace that are in Christ, without honors and without riches, etc. “Whoever drinks the water I give him will never thirst.” The riches of poor saints are lasting; they will share bed and board with them; they297 will go with them to prison, to a sickbed, to the grave, indeed to heaven. The spiritual riches of poor saints are as wine to cheer them, as bread to strengthen them, as clothes to warm them, and as armor to protect them. Now all of you+ who know anything know that the riches of this world cannot satisfy the souls of men, and that they are as fading as a flower, or as their owners are, etc.

The fourth remedy against this device is to consider seriously that though the saints, considered comparatively, are few; though they are “a little, little flock,”298 a remnant, “a garden locked up, a spring enclosed,”299 “a fountain sealed”; though they are like the summer gleanings, one from a city and two from a tribe; though they are300 only a handful to a houseful, a spark to a flame, a drop to the ocean; yet consider them simply in themselves, and they are an innumerable number that cannot be counted, as John says: “After this I looked and saw a multitude too large to count, from every nation301 and tribe and people and tongue, standing before the throne and before the Lamb. They were wearing white robes and holding palm branches in their hands.” So Matthew says: “I say302 to you+ that many will come from the east and the west to share the banquet with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven.” So Paul: “But you+ have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem. You+ have come to an innumerable company of angels in joyful assembly, to the congregation of the firstborn, enrolled in heaven. You+ have come to God the Judge of all, to the spirits of the righteous made perfect.”

The fifth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider seriously that it will be but as a day before these poor despised saints shine brighter than the sun in its glory. It will not be long before you+ will wish, “Oh, that we were now among the poor, lowly, despised ones, in the day that God comes to gather up his jewels!” It will not be long before these poor, few saints are lifted up on their thrones to judge the multitude, the world, as the apostle says: “Do you+ not know that the saints will judge the world?” And in that day, oh, how the great and the rich, the303 learned and the noble will wish that they had lived and spent their days with these few, poor, despised people in the service of the Lord! Oh, how this wicked world will curse the day that they ever had such base thoughts of the poor, lowly saints, and that their poverty became a stumbling block to keep them from the ways of holiness! I have read of Ingo, an ancient king of the Draves, who, making a stately feast, appointed his nobles, at that time pagans, to sit in the hall below, and commanded certain poor Christians to be brought up into his presence chamber, to sit with him at his table and eat and drink of his kingly fare. When many wondered at this, he said that he counted Christians, however poor, a greater ornament at his table, and more worthy of his company, than the greatest peers unconverted to the Christian faith; for while these might be thrust down to hell, those might be his companions and fellow princes in heaven. You+ know how to apply it. Although you+ sometimes see the stars by their reflection in a puddle, or in the bottom of a well, indeed, in a stinking ditch, yet the stars have their place in heaven. So, though you+ see a godly man in a poor, miserable, low, despised condition as to the things of this world, yet he is fixed in heaven, in the region of heaven. “He raised us up,” says the apostle, “and seated us with Him in the heavenly realms in Christ Jesus.” Oh, therefore, say to your+ own souls (when they begin to turn from the ways of Zion because of the poverty and fewness of those who walk in them), “The day is at hand when these few, poor, despised saints will shine in glory, when they will judge this world, and when all the wicked of the world will wish that they were in their condition, and would give ten thousand worlds (were it in their power) just to have the honor and happiness of waiting on those whom they have neglected and despised in this world for their poverty and fewness.”

The sixth and last remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that there will come a time, even in this304 life, in this world, when the reproach and contempt now cast on the ways of God, because of the poverty and fewness of those who walk in them, will be quite taken away. God will do it by making those the head who have been the tail for days without number, and by raising to much outward riches, prosperity and glory those who have been like outcasts because of their poverty and fewness. John, speaking of the glory of the church, the new Jerusalem that came down from heaven, in Revelation 21, tells us: “By its light the nations of those who are saved will walk, and into it the kings of the earth will bring their glory.” So the prophet Isaiah: “They will bring their sons from afar, and their silver and gold with305 them,” v. 9. “Instead of bronze I will bring gold; I will bring silver in place of iron, bronze instead of wood, and iron instead of stones,” v. 17. And so the prophet Zechariah speaks, Zech 14:14: “And the wealth of all the surrounding nations will be collected: gold, silver, and apparel in great abundance.” The Lord has promised “that the meek will inherit the earth,” and that heaven and earth will pass away before one jot or the smallest stroke of his word goes unfulfilled. Ah, poor saints! Now some push hard against you+, others look askance at you+, others shut the door against you+, others turn their backs on you+; and most men (except a few who live much in God and are filled with the riches of Christ) either neglect you+ or despise you+ because of your+ poverty. But the day is coming when you+ will be lifted up above the dunghill, when you+ will exchange poverty for riches, your+ rags for robes, your+ reproach for a crown of honor, your+ infamy for glory, even in this world.

And this is not all: God will also mightily increase the number of his chosen ones; multitudes will be converted to him. “Who has heard306 of such as this? Who has seen such things? Can a country be born in a day or a nation be delivered in an instant? Yet as soon as Zion was in labor, she gave birth to her children. And they will bring all your+ brothers from all the nations as a gift to the Lord on307 horses and chariots and wagons, on mules and camels, to My holy mountain Jerusalem,” says the Lord, “just as the Israelites bring an offering in a clean vessel to the house of the Lord.” Does not the Scripture say “that the kingdoms of308 this world must become the kingdoms of our Lord”? Has not God given Christ “the nations” and “the ends of the earth” for his possession? Has not the Lord said “that in the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord309 will be established as the chief of the mountains; it will be raised above the hills, and all nations will stream to it”? Please read310 and meditate on the sixtieth chapter of Isaiah, and the sixty-sixth chapter, and the first five verses of the second chapter of Isaiah, and there you+ will find the multitudes that will be converted to Christ. And oh, that you+ would be mighty in believing and in wrestling with God, that he would hasten the day of his glory, so that the reproach now on his people and ways may cease!

6. The Example of the World

The sixth device that Satan has to keep souls away from religious services is,

By presenting before them the examples311 of the greatest part of the world, who walk in the ways of their own hearts and who make light and slight of the ways of the Lord. “Why,” says Satan, “do you not see that the great and the rich, the noble and the honorable, the learned and the wise, indeed the greatest number of men, never trouble themselves about such and such ways? Why then should you be odd and fastidious? You would do far better to do as most do,” etc.

Now the remedies against this device of Satan are as follows.

The first remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly those Scriptures that speak directly against following the sinful examples of men, such as that in Exodus: “You shall not312 follow a multitude in wrongdoing. When you testify in a lawsuit, do not pervert justice by siding with the multitude.” The multitude are generally ignorant and do not know the way of the Lord; therefore they speak evil of what they do not know. They are envious and maliciously set against the service and way of God, and therefore they cannot speak well of the ways of God. “This way is everywhere spoken against,” they said. So in Num 16: “Separate yourselves from them, and come out from among them.” So the apostle: “Have no fellowship with the fruitless deeds of darkness.” So Solomon: “Do not set foot313 on the path of the wicked”; “Leave the foolish behind, and you will live.” Those who walk with the most will perish with the most. Those who do as the most do will before long suffer with the most; those who live as the most live must die with the most, and go to hell with the most.

The second remedy against this device of Satan is to consider seriously that if you+ will sin with the multitude, all the angels in heaven and men on earth cannot keep you+ from suffering314 with the multitude. If you+ will be wicked with them, you+ must unavoidably be miserable with them. Say to your soul, “O my soul, if you will sin with the multitude, you must be shut out of heaven with the multitude; you must be cast down to hell with the multitude,” etc. “Then I heard another voice from heaven say: ‘Come out of her, My people, so that you+ will not share in her sins or contract any of her plagues.’” Come out in affection, in action, and in habitation; otherwise the infection of sin will bring on you+ the infliction of punishment. So says the wise man: “He who walks with the wise will become wise, but the companion of fools will be destroyed,” or, as the Hebrew315 has it, will be broken in pieces. Multitudes may help you into sin; indeed, one may draw you into sin; but it is not multitudes that can help you to escape punishment. You+ may see this in Moses and Aaron, who were provoked to sin by the multitude, yet were shut out of the pleasant land and fell by a hand of justice as well as others.

The third remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly the worth and excellence of your immortal soul. Your soul is a jewel worth more316 than heaven and earth. The loss of your soul is incomparable, irreparable, and irrecoverable; if that is lost, all is lost, and you are undone forever. Is it madness and folly for a man to kill himself for company? And is it not greater madness or folly to break the neck of your soul, and to damn it for company? Suspect that way in which you see multitudes walking, the multitude being a stream that you must row hard against, or you will be carried into that gulf out of which angels cannot deliver you. Is it not better to walk in a narrow way alone than to wander into crooked ways with company? Surely it is better to go to heaven alone than to hell with company. I might add other things, but these may suffice for the present; and I am afraid that if these arguments do not stir you+, other arguments will work little on you+.

7. Vain Thoughts in Duty

The seventh device that Satan has to keep souls from holy and heavenly services, is,

By casting in a multitude of vain thoughts while the soul is seeking God, or waiting on God. By this device he has cooled some men’s spirits in heavenly services, and drawn many precious317 souls away (at least for a time) from religious exercises. I have no heart to hear, no heart to pray, no delight in reading, nor in the company of the saints, etc. Satan so dogs and follows my soul, and is always casting in such a multitude of vain thoughts concerning God, the world, and my own soul, etc., that I even tremble to think of waiting on God in any religious service. Oh, the vain thoughts that Satan casts in so sour my soul, and so grieve, vex, perplex, and distract my soul, that they even make me weary of holy duties, yes, of my very life! Oh, I cannot be so raised and enraptured, so heated and melted, so revived and set free, so comforted and refreshed as I should be, as I might be, and as I would be in religious services, because of the multitude of vain thoughts that Satan is injecting, or casting into my soul, etc.

Now the remedies against this device of Satan are as follows.

The first remedy against this device318 of Satan is to have your+ hearts strongly moved by the greatness, holiness, majesty, and glory of the God before whom you+ stand, and with whom your+ souls commune in religious services. Oh, let your+ souls be greatly moved by the presence, purity, and majesty of the God before whom you stand! A man would be afraid of playing with a feather when he is speaking to a king. Ah, when men have poor, low, light, slight, etc. thoughts of God in their drawing near to God, they tempt the devil to stir himself, and to cast in a multitude of vain thoughts to disturb and distract the soul in its waiting on God. Nothing will contribute so much to keeping out vain thoughts as to look on God as an omniscient God, an omnipresent God, an omnipotent God, a God full of all glorious perfections, a God whose majesty, purity, and glory will not allow him to look on the least iniquity. The reason the blessed saints and glorious angels in heaven do not have so much as one vain thought is that they are greatly moved by the greatness, holiness, majesty, purity, and glory of God.

The second remedy against this device of Satan is to be determined in religious services, notwithstanding all the wandering thoughts the soul319 is troubled with. It will be a sweet help against them for the soul to be resolute in waiting on God, whether it is troubled with vain thoughts or not, and to say, “Well, I will go on praying, and go on hearing, and go on meditating, and go on keeping fellowship with the saints.” Many precious souls can say from experience that when their souls have been determined in their waiting on God, Satan has left them, and has not been so busy vexing their souls with vain thoughts. Satan may perceive that all320 the trifling vain thoughts he casts into the soul only vex the soul into greater diligence, carefulness, watchfulness, and determination in holy and heavenly services, and that the soul loses nothing of its zeal, piety, and devotion, but doubles its care, diligence, and earnestness. When he does, he often stops throwing in his trifles and vain thoughts, as he stopped tempting Christ when Christ was determined in resisting his temptations.

The third remedy against this device of Satan is to consider that the vain and trifling thoughts that are cast321 into our souls when we are waiting on God in this or that religious service are not sins upon our souls, if they are not cherished and indulged, but abhorred, resisted, and disowned. They may be troubles to our minds, but they will not be put to our account, nor keep mercies and blessings from being enjoyed by us. Suppose a soul can in uprightness look God in the face and say, “Lord, when I draw near to you, a world of vain thoughts crowds in on me, disturbing my soul, weakening my faith, and lessening my comfort and spiritual strength. Oh, these are my clog, my burden, my torment, my hell! Oh, execute justice on these! Free me from these, so that I may serve you with more freedom, singleness, spirituality, and sweetness of spirit.” Then these thoughts may vex that soul, but they will not harm that soul, nor keep a blessing from that soul. If vain thoughts that are resisted and lamented could stop the current of mercy and make a soul unhappy, there would be no one on earth who would ever taste mercy, or be everlastingly happy, etc.

The fourth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that watching against sinful thoughts, resisting sinful thoughts, lamenting and weeping over sinful thoughts, carries322 with it the sweetest and strongest evidence of the truth and power of grace, and of the sincerity of your+ hearts, and is the readiest and surest way to be rid of them. Many low and carnal considerations may move men to watch their words, their lives, their actions, such as the hope of gain, or the wish to please friends or to get a name in the world, and many other such considerations. Oh, but to watch our thoughts, to weep and lament over them, etc., must come from some noble, spiritual, and inward principle, such as love to God, a holy fear of God, a holy care and delight to please the Lord, etc. The schoolmen rightly observe that outward sins are of greater323 infamy, but inward heart sins are of greater guilt, as we see in the devils. Nothing shows a man to have been thoroughly and genuinely worked upon so much as his having his thoughts324 brought into obedience, as the apostle says. Grace has grown to a very great height in the soul where it prevails to the subduing of the vain thoughts that walk up and down in the soul. Well, though you+ cannot be325 rid of them, yet resist and oppose their first risings. When sinful thoughts arise, then think this way: The Lord takes notice of these thoughts; he knows them “from afar,” as the psalmist says. He knew Herod’s bloody thoughts, and Judas’s betraying thoughts, and the Pharisees’ cruel and blasphemous thoughts from afar. Oh, think this way: All these sinful thoughts defile and pollute the soul; they deface and spoil much of the inward beauty and glory of the soul. If I commit this or that sin to which my thoughts incline me, then either I must326 repent, or not repent. If I repent, it will cost me more grief, sorrow, shame, heartbreak, and soul-bleeding before my conscience is quieted, divine justice pacified, my comfort and joy restored, my evidences cleared, and my pardon sealed in the court of conscience, than the imagined profit or seeming sensual pleasure can be worth. “What fruit did you+ reap at that time from the things of which you+ are now ashamed?”

If I never repent, oh, then my sinful327 thoughts will be the scorpions that will eternally vex me, the rods that will eternally lash me, the thorns that will everlastingly prick me, the dagger that will be eternally stabbing me, the worm that will be forever gnawing me. Oh, therefore watch against them, be constant in resisting them, and in lamenting and weeping over them, and then they will not hurt you, though they may trouble you for a time. And remember this: he who does this does more than the most glittering and blustering hypocrite in the world does.

The fifth remedy against this device328 of Satan is to labor more and more to be filled with the fullness of God, and to be enriched with all spiritual and heavenly things. What is the reason that the angels in heaven do not have so much as an idle thought? It is because they are filled with the fullness of God. Take it as a truth proved by experience: the more the soul is filled with the fullness of God, and enriched with spiritual and heavenly things, the less room there is in that soul for vain thoughts. The fuller the vessel is of wine, the less room there is for water. Oh, lay up much of God, of Christ, of precious promises, and of choice experiences in your+ hearts, and then you+ will be less troubled with vain thoughts! “The good man brings good things out of the good treasure329 of his heart.”

The sixth remedy against this device of Satan is to keep up holy and spiritual affections, for as your affections are, so will your thoughts be. “Oh,330 how I love Your law! All day long it is my meditation.” What we love most, we muse on most. “When I awake, I am still with You.” What we greatly like, we will greatly think on. Those who are frequent in their love to God and his law will be frequent in thinking of God and his law. A child will not forget his mother.

The seventh remedy against this device331 of Satan is to avoid a multiplicity of worldly business. Oh, do not let the world take up your+ hearts and thoughts at other times! Souls that are torn in pieces with the cares of the world will always be vexed and tormented with vain thoughts in all their approaches to God. Vain thoughts will always be crowding in on him who lives in a crowd of business. The stars that have the smallest circuit are nearest the pole, and the men who are least entangled with business are commonly nearest to God.

8. Resting in Performances

The eighth device that Satan has to keep souls from religious services, from holy performances, is,

By leading them to rest in their performances: to rest in prayer, and to rest in hearing, reading and the communion332 of saints, etc. And when Satan has drawn the soul to rest on the service done, then he will help the soul to reason like this: “Why, you might as well never pray as pray and rest in prayer; as well never hear as hear and rest in hearing; as well never be in the communion of saints as be in it and rest in the communion of saints.” By this device he stops many souls in their heavenly race, and draws poor souls away from the services that should be their joy and crown.

Now the remedies against this device of Satan are as follows.

The first remedy against this device of Satan is to dwell much on the imperfections and weaknesses that333 attend your+ choicest services. Oh, the spots, the blots, the blemishes that are to be seen on the face of our fairest duties! When you have done all you can, you need to close it all with this: “Do not bring Your servant into judgment, O Lord, because of the weaknesses that cling to my best services.” We may all334 say with the church, “All our righteous acts are like filthy rags.” If God were strict to mark what is done amiss in our best actions, we would be undone. Oh, the water that is mingled with our wine, the dross that clings to our gold!

The second remedy against this device of Satan is to consider the powerlessness and inability of any of your+ best services to comfort, refresh and bear up your+ souls divinely from fainting and sinking in days of trouble, when darkness is all around you+, when God says to you+, as he once did335 to the Israelites, “Go and cry out to the gods you+ have chosen. Let them save you+ in your+ time of trouble.” So when God says in the day of your+ troubles, “Go to your+ prayers, to your+ hearing and to your+ fasting, etc., and see if they can help you+, if they can support you+, if they can deliver you+”: if God in that day only withholds the influence of his grace from you, your former services will be but poor heart-medicines to comfort you. And then you must and will cry out, “Oh, none but Christ, none336 but Christ! Oh, my prayers are not Christ, my hearing is not Christ, my fasting is not Christ, etc.” Oh, one smile of Christ, one glimpse of Christ, one good word from Christ, one nod of love from Christ in the day of trouble and darkness will revive and refresh the soul more than all your+ former services, in which your+ souls rested as if they were the bosom of Christ, which should be the only center of our souls. Christ is the crown of crowns, the glory of glories, and the heaven of heaven.

The third remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that good things rested on will as surely undo us and everlastingly destroy us as the greatest enormities we can commit. Those souls who, after they have done all, do not look up as high as Christ, and rest and center in Christ alone, laying down their services at the footstool of Christ, must lie down in sorrow; their bed is prepared for them in hell. “Behold, all337 you+ who kindle a fire, who array yourselves+ with firebrands, walk in the light of your+ fire and of the firebrands you+ have lit! This is what you+ will receive from My hand: You+ will lie down in sorrow.” Is it good to dwell with everlasting burnings, with a devouring fire? If it is, then go on resting in your+ duties; if not, then see that you+ center only in the bosom of Christ.

The fourth and last remedy against this device of Satan is to dwell much on the necessity and excellence of that resting place which God has provided for you+ above all other resting places. He himself is your+ resting place; his free mercy and love is your+ resting place; the pure, glorious, matchless and spotless righteousness of Christ is your+ resting place. Ah, it is sad to think that most men have forgotten their resting place, as the Lord complains: “My people are lost sheep; their shepherds have led them338 astray, causing them to roam the mountains. They have wandered from mountain to hill; they have forgotten their resting place.” So poor souls who do not see the excellence of the resting place that God has appointed for their souls to lie down in wander from mountain to hill, from one duty to another; here they will rest, and there they will rest. But souls who see the excellence of the resting place that God has provided for them will say, “Farewell prayer, farewell hearing, farewell fasting, etc. I will rest no more in you+, but now will rest only in the bosom of Christ, the love of Christ, the righteousness of Christ.”

332. Isa 58:1, 2, 3. Zech 7:4, 5, 6. Matt 6:2. Rom 2:17.

333. “Pride and high confidence are most apt to creep in upon duties well done,” says one.

334. Isa 64:6.

335. Judg 10:14.

Part III. Devices to Keep Souls Doubting

1. Poring on Sin More than on the Savior

The third thing to be shown is the various devices that Satan has to keep souls in a sad, doubting, questioning, and comfortless condition.339

Though Satan can never rob a believer of his crown, yet such is his malice and envy that he will leave no stone unturned, no means untried, to rob believers of their comfort and peace, to make their life a burden and a hell to them, to cause them to spend their days in sorrow and mourning, in sighing and complaining, in doubting and questioning: surely we have no share in Christ; our graces are not true; our hopes are the hopes of hypocrites; our confidence is only presumption; our enjoyments are only delusions, etc.

I will show you this in some particulars.

The first device that Satan has to keep souls in a sad, doubting, and questioning condition, and so to make their life a hell, is,

BY causing them to be always poring340 and musing on sin, to think on their sins more than their Savior; yes, so to think on their sins as to forget, yes, to neglect their Savior, so that, as the psalmist says, “The Lord is not in all their thoughts.” Their eyes are so fixed on their disease that they cannot see the remedy, though it is near; and they so muse on their debts that they have neither mind nor heart to think of their surety, etc.

Now the first remedy against this device of Satan is,

For weak believers to consider that though Jesus Christ has not freed them from the presence of sin, yet he341 has freed them from the damning power of sin. It is most true that sin and grace were never born together, and sin and grace will not die together; yet while a believer breathes in this world, they must live together; they must keep house together. Christ in this life will not free any believer from the presence of any one sin, though he does free every believer from the damning power of every sin: “There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, who do not walk according to the flesh but according to the Spirit.” The law cannot condemn a believer, for Christ has fulfilled it for him. Divine justice cannot condemn him, for Christ has satisfied it. His sins cannot condemn him, for they are pardoned in the blood of Christ. And his own conscience (on righteous grounds) cannot condemn him, because Christ, who is greater than his conscience, has acquitted him, etc.

The second remedy against this device of Satan is to consider that though Jesus Christ has not freed you from the harassing and vexing power of sin, yet he has freed you from the reign and342 dominion of sin. You say that sin so harasses and vexes you that you cannot think of God, nor go to God, nor speak with God. Oh, but remember, it is one thing for sin to harass and vex you, and another thing for sin to reign and have dominion over you. “For sin shall not have dominion over you+, because you+ are not under law, but under grace.” Sin may rebel, but it will never reign in any saint. It goes with sin in the regenerate as with those beasts that Daniel speaks of: “their dominion was removed,343 but they were granted an extension of life for a season and a time.”

Now sin reigns in the soul when the soul willingly and readily obeys it, and submits to its commands, as subjects actively obey and embrace the commands of their prince. The commands344 of a king are readily embraced and obeyed by his subjects, but the commands of a tyrant are embraced and obeyed unwillingly. All the service done to a tyrant comes from violence, and not from obedience. A free and willing subjection to the commands of sin shows the soul to be under the reign and dominion of sin; but from this plague, this hell, Christ frees all believers. Sin cannot say of a believer what the centurion said of his servant: “I tell one to go, and he goes; and another to come, and he comes. I tell my servant to do something, and he does it.” No, the heart of a saint rises against the commands of sin; and when sin would carry his soul to the devil, he drags his sin before the Lord and cries out for justice. “Lord,” says the believing soul, “sin plays the tyrant, the devil, in me. It would have me do what works against your holiness as well as against my happiness, against your honor and glory as well as my comfort and peace. Therefore do me justice, you righteous Judge of heaven and earth, and let this tyrant sin die for it,” etc.

The third remedy against this device of Satan is constantly to keep one eye on the promises of the remission of sin,345 as well as the other eye on the inward operations of sin. It is most certainly true that God will graciously pardon to his people the sins that he will not fully subdue in his people in this life. Paul prays three times, that is, often, to be delivered from the thorn in the flesh, and all he can get is, “My grace is sufficient for you.” “I will graciously pardon you what I will not conquer in you,”346 says God. “And I will cleanse them from all the iniquity they have committed against Me, and will pardon all their sins of rebellion against Me.” “I, yes I, am He who blots out your transgressions for My own sake and remembers your sins no more.” Ah, you+ lamenting souls, who spend your+ days sighing and groaning under the sense and burden of your+ sins, why do you+ deal so unkindly with God, and so injuriously with your+ own souls, as not to cast an eye on those precious promises of the remission of sin, which may hold up and refresh your+ spirits in the darkest night, and under the heaviest burden of sin?

The fourth remedy against this device of Satan is to look on all your sins as charged to the account of Christ, as debts that the Lord Jesus has fully satisfied. And indeed, if there were but one farthing of the debt unpaid that Christ was bound to satisfy, it would not have agreed with the unspotted justice of God to let him come into heaven and sit down at his own right hand. But since all our debts have been discharged by his death, we are freed, and he is exalted to sit down at the right hand of his Father, which is the height of his glory, and the greatest pledge of our happiness. “God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our347 behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God,” says the apostle. All our sins were made to meet on Christ, as that evangelical prophet has it: “He was pierced for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was upon Him, and by His stripes we are healed. We all like sheep have gone astray, each one has turned to his own way; and the Lord has laid upon Him the iniquity of us all”; or, as the Hebrew has it, he has made the iniquity of us all to meet in him. In law, we know, all the debts of the wife are charged to the husband. The wife says to one and to another, “If348 I owe you anything, go to my husband.” So a believer may say to the law, and to the justice of God, “If I owe you anything, go to my Christ, who has stood surety for me. I must not sit down discouraged at the thought of those debts that Christ has fully satisfied to the last farthing.” Would it not show much weakness (I had almost said much madness) for a debtor to sit down discouraged when he looks over the debts that his surety has readily, freely, and fully satisfied? The sense of his surety’s great love should bind a man for349 ever to love and honor his surety, and to bless the hand that has paid the debt and crossed out the account, etc. But to sit down discouraged when the debt is satisfied is a sin that calls for repentance, etc.

Christ has cleared all reckonings between God and us. You remember the scapegoat: “all the iniquities350 of the Israelites and all their rebellious acts in regard to all their sins” were confessed351 over its head and put on it, “and the goat will carry on itself all their iniquities,” etc. Why, the Lord Jesus is that blessed scapegoat on whom all our sins were laid, and who alone has carried our sins away into the land of forgetfulness, where they will never, never be remembered again. A believer under the guilt of his sin may look the Lord in the face, and sweetly plead with him this way: “It is true, Lord, I owed you352 much, but your Son was my ransom, my redemption. His blood was the price; he was my surety, and undertook to answer for my sins. I know you must be satisfied, and Christ has satisfied you to the last farthing, not for himself, for what sins did he have of his own? But for me: they were my debts that he satisfied. Be pleased to look over the book, and you will find that it is crossed out by your own hand, on this very ground, that Christ has suffered and satisfied for them.”

The fifth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly the reasons why the Lord is pleased to have his people exercised, troubled, and vexed with the operations of sinful corruptions;353 and they are these: partly to keep them humble and low in their own eyes; and partly to set them on the use of all divine helps by which sin may be subdued and mortified; and partly that they may live on Christ for the perfecting of the work of sanctification;354 and partly to wean them from things below, and to make them heartsick at their absence from Christ, and to keep alive in them a tender compassion toward others who are subject to the same weaknesses as they are; and that they may distinguish between a state of grace and a state of glory, and that heaven may be the sweeter to them in the end. Now since the Lord, for these weighty reasons, allows his people to be exercised and harassed with the operations of sinful corruptions, oh, then let no believer speak, write, or conclude bitter things against his own soul and its comforts because sin troubles and vexes his righteous soul, etc. Let him rather lay his hand on his mouth and be silent, because the Lord will have it so, on such weighty grounds as the soul is not able to withstand.

The sixth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that believers must repent of their being355 discouraged by their sins. Their being discouraged by their sins will cost them many a prayer, many a tear, and many a groan, because their discouragements under sin flow from ignorance and unbelief. They spring from their ignorance of the riches, freeness, fullness, and everlastingness of God’s love; and from their ignorance of the power, glory, sufficiency, and efficacy of the death and sufferings of the Lord Jesus Christ; and from their ignorance of the worth, glory, fullness, largeness, and completeness of the righteousness of Jesus Christ; and from their ignorance of the real, close, spiritual, glorious, and inseparable union that exists between Christ and their precious souls. Ah, if precious souls knew and believed the truth of these things as they should, they would not sit down dejected and overwhelmed under the sense and operations of sin, etc.

339. The blessed Bradford, in one of his letters, says this: “O Lord, at times it seems to me that I feel it so with me, as if there were no difference between my heart and the wicked. I have a blind mind, as they do; a proud, stubborn, rebellious, hard heart, as they do,” and so he goes on, etc.

340. A Christian should wear Christ in his bosom as a flower of delight, for he is a whole paradise of delight. He who does not think on Christ more than his sin can never be as thankful and fruitful as he should be.

341. Peccata enim non nocent, si non placent: my sins do not hurt me, if they do not please me. Sin is like that wild fig tree, or the ivy in the wall: cut off stump, trunk, bough, and branches, and yet some root or other will sprout out again until the wall is pulled down. Rom 8:1.

342. The early Christians chose rather to be thrown to lions without than left to lusts within. Ad leonem magis quam ad lenonem, says Tertullian. Rom 6:14.

344. It is a sign that sin has not gained your+ consent, but has committed a rape on your+ souls, when you+ cry out to God. If the violated virgin under the law cried out, she was guiltless (Deut 22:27). So when sin plays the tyrant over the soul, and the soul cries out, it is guiltless; those sins will not be charged to the soul.

345. Isa 44:22. Mic 7:18, 19. Col 2:13, 14. The promises of God are a precious book; every leaf drops myrrh and mercy.

346. Though the weak Christian cannot open, read, and apply them, Christ can and will apply them to their souls. Jer 33:8. Isa 43:25. מחה, a Hebrew participle, denotes a constant, a continued act of God: I, I am he, blotting out your transgressions, today, and tomorrow, etc.

348. Christ has the greatest worth and wealth in him. As the worth and value of many pieces of silver is in one piece of gold, so all the excellencies scattered throughout created things are united in Christ.

349. The whole volume of perfections that is spread through heaven and earth is summed up in him.
