351. Christ is (Canalis gratiae) the channel of grace from God.

352. The bloods of Abel, for so the Hebrew has it (as if the blood of one Abel had as many tongues as drops), cried for vengeance against sin; but the blood of Christ cries louder for the pardon of sin.

353. Augustine says that the first, second, and third virtue of a Christian is humility.

354. Lilmod lelammed, we learn so that we may teach, is a proverb among the rabbis. After the Trojans had been wandering and tossing up and down the Mediterranean Sea, as soon as they caught sight of Italy, they cried out with exulting joy, “Italy, Italy!” So will saints when they come to heaven.

355. God never gave a believer a new heart so that it would always lie bleeding, and always be rent and torn in pieces with discouragements.

2. False Definitions of Grace

The second device that Satan has to keep souls in a sad, doubting, and questioning condition, is,

BY leading them to make false definitions of their graces. Satan knows that as false definitions of sin wrong the soul one way, so false definitions of grace wrong the soul another way.

I will give an instance only in faith. Oh, how Satan labors with all his might to lead men to make false definitions of faith! Some he leads to define faith too high: that it is a full assurance of the love of God to a man’s soul in particular, or a full persuasion of the pardon and remission of a man’s own sins in particular. Satan says, “Why do you talk of faith? Faith is an assurance of the love of God, and of the pardon of sin, and this you do not have. You know you are far from this; therefore you have no faith.” And by drawing men to make such a false definition of faith, he keeps them in a sad, doubting, and questioning condition, and makes them spend their days in sorrow and sighing, so that tears are their drink, and sorrow is their food, and sighing is their work all the day long, etc.

The philosophers say there are eight degrees of heat; we discern three. Now if a man were to define heat only by the highest degree, then all the other degrees would be cast out from being heat. So if men define faith only by the highest degrees, by assurance of the love of God, and of the pardon of his sins in particular, what will become of the lesser degrees of faith?

If a man were to define a living man only by the highest and strongest signs of life, such as laughing, leaping, running, working, walking, etc., would not many thousands who groan under inward and outward weaknesses, and who cannot laugh, nor leap, nor run, nor work, nor walk, be found dead men by such a definition, though we know them to be alive? It is so here, and you know how to apply it, etc.

Now the remedies against this device of Satan are as follows.

The first remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that there may be true faith, yes, great measures of faith, where there is no assurance. The Canaanite woman in the Gospel had strong faith, yet no assurance that we read of. “I have written these things to you+” (says John) “who believe in the name of the Son of God, so that you+ may know that you+ have eternal life, and so that you+ may believe in the name of the Son of God.” In these words you see that they did believe, and had eternal life: in respect of the purpose and promise of God; and in respect of its seeds and beginnings in their souls; and in respect of Christ their head, who sits in heaven as a public person, representing all his chosen ones: “God raised us up with Christ356 and seated us with Him in the heavenly realms in Christ Jesus.” And yet they did not know that they had eternal life. It is one thing to have a right to heaven, and another thing to know it; it is one thing to be beloved, and another thing for a man to know that he is beloved. It is one thing for God to write a man’s name in the book of life, and another thing for God to tell a man that his name is written in the book of life, and to say to him, “Rejoice that your name is written in heaven.”

So Paul: “In Him you+ also trusted, after357 you+ heard the word of truth, the gospel of your+ salvation; in Him also, after you+ believed, you+ were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit.”

So Micah: “Do not gloat over me, my enemy! Though I have fallen, I will arise; though I sit in darkness, the Lord will be my light. Because I have sinned against Him, I must endure the indignation of the Lord,” etc.; or “the sad countenance of God,” as the Hebrew has it. This soul had no assurance, for he sits in darkness, and was under the sad countenance of God; and yet he had strong faith, as appears in these words: “Though I have fallen, I will arise; though I sit in darkness, the Lord will be my light. … He will bring me out into the light, and I will see His righteousness.” Let this suffice for the first answer.

The second remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that God in the Scriptures defines358 faith otherwise. God defines faith as a receiving of Christ: “To all who did receive Him, He gave the right to become359 children of God, to those who believed in His name.” He defines it as a cleaving of the soul to God, though no joy, but afflictions, attend the soul. Yes, the Lord defines faith as a coming to God in Christ,360 and often as a resting, and staying, or rolling of the soul on Christ. It is safest and sweetest to define both vices and graces as God defines them. This is the only way to settle the soul, and to secure it against all the wiles of men and devils, who labor by false definitions of grace to keep precious souls in a doubting, staggering, and languishing condition, and so make their lives a burden, a hell to them.

The third remedy against this device of Satan is to consider seriously that there may be true faith where there361 are many doubts. Witness those frequent sayings of Christ to his disciples: “You+ of little faith, why are you+ so afraid?”362 Persons may be truly believing who nevertheless are at times doubting. In the same persons (whom the Scriptures mentioned above speak of) you may see their faith commended and their doubts condemned, which necessarily presupposes that both are present.

The fourth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that assurance is an effect of faith; therefore it cannot be faith. The cause cannot be the effect, nor the root the fruit. As the effect flows from the cause, the fruit from the root, the stream from the fountain, so assurance flows from faith. I will prove this truth as follows.

The assurance of our salvation and of the pardon of sin arises primarily from the witness of the Spirit of God that363 we are the children of God. And the Spirit never witnesses this until we are believers, “for we are sons by faith in364 Christ Jesus.” Therefore assurance is not faith, but follows it, as the effect follows the cause.

Again, no man can be assured and persuaded of his salvation until he is united to Christ, until he is grafted into Christ; and a man cannot be grafted into Christ until he has faith. He must first be grafted into Christ by faith before he can have assurance of his salvation, which clearly shows that assurance is not faith, but an effect and fruit of faith, etc.

Again, faith cannot be lost, but assurance may; therefore assurance is not faith. Though assurance is a precious365 flower in the garden of a saint, and is infinitely more sweet and delightful to the soul than all outward comforts366 and contentments, yet it is only a flower that is subject to fade, and to lose its freshness367 and beauty, as saints find by sad experience, etc.

Again, a man must first have faith before he can have assurance; therefore assurance is not faith. And that a man must first have faith before he can have assurance is clear from this: a man must first be saved before he can be assured of his salvation, for he cannot be assured of what does not exist; and a man must first have a saving faith before he can be saved by faith, for he cannot be saved by what he does not have. Therefore a man must first have faith before he can have assurance, and so it plainly follows that assurance is not faith, etc.

361. Matt 6:30 ch. 14:31 and ch. 16:8.

362. Luke 12:28.

363. Eph 1:13. Gal 5:6.

367. There are many thousands of precious souls, of whom this world is not worthy, who have the faith of reliance and yet lack assurance and its effects, such as high joy, glorious peace, and vehement longings for the coming of Christ.

3. Adverse Providences

The third device that Satan has to keep the soul in a sad, doubting, and questioning condition, is,

BY leading the soul to draw false368 inferences from the adverse actings of providence. Satan says, “Do you not see how providence thwarts your prayers, and thwarts your desires, your tears, your hopes, your endeavors? Surely, if his love were toward you, if his soul delighted and took pleasure in you, he would not deal with you this way,” etc.

Now the remedies against this device of Satan are as follows.

The first remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that many things may be contrary to our desires that are not contrary to our good. Abraham, Jacob, David, Job, Moses, Jeremiah,369 Jonah, Paul, etc. met with many things that were contrary to their desires and endeavors, that were not contrary to their good, as all know who have wisely compared their desires and endeavors with God’s actings. Medicine often works contrary to the patient’s desires when it does not work contrary to his good. I remember a story of a godly man who had a great desire to go to France. As he was going to take ship, he broke his leg; and it pleased providence so to order it that the ship he would have gone in was wrecked at that very time, and not a man saved; and so by breaking a bone his life was saved. Though providence worked against his desires, yet it did not work against his good, etc.

The second remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that the hand of God may be against a man when the love and heart of God are much set on that man. No man can conclude how the heart of God stands by his hand. The hand of God was against Ephraim, and yet his love, his heart, was370 dearly set on Ephraim: “I have surely heard Ephraim’s moaning: ‘You disciplined me severely, like an untrained calf. Restore me, that I may return, for You are the Lord my God. After I returned, I repented; and after I was instructed, I struck my thigh in grief. I was ashamed and humiliated because I bore the disgrace of my youth.’ Is not Ephraim a dear son to Me, a delightful child? Though I often speak against him, I still remember him. Therefore My heart yearns for him; I have great compassion for him,” declares the Lord.

God can look sourly, and chide bitterly, and strike heavily, even where and when he loves dearly. The hand of God was very much against Job, and yet his love, his heart, was very much set on Job, as you may see by comparing the first two chapters of Job with the last two. The hand of God was heavy against David and Jonah when his heart was much set on them. He who concludes that the heart of God is against those whom his hand is against will condemn the generation of the just, whom God would not have anyone condemn unjustly.

The third remedy against this device of Satan is to consider that all the adverse providences that befall the saints are only in order to some noble good that God intends to confer on them. Providence worked against David’s desire in taking away the child sinfully conceived, but yet not against a more noble good. For was it not far better for David to have such a lawful heir as Solomon was, than that a bastard should wear the crown and wield the scepter?

Joseph, you know, was sold into a far country by the envy and malice of his brothers, and afterwards imprisoned because he would not be a prisoner to the lusts of his master’s wife. Yet all these adverse providences wonderfully served his advancement, and the preservation of his father’s family, which was then the visible church of Christ. It was so ordered by a noble hand of providence that what they sought to prevent, they promoted. Joseph was sold by his brothers so that he would not be bowed down to, and yet he was bowed down to because he was sold.

David was appointed to a kingdom; but oh, the straits, troubles, and dangers of death that he ran through before he felt the weight of the crown! And all this was only in order to sweeten his crown, and to settle it more firmly and gloriously on his head. God so contrived it that Jonah’s offense, and those contrary actings of his that attended it, should advance the very end they seemed most directly371 to oppose. Jonah flees to Tarshish, is then cast into the sea, then saved by a miracle. Then the mariners who cast Jonah into the sea, as is very probable, declared to the Ninevites what had happened: that therefore he must be a man sent by God, and that his threatenings must be believed and heeded, and therefore they must repent and humble themselves, so that the wrath threatened might not be carried out, etc.

The fourth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider seriously that all the strange, dark, deep, and changeable providences that believers meet with will further them in their way to heaven, in their journey to happiness. Divine wisdom and love will so order all things here below that they will work for the real, internal, and eternal good of those who love him. All the rugged providences that David met with contributed to372 bringing him to the throne; and all the rugged providences that Daniel and the three young men met with contributed to their great advancement. So all the rugged providences that believers meet with will all contribute to the lifting up of their souls above all things below God. As the waters lifted Noah’s ark nearer heaven, and as all the stones that flew about Stephen’s ears only knocked him closer to Christ, the cornerstone, so all the strange, rugged providences that we meet with will raise us nearer heaven, and knock us nearer to Christ, that precious cornerstone, etc.

369. The Circumcellians, not being able to withstand the preaching and writing of Augustine, sought his destruction, and beset the road he was to take on his pastoral visit; but by God’s providence he missed his way and escaped the danger.

370. Jer 31:18, 19, 20. God’s providential hand may be with persons when his heart is set against them. God’s providential hand was for a time with Saul, Haman, Ashur, and Jehu, and yet his heart was set against them. “No man knows love or hatred by all that is before him” (Eccl 9:1, 2).

371. The workings of divine providence are so dark, so deep, so changeable, that the wisest and noblest souls cannot tell what conclusions to draw.

372. Orosius, speaking of Valentinian, says that he who for Christ’s name’s sake had lost a tribuneship, a while after succeeded his persecutor in the empire.

4. Counterfeit Graces

The fourth device that Satan has to keep the soul in a sad, doubting, and questioning condition, is,

BY suggesting to them that their graces are not true, but counterfeit. “All is not gold that glitters,” says Satan; “all is not grace that you count grace, that you call grace. That which373 you call faith is only a fancy, and that which you call zeal is only unnatural heat and passion. And that light you have is only common; it falls short of what many have attained who are now in hell,” etc. Satan does not labor more mightily to persuade hypocrites that their graces are true, when they are counterfeit, than he does to persuade precious souls that their graces are counterfeit, when indeed they are true, and such as will bear the touchstone of Christ, etc.

Now the remedies against this device of Satan are as follows.

The first remedy against this device of Satan is to consider seriously that grace is taken in two ways.

First, it is taken for the gracious goodwill and favor of God, by which he is pleased, of his own free love, to accept some in Christ as his own. Some call this the first grace, because it is the fountain of all other graces, and the spring from which they flow. And it is called grace because it makes a man gracious with God; but this is only in God.

Secondly, grace is taken for the gifts of grace, and they are of two sorts, common or special.

Some are common to believers and hypocrites, such as a gift of knowledge, a gift of prayer, etc.374

Some are special graces, and they belong distinctively and only to the saints, such as faith, humility, meekness, love, patience, etc.

The second remedy against this device of Satan is to consider wisely the differences between renewing grace and375 restraining grace, between sanctifying grace and temporary grace. I will show you this in the following particulars:

1. True grace makes all glorious within and without: “The king’s daughter is all glorious within; her gown is embroidered with gold.” True grace makes the understanding glorious, the will glorious, the affections glorious; it casts a general glory on all the noble parts of the soul: “The king’s daughter is all glorious within.” And as it makes the inside glorious, so it makes the outside glorious: “Her gown is embroidered with gold.” It makes men look gloriously and speak gloriously, and walk and act gloriously, so that worldly souls will be376 forced to say that these are the ones who have seen Jesus. As grace is a fire to burn up and consume the dross and filth of the soul, so it is an ornament to377 beautify and adorn the soul. True grace makes all new, the inside new and the outside new: “If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.” But temporary grace does not do this. True grace changes the very nature of a man; moral virtue only restrains or chains up the outward man, and does not change the whole man. A lion in a cage is a lion still: he is restrained, but not changed, for he keeps his lion-like nature still. So temporary graces restrain many men from this and that wickedness, but they do not change and turn their hearts from wickedness. But true grace turns a lion into a lamb, as you may see in Paul,378 and a notorious prostitute into a blessed and glorious penitent, as you may see in Mary Magdalene, etc.379

2. The objects of true grace are supernatural. True grace is occupied with the choicest and the highest objects,380 with the most soul-ennobling and soul-enlarging objects: God, Christ, precious promises that are worth more than a world, a kingdom that cannot be shaken, a crown of glory that does not wither, and heavenly treasures that do not rust. The objects of temporary grace are low and poor, and always within the compass of reason’s reach.

3. True grace enables a Christian (when he is himself) to do spiritual actions with real pleasure and delight. To souls truly gracious, Christ’s “yoke is381 easy,” and his “burden is light”; his “commandments are not burdensome,” but joyous. “In my inner being I delight in God’s law,” says Paul. The blessed man is described by this, that “his delight is in the Law382 of the Lord.” “It is a joy to the righteous to do justice,”383 says Solomon. To a gracious soul all the ways of the Lord are pleasant, and all his paths are peace. But to souls that have only temporary grace, only moral virtues, religious services are a toil, not a pleasure; a burden, and not a delight. “Why have we fasted,” they say,384 “and You have not seen? Why have we humbled385 ourselves, and You have not noticed?” etc. So in Malachi: “You+ have said, ‘It is futile to serve God. What have we gained by keeping His requirements and walking mournfully before the Lord of Hosts?’” “When will the New Moon be over” (say those in Amos), “that386 we may sell grain? When will the Sabbath end, that we may market wheat? Let us reduce the ephah and increase the shekel; let us cheat with dishonest scales.”

Fourthly, true grace makes a man most careful and most fearful about his own heart. It makes him most studious of his own heart, instructing it, examining it, and387 watching over it. But temporary grace, moral virtues, make men more mindful and careful of others, to instruct them, counsel them, stir them up, and watch over them, etc. This demonstrates with open mouth that their graces are not saving graces belonging only to saints, but that they are temporary, and no more than what Judas, Demas, and the Pharisees had, etc.

5. Grace will move a man’s heart to love and cling to the strictest and holiest ways and things of God, for their purity and holiness, in the face of all dangers and hardships: “Your word is completely388 pure; therefore Your servant loves it.” Others love it and like it and follow it for the credit, the honor, the advantage that they get by it; but I love it for its spiritual beauty and purity. So the psalmist: “All this has come upon us,389 though we have not forgotten You or betrayed Your covenant. Our hearts have not turned back; our steps have not strayed from Your path, though You have crushed us in the lair of jackals and covered us with deepest darkness.” But temporary grace will not bear up the soul against all oppositions and discouragements in the ways of God, as is clear from their falling away in John 6390 and from the stony ground’s falling away, etc.

6. True grace will enable a man to step over the world’s crown to take up Christ’s cross, to prefer the cross of Christ above the glory and splendor of this world. It enabled Abraham and Moses and Daniel, with those other391 worthies in Hebrews 11, to do so.

Godfrey of Bouillon, first king of Jerusalem, refused to be crowned with a crown of gold, saying that it was392 not fitting for a Christian to wear a crown of gold where Christ had worn a crown of thorns. Oh, but temporary grace cannot bring the soul to prefer Christ’s cross above the world’s crown. When these two meet, a temporary Christian steps over Christ’s cross to take up and keep up the world’s crown: “Demas, in his love of this world, has deserted me.” So the young man in the gospel had many good things in him; he seemed well set for heaven, and came near to heaven. But when Christ set his cross before him, he stepped over that to enjoy the world’s crown. When Christ told him to “go, sell your possessions and give to the poor,” etc., “he went away in sorrow, because he had great wealth.” If heaven is to be had on no other terms, Christ may keep his heaven to himself; he will have none of it, etc.

Then, in the seventh place, consider this: sanctifying grace, renewing grace, sets the soul on spiritual duties from spiritual and inward motives, such as the sense of divine love, which constrains the soul to wait on393 God and to act for God; and the sense of the excellency and sweetness of communion with God; and the choice and precious revelations that the soul has had in the past of the beauty and glory of God, while it was in the service of God. The kind looks, the kind words, the blessed love letters, the glorious kisses, and the sweet embraces that gracious souls have had from Christ in his service stir them up and move them to wait on him in holy duties. Ah, but restraining grace, temporary grace, sets men on religious duties only from outward motives: the ear of men, the eye of men, the rewards of men, the keeping up of a name among men, and a thousand such considerations, as you may see in Saul, Jehu, Judas, Demas, and the scribes and Pharisees, etc.

The abbot in Melanchthon’s story lived strictly, walked demurely, and looked humble, as long as he was only a monk. But when, by his seeming extraordinary holiness, he became abbot, he grew intolerably proud and insolent. When he was asked the reason for it, he confessed that his former lowly look was only to see if he could find the keys of the abbey. Such poor, low, vain motives move temporary souls to all the service they perform, etc.

8. Saving grace, renewing grace, will cause a man to follow the Lord fully, in forsaking all sin and in keeping all God’s precepts. Joshua and394 Caleb followed the Lord fully. Zechariah and Elizabeth were righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord. The saints in Revelation are described by this, that “they follow the Lamb wherever He goes.” But restraining grace, temporary grace, cannot enable a man to follow the Lord fully. All that temporary grace can enable a man to do is to follow the Lord partially, unevenly, and haltingly, as you may see in Jehu, Herod, Judas, and the scribes and Pharisees, who paid tithes of mint and anise and cumin, but neglected the weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy, and faith, etc.

True grace moves the heart to the395 hatred of all sin and to the love of all truth. It moves a man to hate those sins that for the life of him he cannot conquer, and to loathe those sins that he would give all the world to overcome. So a soul truly gracious can say, “Though no one sin is mortified and subdued in me as it should be and as I would have it, yet every sin is hated and loathed by me.” So a soul truly gracious can say, “Though I do not obey any one command as I should and as I would, yet every word is sweet, every command of God is precious. I dearly prize and greatly love those396 commands that I cannot obey. Though there are many commands that I cannot fulfill in a strict sense, yet there is no command that I would not fulfill, and none that I do not exceedingly love.” “I love Your commandments more than gold, even the purest gold.” “I obey Your testimonies and love them exceedingly.”

9. True grace leads the soul to rest in Christ as in its chief good (summum bonum); it works the soul to center in Christ as in its highest and ultimate end. “To whom would we go? You have397 the words of eternal life.” “My beloved is dazzling and ruddy, outstanding among ten thousand.” “I found the one my soul loves. I held him and would not let go.”

That wisdom a believer has from Christ leads him to center in the wisdom of Christ; that love the soul has from Christ leads the soul to center in the love of Christ; and that righteousness the soul has from Christ leads the soul to rest and center in the righteousness of Christ.398 True grace is a beam of Christ, and where it is, it will naturally lead the soul to rest in Christ. The stream does not lead more naturally to the fountain, nor the effect to the cause, than true grace leads the soul to Christ. But restraining grace, temporary grace, works the soul to center and rest in things below Christ. At times it works the soul to center in the praises of men, at times to rest in399 the rewards of men. “Truly I tell you, they already have their full reward,” says Christ; and so in a hundred other things, etc.

10. True grace will enable a soul to sit down satisfied and content with the bare enjoyment of Christ. The400 enjoyment of Christ without honor will satisfy the soul; the enjoyment of Christ without riches, the enjoyment of Christ without pleasures and without the smiles of men, will content and satisfy the soul. “It is enough; Joseph is alive.” So says a gracious soul: “Though honor is not, and riches are not, and health is not, and401 friends are not, etc., it is enough that Christ is, that he reigns, conquers, and triumphs.” Christ is the jar of manna, the jug of oil, a bottomless ocean of all comfort, contentment, and satisfaction. He who has him lacks nothing; he who lacks him enjoys nothing. “Having nothing” (says Paul), “and yet possessing402 all things.” Oh, but a man who has only temporary grace, who has only restraining grace, cannot sit down satisfied and content when he lacks outward comforts. “Christ is good with honors,” says such a soul, “and Christ is good with riches, and Christ is good with pleasures, and he is good with such and such outward comforts. I must have Christ and the world, or else, like the young man in the gospel (in spite of my soul), I will forsake Christ to follow the world.” Ah, how many shining professing Christians there are in the world who cannot sit down satisfied and content when they lack this or that outward comfort and contentment, but are like the madmen of Bedlam, fretting and vexing, raging and raving, as if there were no God, no heaven, no hell, no Christ to make up all such outward lacks to souls! But a soul truly gracious can403 say, “In having nothing, I have all things, because I have Christ. Having therefore all things in him, I seek no other reward, for he is the universal reward.” Such a soul can say, “Nothing is sweet to me without the enjoyment of Christ in it. Neither honors nor riches nor the smiles of men are sweet to me any further than I see Christ and taste Christ in them. The confluence of all outward good cannot make a heaven of glory in my soul if Christ, who is the height of my glory, is absent.” As Absalom said, “What is all this to me, as long as I cannot see the king’s face?” So says the soul: “Why do you tell me of this and that outward comfort, when I cannot see his face whom my soul loves? Why, my honor is not my Christ, nor are riches Christ, nor is the favor of men Christ. Let me have him, and let the men of this world take the world and divide it among themselves. I prize my Christ above all; I would enjoy my Christ before all other things in the world. His presence will make up for the absence of all other comforts, and his absence will darken and embitter all my comforts, so that my comforts will neither taste like comforts, nor look like comforts, nor warm like comforts, etc., when he who should404 comfort my soul stands far off,” etc. Christ is all, and in all, to souls truly gracious. We have all things in Christ, and Christ is all things to a Christian.405 If we are sick, he is a physician; if we thirst, he is a fountain; if our sins trouble us, he is righteousness; if we need help, he is mighty to save; if we fear death, he is life; if we are in darkness, he is light; if we are weak, he is strength; if we are in poverty, he is plenty; if we desire heaven, he is the way. The soul cannot say, “This I would have, and that I would have,” but Christ says, “It is in me, it is in me, eminently, perfectly, eternally.”

373. Yet it must be granted that many a fair flower may grow out of a stinking root, and many sweet dispositions and fair actions may be where there is only the corrupt root of nature.

376. Acts 4:8-15.

379. Luke 7.

392. Few are of Jerome’s mind, who would rather have St. Paul’s coat with his heavenly graces than the purple of kings with their kingdoms. 2 Tim 4:10. Matt 19:20, 21, 22. The king of Navarre told Beza that in the cause of religion he would launch no further into the sea than he could be sure of returning safe to the harbor.

393. “As what I have, if offered to you without myself, does not please you, O Lord, so the good things we have from you, though they may refresh us, yet do not satisfy us without yourself.” Bernard. It is an excellent saying of Bernard (bonus es domine, animae quaerenti; quid invenienti?): “You are good, O Lord, to the soul that seeks you; what are you then to the soul that finds you?”

402. 2 Cor 6:10. St. Augustine, on Ps 12, brings in God rebuking a discontented Christian thus: “What is your faith? Have I promised you these things? What, were you made a Christian so that you should flourish here in this world?”

403. Contentment is the deputy of outward happiness, and supplies its place where it is absent. As the Jews throw the book of Esther to the ground before they read it, because the name of God is not in it, as the rabbis have observed, so in some sense do saints with those blessings in which they do not read Christ’s name and see Christ’s heart. Luther said he would rather be in hell with Christ than in heaven without him.

5. Conflict as in Hypocrites

The fifth device that Satan has to keep souls in a sad, doubting, and questioning condition, is,

BY suggesting to them that the conflict406 that is in them is not a conflict found only in saints, but such a conflict as is found in hypocrites and profane souls; when the truth is, there is as much difference between the conflict that is in them and that which is in wicked men as there is between light and darkness, between heaven and hell. And I will make the truth of this plain to you in the following particulars.

1. The whole frame of a believer’s soul is against sin: understanding, will, and affections, all the powers and faculties407 of the soul, are in arms against sin. A covetous man may condemn covetousness, and yet the frame and bent of his heart may be toward it. A proud person may condemn pride, and yet the frame of his spirit may be toward it. The drunkard may condemn drunkenness, and yet the frame of his spirit may be toward it. A man may condemn stealing and lying, and yet the frame of his heart may be toward them. “You who preach against stealing, do you steal? You who forbid adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you rob temples? You who boast in the law, do you dishonor God by breaking the law?” But a saint’s will is against sin: “I keep on doing the evil I do not want to do.” And his affections are against408 it: “What I hate, I do.”

2. A saint fights against sin universally,409 the least as well as the greatest, the most profitable and the most pleasing sin as well as those that are less pleasing and profitable. He will do battle with all, though he cannot conquer one as he should and as he would. He knows that all sin strikes at God’s holiness as well as at his own happiness, at God’s glory as well as at his soul’s comfort and peace.

He knows that all sin is hateful to God, and that all sins are traitors to the crown and dignity of the Lord Jesus. He looks on one sin and sees410 that it threw down Noah, the most righteous man in the world; and he looks on another sin and sees that it cast down Abraham, the greatest believer in the world; and he looks on another sin and sees that it threw down David, the best king in the world; and he looks on another sin and sees that it cast down Paul, the greatest apostle in the world. He sees that one sin threw down Samson, the strongest man in the world; another cast down Solomon, the wisest man in the world; another, Moses, the meekest man in the world; and another sin cast down Job, the most patient man in the world. And this raises a holy indignation in his soul against all, so that nothing can satisfy and content411 his soul but the destruction of all those lusts and vermin that vex and rack his righteous heart. It will not satisfy a gracious soul to see justice done on one sin; he cries out for justice on all. He would not have some crucified and others spared, but cries out, “Lord, crucify them all, crucify them all.” Oh, but the conflict that is in wicked men is partial. They frown on one sin and smile on another; they strike at some sins but stroke others; they thrust some out of doors but keep others close in their bosoms, as you may see in Jehu, Herod, Judas, Simon Magus, and Demas. Wicked men strike at gross sins, such as are against not only the law of God but the laws of nature and nations; but they make nothing of lesser sins, such as vain thoughts, idle words, sinful impulses,412 petty oaths, etc. They fight against those sins that fight against their honor, profits, pleasures, etc., but make a truce with those that are as right hands and right eyes to them, etc.

3. The conflict that is in a saint against sin is maintained by spiritual arguments: by arguments drawn from413 the love of God, the honor of God, the sweetness of communion with God, and from the spiritual and heavenly blessings and privileges that are conferred on them by God; by arguments drawn from the blood of Christ, the glory of Christ, the eye of Christ, the kisses of Christ, and the intercession of Christ; and by arguments drawn from the earnest of the Spirit, the seal of the Spirit, the witness of the Spirit, the comforts of the Spirit. Oh, but the conflict that is in wicked men comes from low, carnal, and legalistic arguments, drawn from the eye, ear, or hand of man, or drawn from shame, hell, the curses of the law, etc.

4. The conflict that is in saints is a414 constant conflict. Though sin and grace were not born together in the heart of a saint, and though they will not die together, yet while a believer lives they must be in conflict together. Paul had been converted about fourteen years when he cried out, “I see another law at work in my body, warring against the law of my mind and holding me captive to the law of sin.”

Pietro Candiano, one of the doges of Venice, died fighting against the Narentines with his weapons in his hands. So a saint lives fighting and dies fighting; he stands fighting and falls fighting, with his spiritual weapons in his hands. But the conflict that is in wicked men is inconstant. Now they fall out with sin, and the next moment they fall in with sin; now it is bitter, the next moment it is sweet. Now the sinner turns from his sin, and soon he turns back to wallowing in sin, as the pig does to wallowing in the mire. One hour you will find him415 praying against sin, as if he feared it more than hell, and the next hour you will find him pursuing sin, as if there were no God to punish him, no justice to damn him, no hell to torment him.

5. The conflict that is in the saints is in the same faculties: there is the judgment against the judgment, the mind against the mind, the will against the will, the affections against the affections;416 that is, the regenerate part against the unregenerate part, in all the parts of the soul. But in wicked men the conflict is not in the same faculties, but between the conscience and the will. The will of a sinner is bent strongly toward such and such sins; but conscience steps in and tells the sinner, “God has made me his deputy; he has given me power to hang and draw, to examine, scourge, judge, and condemn. If you do such and such wickedness, I will be your jailer and your tormentor. I do not bear the rod or the sword in vain,” says conscience. “If you sin, I will do my office, and then your life will be a hell.” And this raises a tumult in the soul.

6. The conflict that is in the saints is a more blessed, successful, and prevailing conflict. A saint by his conflict with sin gains ground on his sin. “Those who belong to Christ” (says the apostle) “have417 crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.” Christ puts his hand to it and helps them to lead captivity captive, and to set their feet on the necks of those lusts that once trampled on their souls and their comforts. As the house of Saul grew weaker and weaker, and the house of David grew stronger and stronger, so the Lord, by the revelations of his love and by the influences of his Spirit, causes grace, the noble part of a saint, to grow stronger and stronger, and corruption, like the house of Saul, to grow weaker and weaker. But sin in a wicked heart gains ground and grows stronger and stronger. For all his conflicts, his heart is more encouraged, emboldened, and hardened in a way of sin, as you may see in the Israelites, Pharaoh, Jehu, and Judas, who no doubt felt many strange conflicts, tumults, and mutinies in their souls when God spoke such bitter things against them and executed such justice on them.

But remember this by way of caution: though Christ has given sin its death wound (by his power, Spirit, death, and resurrection), yet it will die only a lingering death. As a man who is mortally wounded dies little by little, so does sin in the heart of a saint. The death of Christ on the cross was a lingering death; so the death of sin in the soul is a lingering death: now it dies a little, and then it dies a little more, etc. As the psalmist says, “Do not kill them, or my people will forget. Scatter them by Your power, and bring them down, O Lord, our shield.” He would not have them utterly destroyed, but some remnants preserved as a memorial. So God deals with sin: it is wounded and brought down, but not wholly slain. Something is still left as a monument of divine grace, and to keep us humble, wakeful, and watchful, and so that our armor may always be kept on, and our weapons always in our hands. The best men’s souls in this life hang between the flesh and the spirit, as it were, like Muhammad’s tomb at Aleppo between two lodestones; like Erasmus, as the papists paint him, between418 heaven and hell; like the tribe of Manasseh, half on this side of the Jordan, in the land of the Amorites, and half on that side, in the Holy Land. Yet in the end they will overcome the flesh and trample on the necks of their spiritual enemies.

406. John 8:44. The devil is a liar, and the father of it. “The devil’s breasts,” says Luther, “are very fruitful with lies.”

407. It was a good prayer of the man who said (Domine libera me a malo homine meipso): “Lord, deliver me from an evil man, myself.” Augustine complains that men do not tame the beasts in their own bosoms. Rom 2:21, 22, 23.

408. Rom 7:19, 15.

409. Ps 119:104. “I hate every false way.” Sanethi, from שנא, which signifies to hate with a deadly and irreconcilable hatred.

410. He knows that all the parts of the old man have played, and do play, the part of a treacherous friend and a friendly traitor; therefore his heart strikes at all. “The greater the combat is, the greater will be the rewards that follow,” says Tertullian.

411. True hatred is πρὸς γένη, against the whole kind. Plutarch reports of one who would not have his doubts resolved, because he would not lose the pleasure of seeking a resolution. So wicked men will not be rid of some sins, because they would not lose the seeming pleasure of sinning.

412. John 3:20.

413. Though to be kept from sin brings comfort to us, yet for us to oppose sin from spiritual and heavenly arguments, and for God to pardon sin, brings most glory to God. 2 Cor 12:7, 8, 9.

414. It was an excellent saying of Eusebius Emesenus: “Our fathers overcame the torments of the flames; let us overcome the fiery darts of vices.” Consider that the pleasure and sweetness that follow victory over sin are a thousand times beyond the seeming sweetness that is in sin.

415. 2 Pet 2:19, 20.

416. A heathen could say that their soul is in a mutiny: a wicked man is not friends with himself; he and his conscience are at odds. Aristotle.

417. These two, grace and sin, are like two buckets at a well: when one is up, the other is down. They are like the two laurels at Rome: when one flourishes, the other withers. The more grace thrives in the soul, the more sin dies in the soul. 2 Tim 3:13. From wicked they grow to be very wicked, and from very wicked to be utterly wicked. Lactantius says of Lucian, Nec diis nec hominibus pepercit, he spared neither God nor man. Mortification is a continued act; it is a daily dying to sin: “I die every day.” A crucified man will strive and struggle, yet in the eyes of the law, and in the account of all who see him, he is dead; it is just so with sin. Ps 59:11. “There is no such pleasure” (says Cyprian) “as to have overcome a pleasure offered, nor is there any greater conquest than that which is gained over a man’s corruptions.”

418. The Romans lost many a battle, and yet in the end were conquerors in all their wars; it is just so with the saints.

6. Lost Joy

The sixth device that Satan has to keep a poor soul in a sad, doubting, and questioning condition, is,

BY suggesting to the soul that surely his state is not good, because he cannot rejoice and delight in Christ as once he could, because he has lost the comfort and joy that once was in his spirit. Says Satan, “You know there was a time when your heart was much carried out in rejoicing and delighting in Christ. You do not forget the time when your heart used to be full of joy and comfort. But now, how you have fallen in your joys and comforts! Therefore your state is not good. You only deceive yourself to think that it was ever good; for surely if it had been, your joy and comfort would have continued.” And at this the soul is apt to take Satan’s part and say, “It is just so. I see all is worthless, and I have only deceived my own soul,” etc.

Now the remedies against this device of Satan are as follows.

The first remedy against this device of Satan is to consider that the loss of comfort is a separable adjunct from grace; the soul may be full of holy affections when it is empty of divine consolations. There may be, and often419 is, true grace, indeed much grace, where there is not a drop of comfort or a dram of joy. Comfort belongs not to the being but to the well-being of a Christian. God has not linked these two choice lovers together so closely that they cannot be420 parted. That wisdom that is from above will never work a man to reason this way: “I have no comfort, therefore I have no grace; I have lost the joy I once had, therefore my condition is not good, and was never good,” etc. But it will enable a man to reason this way: “Though my comfort is gone, yet the God of my comfort abides; though my joy is lost, yet the seeds of grace remain.” The best men’s joys are like glass, bright and brittle, and always in danger of breaking.

The second remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that the precious things that you still enjoy are far better than the joys and comforts that you have lost. Your union with Christ, your communion with Christ, your sonship, your saintship, your heirship, which you still enjoy through Christ, are far better than the comforts you have lost through sin. Even if your comforts are gone, yet your union and communion with Christ remain. Though your comforts are gone, yet you are a son, though421 a comfortless son; an heir, though a comfortless heir; a saint, though a comfortless saint. Though the bag of silver (your comforts) is lost, yet the422 box of jewels (your union with Christ, your communion with Christ, your sonship, your saintship, your heirship), which you still enjoy, is far better than the bag of silver you have lost. Indeed, the least of those precious jewels is worth more than all the comforts in the world. Well, let this be a heart-medicine to comfort you, a star to lead you, and a staff to support you: your box of jewels is safe, though your bag of silver is lost.

The third remedy against this device of Satan is to consider that your condition is no other than what has been the condition of those precious423 souls whose names were written on the heart of Christ, and who are now at rest in the bosom of Christ. One day you will find them praising and rejoicing, the next day mourning and weeping. One day you will find them singing,424 “The Lord is our portion”; the next day sighing and arguing with themselves,425 “Why are you+ downcast, O our souls? Why is our harp turned to mourning, and our flute to the sound of weeping?” etc.

The fourth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that the causes of joy and comfort are not always the same. Perhaps your former joy and comfort sprang from426 the witness of the Spirit, he bearing witness to your soul that your nature was changed, your sins pardoned, your soul reconciled, etc. Now the Spirit may, on some special occasion, bear witness to the soul that the heart of God is dearly set on him, that God loves him with an everlasting love, etc., and yet the soul may never enjoy such a testimony again all the days of his life. Though the Spirit is a witnessing Spirit, it is not his office to witness every day to believers their share in God, Christ, heaven, etc.

Or perhaps your former joy and comfort sprang from the newness and suddenness of the change in your condition. For a man in one hour to have427 his night turned into day, his darkness into light, his bitter into sweet, God’s frowns into smiles, his hatred into love, his hell into a heaven, must greatly gladden and comfort him. It cannot but make the heart leap and dance in him who in one hour sees Satan accusing him, his own heart condemning him, the eternal God frowning on him, the gates of heaven barred against him, all the creation standing armed at the least nod of God to execute vengeance on him, and the mouth of the pit of hell open to receive him. Now in this hour, for Christ to come to the stunned soul and say to it, “I have trodden the winepress of my Father’s wrath for you; I have laid down my life as a ransom for you; by my blood I have satisfied my Father’s justice, and pacified his anger, and procured his love for you; by my blood I have purchased the pardon of your sins, your freedom from hell, and your right to heaven,” etc. Oh, how wonderfully this will cause the soul to leap for joy!

The fifth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider that God will restore and make up the comforts of his people. Though your candle is put out,428 yet God will light it again and make it burn brighter than ever. Though your sun is clouded for the present, yet he who rides on the clouds will scatter those clouds, and cause the sun to shine and warm your heart as in former days. As the psalmist says,429 “Though You have shown me many troubles and misfortunes, You will revive me once again. Even from the depths of the earth You will bring me back up. You will increase my honor and comfort me on every side.” God takes away a little comfort so that he may make room in the soul for a greater degree of comfort. The prophet Isaiah sweetly shows this:430 “I have seen his ways, but I will heal him; I will guide him and restore comforts to him and his mourners.” Bear up sweetly, O precious soul! Your storm will end in a calm, and your dark night in a sunny day; your mourning will be turned into rejoicing, and the waters of consolation will be sweeter and higher in your soul than431 ever. The mercy is surely yours, but the time of giving it is the Lord’s. Wait just a little, and you will find the Lord comforting you on every side.

419. Ps 63:1, 2, 8. Isa 50:10. Mic 7:8, 9. Ps 42:5.

420. Spiritual joy is a sun that is often clouded; though it is as precious a flower as most that Paradise affords, yet it is subject to fade and wither.

421. Jer 31:18, 19, 20.

422. When someone reproached Faninus for his cheerfulness, set against Christ’s agony and sadness, he answered, “Christ was sad so that I might be merry; he had my sins, and I have his righteousness.”

423. Ps 51:12. Ps 30:6, 7. Job 23:6, 8, 9; 30:31. Lam 1:16. Matt 27:46.

424. Ps 42:5.

425. Lam 5:15.

426. The Spirit does not make a feast in the soul every day; he does not make every day a day of wearing the wedding robes.

427. A pardon given unexpectedly into the hand of a criminal, when he is on the last step of the ladder, ready to be hanged, will cause much joy and rejoicing; the newness and suddenness of the change in his condition will cause his heart to leap and rejoice. Yet in the course of time much of his joy will abate, though his life is as dear to him still as ever it was.

So Mr. Glover, when he was within sight of the stake, cried out to his friend, “He has come, he has come,” meaning the Comforter whom Christ promised to send.

7. Relapses

The seventh device that Satan has to keep souls in a doubting and questioning condition is,

BY suggesting to the soul his frequent relapses into the same sin that he has formerly opposed with particular sorrow, grief, shame and tears, and has prayed, complained and resolved against. Satan says, “Your heart is not right with God. Surely your state is not good. You only flatter yourself if you think that God will ever eternally acknowledge and embrace such a one as you are, who complain against sin and yet relapse into the same sin, who confess your sin with tears and groans and yet again and again fall into the same sin, etc.”

I confess this is a very sad condition for a soul: after he has obtained mercy and pity from the Lord, after God has spoken peace and pardon to him, wiped the tears from his eyes and set him on his feet, to return to folly. Ah! how relapses lay men open to the greatest afflictions and the worst432 temptations! How they make the wound bleed afresh! How they darken and cloud former assurances and evidences for heaven! How they put a sword into the hand of conscience to cut and slash the soul! They raise such fears, terrors, horrors and doubts in the soul that the soul cannot be as frequent in duty as before, nor as fervent in duty as before, nor as confident in duty as before, nor as bold, familiar and delighting in God in duty as before, nor as constant in duty as before. They give Satan an advantage to triumph over Christ. They make the work of repentance more difficult. They make a man’s life a burden, and they make death very terrible to the soul, etc.

Now the remedies against this device of Satan are as follows.

The first remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that there are many scriptures that clearly show it is possible for the saints to fall into the same sins of which they have formerly repented.433 “I will heal their backsliding; I will freely love them, for My anger has turned away from them,” says the Lord by the prophet Hosea. So the prophet Jeremiah speaks:434 “Go, proclaim these words toward the north, and say: ‘Return, O backsliding Israel,’ declares the Lord. ‘I will no longer look on you+ with anger, for I am merciful,’ declares the Lord.435 ‘I will not be angry forever.’ … ‘Return, O backsliding children,’ declares the Lord, ‘for I am your+ master, and I will take you+, one from a city and two from a family, and bring you+ to Zion.’” So the psalmist: “They turned back and were faithless like their fathers, twisted like a faulty bow.” And no wonder; for though their repentance is ever so sincere and sound, yet their graces are only weak, and their mortification imperfect in436 this life. Though by grace they are freed from the dominion of sin, from the condemning power of every sin and from the love of all sin, yet grace does not free them from the seed of any one sin. Therefore it is possible for a soul to fall again and again into the same sin. If the fire is not wholly put out, who would think it impossible that it should catch and burn again and again?

The second remedy against this device of Satan is to consider seriously that God has nowhere bound himself by any particular promise that souls converted and united to Christ will not fall again and again into the same sins after conversion. I cannot find anywhere in the whole Book of God where he437 has promised any such strength or power against this or that particular sin that the soul will be forever (in this life) put beyond the possibility of falling again and again into the same sins. And where God has no mouth to speak, I must have no heart to believe. God will graciously pardon to his people those sins that he will not effectually subdue in his people in this life. I would go far to speak with the soul that can show a promise that, when our sorrow and grief for this or that sin has been so great or so much, God will then keep us from ever falling into the same sin. The sight of such a promise would be like life from the dead to many a precious soul who desires nothing more than to keep close to Christ, and fears nothing more than backsliding from Christ.

The third remedy against this device of Satan is to consider seriously that the most renowned saints, now crowned, relapsed in the days of their life on earth into one and the438 same sin. Lot was twice overcome with wine; John twice worshiped the angel; Abraham often dissembled and laid his wife open to adultery to save his own life, which some heathens would not have done: “So when439 God had me journey from my father’s house, I said to her, ‘This is how you can show your loyalty to me: Wherever we go, say of me, “He is my brother.”’” David in his440 wrath was resolved, if ever a man was, to be the death of Nabal and all his innocent family; and after this he fell into the foul murder of Uriah. Though Christ told his disciples that his kingdom was not of this world, yet again and again and again, three separate times, they would insist on being on horseback; they longed to be high, great and glorious in this world. Their pride and ambitious spirit set them (who were only like so many beggars) striving for preeminence and greatness in the world, when their Lord and master had told them three separate times of his sufferings in the world and of his going out of the world. Jehoshaphat,441 though a godly man, still allies himself by marriage with wicked Ahab; and though he was saved by a miracle, yet soon after he falls into the same sin and makes an alliance with442 Ahaziah king of Israel, who acted very wickedly. Samson is numbered by the Spirit of the Lord among the faithful worthies,443 and yet he often fell into one gross sin, as is evident in the book of Judges.444 Peter, you know, relapsed often, and so did Jonah. And this comes about so that they may see their own inability to stand, to resist or to overcome any temptation or corruption; so that they may be taken off all false confidences and rest wholly on God, and only on God, and always on God; and for the praise and honor of the power, wisdom, skill, mercy and445 goodness of the physician of our souls, who can heal, help and cure when the disease is most dangerous, when the soul has relapsed and grows worse and worse, when others say there is no help for him in his God, and when his own heart and hopes are dying.

The fourth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider that there are relapses into enormities, and there are relapses into infirmities. Now it is not usual for God to leave his people446 to relapse frequently into enormities; for by his Spirit and grace, by his smiles and frowns, by his word and rod, he usually preserves his people from relapsing frequently into enormities. Yet he does leave his choicest ones to relapse frequently into infirmities (and of his grace he pardons them as a matter of course), such as idle words, anger, vain thoughts, etc. Though gracious souls strive against these, complain of these and weep over these, yet the Lord, to keep them humble, leaves them to relapse frequently into these. And these frequent relapses into infirmities will never be their bane, because they are their burden.

The fifth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider that there are447 involuntary relapses, and there are voluntary relapses. Involuntary relapses are when the resolution and full bent of the heart is against sin, when the soul strives with all its might against sin, by sighs and groans, by prayers and tears, and yet out of weakness is forced to fall back into sin, because there is not spiritual strength enough to overcome. Now though involuntary relapses must humble us, yet they must never discourage or deject us; for God will freely and readily pardon those as a matter of course. Voluntary relapses are when the soul longs and loves to return to the fleshpots of Egypt, when it is a pleasure and a pastime to a man to return to his old ways. Such voluntary relapses declare the man blinded, hardened and ripened for ruin, etc.

The sixth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider that there is no such power or infinite force in the448 greatest horror or sorrow the soul can be under for sin, nor in the sweetest or choicest revelations of God’s grace and love to the soul, as to fence and secure the soul forever from relapsing into the same sin. Grace is only a created habit, which may be overcome by the secret, subtle and strong workings of sin in our hearts. And the revelations that God makes of his love, beauty and glory to the soul do not always remain in their freshness and power on the heart; by degrees they fade and wear off, and then the soul may return to folly again. We see this in Peter. After he had a glorious testimony449 from Christ’s own mouth of his blessedness and happiness, he labors to keep Christ from going up to Jerusalem to suffer, out of base, slavish fears that he and his fellows could not be safe if their master were brought to suffer. And again, after this, Christ took him up onto the mount and there450 showed him his beauty and glory, to strengthen him against the hour of temptation that was coming on him. And yet soon after he had the honor and happiness of seeing the glory of the Lord (which most of the disciples did not have), he basely and most shamefully denies the Lord of glory, thinking451 by that means to provide for his own safety. And yet again, after Christ had broken his heart with a look of love for his most unlovely dealings, and had told those who first learned of his resurrection to go and tell Peter that he was risen, I say, after all this, slavish fears prevail over him, and he basely dissembles and plays the Jew with the Jews and the Gentile with the Gentiles, to the leading astray of Barnabas,452 etc.

Yet by way of caution, know that it is very rare for God to leave his beloved ones to relapse frequently into one and the same gross sin; for the law of nature is up in arms against gross sins, as well as the law of grace, so that a gracious soul cannot, dares not, will not frequently return to gross folly. And God has made even his dearest ones smart dearly for their relapses, as may be seen in his dealings with Samson, Jehoshaphat and Peter. Ah Lord! what a hard heart that man has who can see you stripping and whipping your dearest ones for their relapses, and yet makes nothing of returning to folly, etc.

432. A backslider may say (opera & impensa periit), “All my pains and cost are lost.”

433. Hos 14:4.

434. Jer 3:12, 14.

435. The sin of backsliding is a soul-wounding sin. “I will heal their backsliding”: you read of no armor for the back, though you do for the breast.

436. When a soldier boasted too much of a great scar on his forehead, Augustus Caesar (in whose time Christ was born) asked him whether he had not got it when he looked back as he fled.

437. In some cases the saints have found God better than his word. He promised the children of Israel only the land of Canaan, but besides that he gave them two other kingdoms, which he never promised. And he promised Zechariah to give him back his speech at the birth of the child, but besides that he gave him the gift of prophecy.

438. A sheep may often slip into a bog, as well as a swine.

439. Gen 20:13; ch. 12.

440. Perhaps the prodigal sets before us a Christian who has relapsed; for he was a son before, and with his father, and then went away from him and spent everything; and yet he was not quite undone, but returned again.

441. 2 Chr 18:1, 2, 3, 30, 31.

442. ch. 20:35, 36, 37.

443. Heb 11:32.

444. Judg 14:15; ch. 16.

445. The prodigal saw his father’s compassion as all the greater in receiving him after he had run away from him.

446. Relapses into enormities are (peccata vulnerantia & devastantia) wounding and wasting sins. Therefore the Lord is graciously pleased to put his everlasting arms under his chosen ones and hold them up from frequently falling into them.

447. There is a great difference between a sheep that falls into the mire through weakness and a swine that delights to wallow in the mire; between a woman who is forced, though she struggles and cries out, and an alluring adulteress.

448. Christ rebuked his disciples for their unbelief and hardness of heart, though they had seen his glory, the glory of the only begotten Son of God, full of grace and truth. John 1:14.

449. Matt 16:15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 22, 23, 24.

450. Matt 17:1, 2, 3.
