8. Temptations

The eighth device that Satan has to keep souls in a doubting and questioning condition is,

BY persuading them that their state is not good, their hearts are not upright and their graces are not sound, because they are so followed, vexed and tormented with temptations. It is his method first to vex and weary the soul with temptations, and then to tempt the soul to think that surely it is not beloved,453 because it is so much tempted. By this stratagem he keeps many precious souls in a sad, doubting and mourning state for many years, as many of the precious sons of Zion have found by woeful experience, etc.

Now the remedies against this device of Satan are as follows.

The first remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that those who have been best and most beloved have been most tempted by Satan. Though Satan can never rob a Christian of his crown, yet such is his malice that he will tempt them for this very reason, that he may rob them of their comforts. Such is his enmity to the Father that the nearer and dearer any child is to him, the more Satan will trouble him and vex him with temptations.454 Christ himself was nearest and dearest, most innocent and most excellent, and yet none was so much tempted as Christ. David was dearly beloved, and yet was tempted by Satan to number the people. Job was highly praised by God himself, and yet much tempted; witness those sad things that fell from his mouth when he was wet to the skin. Peter was much prized by Christ; witness that choice testimony Christ gave of his faith and happiness, his showing him his glory on the mount, and that eye of pity he cast on him after his fearful fall, etc. And yet he was tempted by Satan. And the Lord said,455 “Simon, Simon, Satan has asked to sift each of you+ like wheat. But I have prayed for you, that your faith will not fail,” etc.

Paul had the honor of being exalted as high as heaven and of seeing glory that could not be expressed; and yet no sooner had he stepped out of heaven than he was buffeted by Satan, so that he would not be exalted above measure. If456 these who were so really, so gloriously, so eminently beloved by God, if these who have lived in heaven and set their feet on the stars, have been tempted, let no saints judge themselves not to be beloved because they are tempted.

It is as natural for saints who are dearly beloved to be tempted as it is for the sun to shine or a bird to sing. The eagle does not complain of her wings, nor the peacock of his train, nor the nightingale of her voice, because these are natural to them; no more should saints complain of their temptations, because they are natural to them. “For our struggle is not against457 flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the powers of this world’s darkness, and against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms.”

The second remedy against this device of Satan is to consider that all the temptations that befall the saints will be sanctified to them by a hand of love. Ah! the choice experiences the saints gain of the power of God supporting them, of the wisdom of God directing them (so to handle their spiritual weapons, their graces, as not only to resist but to overcome), and of the mercy and goodness of the Lord pardoning and helping them! And therefore Paul says, “I was given … a messenger of458 Satan, to buffet me, so that I would not be exalted, so that I would not be exalted above measure.” It is there twice in that verse: he begins with it and ends with it. If he had not been buffeted, who knows how his heart would have swelled? He might have been carried higher in conceit than he had been before in his ecstasy. The school of temptation is a choice school: a school in which God gives his people the clearest and sweetest revelations of his love; a school in which God teaches his people to be more frequent and fervent in duty (when Paul was buffeted, then he prayed three times, that is, frequently and fervently); a school in which God teaches his people to be more tender, meek and compassionate to other poor tempted souls than ever; a school in which God teaches his people to see a greater evil in sin than ever, a greater emptiness in created things than ever, and a greater need of Christ and free grace than ever; a school in which God will teach his people that all temptations are only his goldsmiths, by which he will try and refine his people and make them more bright and glorious. The outcome of all temptations will be the good of the saints, as you may see by the temptations that Adam and Eve, and Christ, and David, and Job, and Peter, and Paul met with. Those hands of power and love that bring light out of darkness, good out of evil, sweet out of bitter, life out of death, heaven out of hell, will bring much sweetness and good to his people out of all the temptations that come on them.

The third remedy against this device of Satan is to consider wisely that no temptations hurt or harm the saints so long as the saints resist them and the temptations prove the greatest affliction that can befall them. It is not Satan’s tempting but your+ assenting, not his enticing but your+ yielding, that makes temptations hurtful to your+ souls. If the soul, when it is tempted, resists the temptation and says with Christ, “Get behind Me, Satan!” and with that young convert, “I am not the man I459 was,” or, as Luther counsels all men to answer all temptations, with these words (Christianus sum), “I am a Christian”; and if a man’s temptations are his greatest affliction, then the temptation is no sin on his soul, though it is a trouble on his mind. Suppose a soul can look the Lord in the face and say, “Ah Lord! I have many outward troubles on me now. I have lost such and such a near blessing, and such and such dear, desirable blessings. And yet you who know the heart, you know that all my crosses and losses do not make so many wounds in my soul, nor fetch so many sighs from my heart or tears from my eyes, as those temptations do with which Satan pursues my soul.” When it is like this with the soul, then temptations are only the soul’s trouble; they are not the soul’s sin.

Satan is a malicious and envious enemy;460 as his names are, so is he. His names are all names of enmity: the Accuser, the Tempter, the Destroyer, the Devourer, the envious Man. This malice and envy of his he sometimes shows by tempting men to sins quite contrary to the temperament of their bodies, as he tempted Vespasian and Julian, men of sweet and excellent natures, to be most bloody murderers. Sometimes he shows his malice by tempting men to things that will bring him no honor or profit, etc. (“Fall down and worship me”): to blasphemy and atheism, etc., the very thoughts and first stirrings of which make the heart and the flesh tremble. And sometimes he shows his malice by tempting them to sins that they have not found their natures prone to, and that they abhor in others, etc.

Now if the soul resists these, complains of these, groans and mourns under these, and looks up to the Lord Jesus to be delivered from these, then they will not be put down to the soul’s account but to Satan’s; and he will be tormented all the more, the more the saints have been maliciously tempted by him, etc.

Make immediate and peremptory resistance against Satan’s temptations; bid defiance to the temptation at first sight.461 It is safe to resist; it is dangerous to dispute. Eve lost herself and her posterity by entering the lists of dispute, when she should have resisted and stood on terms of defiance with Satan. He who would stand in the hour of temptation must plead with Christ, “It is written”; he who would triumph over temptations must always plead, “It is written.” Satan is bold and impudent, and if you+ are not peremptory in your+ resistance, he will make fresh attacks on you+. It is your+ greatest honor and your+ highest wisdom to withstand the beginnings of a temptation peremptorily, for a remedy afterward often comes too late.

Mrs. Katherine Brettergh, once, after a great conflict with Satan, said, “Do not reason with me; I am only a weak woman. If you have anything to say, say it to my Christ. He is my advocate, my strength and my redeemer, and he will plead for me.”

Men must not seek to resist Satan’s craft with craft (sed per apertum martem) but by open defiance. He who thinks to put Satan off by disputing and reasoning shoots with Satan in his own bow. As soon as a temptation shows its face, say to the temptation, as Ephraim said to his idols, “Get away from me! What more have I462 to do with you+?” Oh! say to the temptation, as David said to the sons of Zeruiah, “What have I to do with you+?”463 You will be too strong for me. He who resists temptations in this way will never be undone by temptation, etc.

Make strong and constant resistance464 against Satan’s temptations. Resist temptations with arguments drawn from the honor of God, the love of God, and your union and communion with God; from the blood of Christ, the death of Christ, the kindness of Christ, the intercession of Christ and the glory of Christ; from the voice of the Spirit, the counsel of the Spirit, the comforts of the Spirit, the presence of the Spirit, the seal of the Spirit, the whisperings of the Spirit, the commands of the Spirit, the assistance of the Spirit, the witness of the Spirit; and from the glory of heaven, the excellence of grace, the beauty of holiness, the worth of the soul, and the vileness, bitterness and evil of sin, the least sin being a greater evil than the greatest temptation in the world.

And see that you+ make constant resistance as well as strong resistance. Be constantly in arms; Satan will come on with new temptations when old465 ones are too weak. In a calm, prepare for a storm. The tempter is restless, impudent and subtle. He will suit his temptations to your+ constitutions and inclinations; Satan loves to sail with the wind. If your+ knowledge is weak, he will tempt you+ to error; if your+ consciences are tender, he will tempt you+ to scrupulosity and too much strictness, such as doing nothing but hearing, praying, reading, etc. If your+ consciences are wide and lax, he will tempt you+ to carnal complacency; if you+ are bold-spirited, he will tempt you+ to presumption; if timid, to despair; if flexible, to inconstancy; if proud and stiff, to gross folly. Therefore always be ready for fresh assaults; make one victory a step to another. When you+ have overcome a temptation, beware of unbending your+ bow, and see to it that your+ bow is always bent and keeps its strength. When you+ have overcome one temptation, you+ must be ready to enter the lists with another. As distrust (in some sense) is the mother of safety, so complacency is the gate of danger. A man needs to fear this most of all, that he does not fear all. If Satan is always roaring, we should always be watching and resisting him. And certainly, he who makes strong and constant resistance to Satan’s temptations will in the end get above his temptations, and for the present is safe enough from being ruined by his temptations, etc.

For a close of this, remember that it is466 dangerous to yield to the least sin to be rid of the greatest temptation. To take this course would be as if a man thought to wash himself clean in ink, or as if a man exchanged a light cross made of paper for an iron cross that is heavy, toilsome and bloody. The least sin set home on the conscience will wound, vex and oppress the soul more than all the temptations in the world can. Therefore never yield to the least sin to be rid of the greatest temptation. Sidonius Apollinaris relates how a certain man named Maximus, who had reached the top of honor by crooked means, was very much wearied on the first day, and fetching a deep sigh, said, “O Damocles! how happy I count you for having been a king only for the length of a dinner. I have been one a whole day, and can bear it no longer.” I will leave you+ to make the application.

453. He may tempt so as to make a saint weary of his life. Job 10:1: “My soul is weary of my life.”

454. Pirates do not usually attack poor, empty vessels, and beggars need not fear the thief. Those who have most of God and are richest in grace will be most attacked by Satan, who is the greatest and wisest pirate in the world.

455. Luke 22:31, 32.

456. 2 Cor 12:2, 7.

457. Eph 6:12.

458. 2 Cor 12:7. Vide Bezam, Grotium, & Estium [See Beza, Grotius and Estius]. Luther said there were three things that made a preacher: meditation, prayer and temptation.

459. Ego non sum ego.

460. Sometimes he shows his malice by leaving with the soul such things as may most vex and plague it, as Gregory observes in his leaving Job’s wife. This was not out of forgetfulness or carelessness, or any love or pity for Job, but to vex and torment him, etc., and to work on him to blaspheme God, despair and die, etc.

461. When the emperor Constantine was told that there was no means to cure his leprosy except bathing his body in the blood of infants, he answered at once (malo semper aegrotare quam tali remedio convalescere), “I would rather not be cured than use such a remedy.”

462. Hos 14.

463. 2 Sam 16:10.

464. I have read of one who, being tempted with offers of money to desert Christ, gave this excellent answer: “Let no man think that he who has forsaken his own goods to follow Christ will take other men’s goods to forsake Christ.”

465. Luke 4:13: “When the devil had finished every temptation, he left Him until an opportune time.” Christ had no rest until he had been thoroughly tried with all kinds of temptations. Calvin.

466. He who will yield to sin to be rid of temptation will be tempted all the more, and be less able to withstand temptations.

Part IV. Devices to Destroy All Ranks of Men

1. The Great: Self-Seeking

The fourth thing to be shown is the various ways and devices that Satan has to destroy and ensnare all sorts and ranks of men in the world.

I will begin with the honorable and the great, and show you the devices that Satan has to destroy them. I will cite only those that are most important.

His first device to destroy the great and honorable of the earth is,

BY working on them to make it their business to seek themselves: to seek how to make themselves great, to raise467 themselves, to enrich themselves, to secure themselves, etc., as you may see in Pharaoh, Ahab, Rehoboam, Jeroboam, Absalom, Joab, Haman, etc. But were the Scripture silent, our own experience abundantly proves this way and method of Satan to destroy the great and the honorable, to bury their names in the dust and their souls in hell: by drawing them to mind themselves wholly, and to mind only themselves, and to mind themselves in all things, and to mind themselves always. “All” (says the apostle) “mind468 themselves.” All, comparatively, in respect of the fewness of others who let their private interests fall, and drown all regard for self in the glory of God and the public good, etc.

Now the remedies against this device of Satan are as follows.

The first remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly469 that self-seeking is a sin that will drive men to a world of sin: to sins not only against the law of God and the rules of the gospel, but against the very laws of nature, which are so much darkened by the fall of man. It drove the Pharisees to oppose Christ, and Judas to betray Christ, and Pilate470 to condemn Christ. It drove Gehazi to lying, and Balaam to cursing, and Saul and Absalom to plotting David’s ruin. It drove Pharaoh and Haman to contrive ways to destroy those Jews whom God purposed to save by his mighty arm. It drives men to use wicked balances and the bag of deceitful weights. It drives men to ways of oppression, “to sell471 the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals,” etc. I know of no sin in the world that this sin of self-seeking will not drive men to, though it be their eternal loss.

The second remedy against this device of Satan is to consider seriously that self-seeking exceedingly abases472 a man. It strips him of all his royalty and glory. From a lord it makes a man a servant to created things, yes, often to the worst of creatures; indeed, a slave to slaves, as you may see in Judas, Demas, Balaam, and the scribes and Pharisees. Self-seekers bow down to created things, as Gideon’s many thousands bowed down to the waters. Self-seeking will make a man say anything, do anything, and be anything, to please the lusts of others and to gain advantages over others. Self-seeking transforms a man into all shapes and forms. Now473 it makes a man appear as an angel of light, and soon after as an angel of darkness. Now self-seekers are seemingly for God, and soon after they are openly against God. Now you will have them crying “Hosanna in the highest,” and soon after “Crucify him, crucify him!” Now you will have them building with the saints, and soon after you will have them plotting the overthrow of the saints, as those self-seekers did in the time of Ezra and Nehemiah. Self-seekers are the basest of all persons; there is no service so base, so poor, so low, that they will not bow to it. They cannot look either above or beyond their own lusts and the enjoyment474 of created things; these are the first and final objects of their aims.

It is said of Tiberius that while Augustus ruled, his reputation was in no way tainted; and that while Drusus and Germanicus were alive, he feigned virtues that he did not have, to keep a good opinion of himself in the hearts of the people. But after he had got himself out of the reach of contradiction and control, there was no deed in which he was not at fault, no crime to which he was not an accessory. My prayer will be that the spirit of Tiberius may not be found in any of our rulers, lest it prove their ruin, as it did his; and that wherever it is, it may be detected, loathed, and cast out, so that neither the state nor souls may be ruined by it, etc.

The third remedy against this device of Satan is to dwell solemnly on those dreadful curses and woes that are pronounced from heaven against self-seekers. “Woe to you+ who add475 house to house and join field to field until no place is left and you+ live alone in the land.” So Habakkuk:476 “Woe to him who amasses what is not his and makes himself rich with many loans! … Woe to him who builds his house by unjust gain, to place his nest on high and escape the hand of disaster! You have plotted shame for your house by cutting off many peoples and forfeiting your life. For the stones will cry out from the wall, and the beam from the woodwork will answer it. Woe to him who builds a city with bloodshed and establishes a town by iniquity!” The materials of the house built up by oppression will come as joint witnesses. The stones of the wall will cry, “Lord, we were built up by blood and violence”; and the beam will answer, “True, Lord, even so it is.” The stones will cry, “Vengeance, Lord, on these self-seekers”; and the beam will answer, “Woe to him, because he built his house with blood.” So Isaiah: “Woe to those who enact unjust statutes and issue oppressive decrees, to deprive the poor of fair treatment and withhold justice from the oppressed of My people, to make widows their prey and orphans their plunder.” So Amos: “Woe477 to those at ease in Zion and those secure on Mount Samaria, the distinguished ones of the foremost nation, to whom the house of Israel comes. You+ dismiss the day of calamity and bring near a reign of violence. You+ lie on beds inlaid with ivory, and lounge upon your+ couches. You+ dine on lambs from the flock and calves from the stall. … You+ drink wine by the bowlful and anoint yourselves+ with the finest oils, but you+ fail to grieve over the ruin of Joseph.” So Micah: “Woe to those who devise iniquity478 and plot evil on their beds! At morning’s light they accomplish it because the power is in their hands. They covet fields and seize them; they take away houses. They deprive a man of his home, a fellow man of his inheritance.”

By these Scriptures you see that self-seekers labor like a woman in childbirth, but their birth proves their death; their pleasure, their pain; their comfort, their torment; their glory, their shame; their exaltation, their desolation. Loss, disgrace, trouble, and shame, vexation and ruin will be the certain portion of self-seekers. When the Tartars had taken the duke of Muscovy in battle, they made a cup of his skull, with this inscription: All covet, all lose.

The fourth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that self-seekers are self-losers and479 self-destroyers. Absalom and Judas seek themselves and hang themselves. Saul seeks himself and kills himself. Ahab seeks himself and loses himself, his crown, and his kingdom. Pharaoh seeks himself and overthrows himself and his mighty army in the Red Sea. Cain sought himself and slew two at once, his brother and his own soul. Gehazi sought a change of clothing, but God changed his clothing into a leprous skin. Haman sought himself and lost himself. The princes and the administrators sought themselves (in the ruin of Daniel), but ruined themselves, their wives, and their children. What self-seekers think should be a staff to support them becomes (by the hand of justice) an iron rod to break them; what they would have as springs to refresh them becomes a gulf to consume them utterly. The crosses of self-seekers will always exceed their blessings; their pain, their pleasure; their torments, their comforts. Every self-seeker is a self-tormentor, a self-destroyer; he carries a hell, an executioner, in his own bosom, etc.

The fifth remedy against this device of Satan is, to dwell much on the famous examples of those worthy saints who have denied themselves and preferred the public good before their own private advantage. As Moses: the Lord said to Moses, “Leave Me alone, so that I may destroy them and blot out their name from under heaven. Then I will make you into a nation mightier and greater than they are.” Oh, but this offer would480 not win Moses. Being a man of a noble public spirit, he is hot in his desires and prayers that the people might be spared and pardoned. He says, “Pardon, I pray, the iniquity of this people, in keeping with the greatness of Your loving devotion, just as You have forgiven them ever since they left Egypt.” And the Lord said, “I have pardoned them as you requested.” Ah, should God make such an offer to many who style themselves Moses, and are called Moses by many, I am afraid they would prefer their own advantage above the481 public good. They would not care what became of the people, so long as they and theirs might be made great and glorious in the world. They would not care, so long as they might have a Babel built for them, though it was on the ashes and ruin of the people. There are no baser spirits than these in hell, no, not in hell; and I am sure there are no such spirits in heaven. Such men’s hearts and principles must be changed, or they will be ruined forever. Nehemiah was a482 choice soul, a man of a noble public spirit, a man who spent his time, his strength, and his estate for the good and ease of his people. “Furthermore” (says he), “from the day King Artaxerxes appointed me to be their governor in the land of Judah, from his twentieth year until his thirty-second year (twelve years total), neither I nor my brothers ate the food allotted to the governor. … Also I devoted myself to the construction of the wall, and all my servants were gathered there for the work; we did not acquire any land. There were 150 Jews and officials at my table, besides the guests from the surrounding nations. Each day one ox, six choice sheep, and some fowl were prepared for me, and once every ten days an abundance of all kinds of wine was provided. But I did not demand the food allotted to the governor, because the burden on the people was so heavy. Remember me favorably, O my God, for all that I have done for this people.” So Daniel was a man of a noble public spirit: “Then the administrators and satraps483 sought a charge against Daniel concerning the kingdom, but they could find no charge or corruption, because he was trustworthy, and no negligence or corruption was found in him. Finally these men said, ‘We will never find any charge against this Daniel, unless we find something against him concerning the law of his God.’”

Christ had a public spirit; he laid himself out, and laid himself down, for a public good. Oh, never stop looking at and meditating on these precious and sweet examples, till your+ souls are enlivened and raised up to act for the public good more than for your+ own private advantage. Many484 heathens have been excellent at this. Macrobius writes of Augustus Caesar (in whose time Christ was born) that he bore such an entire and fatherly affection to the commonwealth that he called it (filiam suam) his own daughter. And therefore he refused to be called (Dominus) the lord or master of his country, and would only be called (pater patriae) father of his country, because he governed it not by fear (per timorem sed per amorem) but by love; and the senate and the people of Rome together hailed him by the name (pater patriae) Father of his Country. The people greatly lamented his death, using this saying: “Would he had485 never been born, or never died.” So Marcus Regulus, to save his country from ruin, exposed himself to the greatest sufferings that the malice and rage of his enemies could inflict. So Titus and Aristides, and many others, have been famous for preferring the public good above their own advantage. My prayer is, and will be, that all our rulers may be so filled with this spirit by God that they may be willing to be anything, to be nothing, to deny themselves, and to trample their sinful selves underfoot, for the honor of God and a public good; so that neither saints nor heathens may be witnesses against them in that day in which the hearts and practices of all the rulers in the world will be open and bare before him who will judge the world in righteousness and justice, etc.

The sixth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider seriously that self is a great hindrance to divine things; that is why the prophets and apostles were usually carried out of themselves when they had their clearest, choicest, highest, and most glorious visions. Self-seeking blinds the soul, so that it cannot see a beauty in Christ, nor an excellence in holiness. It disorders the palate, so that a man cannot taste sweetness in the word of God, nor in the ways of God, nor in the company of the people of God. It shuts the hand against all the soul-enriching offers of Christ; it hardens the heart against all the knocks and entreaties of Christ; it makes the soul like an empty vine and a barren wilderness. “Israel is an empty486 vine, yielding fruit for himself.” There is nothing that shows a man to be more empty and void of God, Christ, and grace than self-seeking. The Pharisees487 were great self-seekers, and great undervaluers of Christ, his word, and his Spirit. There is no greater hindrance to all the duties of piety than self-seeking. Oh, this is what keeps many a soul from seeking after God and the precious things of eternity. They cannot wait on God, nor act for God, nor abide in those ways in which they might meet with God, because of self. Self-seeking is what drives many a man to neglect and slight the things of his peace. Self-seekers will neither go into heaven themselves, nor allow others to enter who are ready to take the kingdom by force, as you may see in the scribes and Pharisees. Oh, but a gracious spirit is moved quite otherwise, as you may see in that sweet Scripture, Song 7:13: “At our gates are all kinds of choice fruits, new488 as well as old, that I have laid up for you, my beloved.” All that the church has and is, is489 only for him. Let others bear fruit to themselves and lay up for themselves; gracious spirits will store up for Christ and lay up for Christ. All the divine endeavors and productions of saints fall into God’s bosom and empty themselves into his lap. As Christ lays up his merits for them, his graces for them, his comforts for them, his crown for them, so they lay up all their fruits, and all their loves, all their graces, and490 all their experience, and all their services, only for him who is the soul of their comforts, and the crown and top of all their royalty and glory, etc.

467. Self-seeking, like the deluge, overflows the whole world.

468. Phil 2:21.

469. Self-love is the root of hatred of others. 2 Tim 3:2: first “lovers of themselves,” and then “fierce,” etc.

470. The naturalist observes that the beasts that are most cruel to others are most loving to their own.

472. A self-seeker is a Cato outside, but a Nero within. Domitian would seem to love best those whom he least wished to live, and that is the very spirit of self-seekers.

473. It was death under the rites of Moses to counterfeit that ceremonial and figurative ointment (Exod 30). What then will it be to counterfeit the spirit of life and holiness?

474. Rom 1:25.

475. Isa 5:8.

476. Hab 2:6, 9, 10, 11, 12. Crassus, a very rich Roman and a great self-seeker, waged war against the Parthians out of greedy desire for gold, and by them both he and 30,000 Romans were slain. And because the barbarians guessed that he had made this assault on them for their gold, they melted gold and poured it into his dead body, saying (satura te auro), “Satisfy yourself with gold.” Isa 10:1, 2.

478. Mic 2:1, 2. The word of Tacitus, the Roman emperor, was (sibi bonus aliis malus): he who is too much for himself fails to be good to others.

479. Adam seeks himself, and loses himself, Paradise, and that blessed image that God had stamped on him. Lot seeks himself (Gen 13:10, 11) and loses himself and his goods, etc. Peter seeks to save himself, and miserably loses himself. Hezekiah, in the business of the ambassadors, seeks himself, and loses himself, and would have lost his life too, had not God saved him by a miracle.

481. The ancients used to place the statues of their princes by their fountains, implying that they were (or at least should be) fountains of the public good.

482. A certain great emperor, coming into Egypt, to show the zeal he had for the public good, said to the Egyptians, “Draw from me as from your river Nile.”

483. The Counselor says a statesman should be divided thus into three parts: his will to God, his love to his master, his heart to his country, his secret to his friend, his time to business.

484. Solomon’s judgment seat was propped up with lions, to show what spirit and mettle a magistrate should be made of.

2. The Great: Against the Saints

The second device that Satan has to ensnare and destroy the great and honorable of the earth is,

BY setting them against the people of the Most High, against those who are his jewels, his pleasant portion, the delight of his eye and the joy of his heart, etc. So he drew Pharaoh to engage491 against the children of Israel, and that was his overthrow. So he set492 Haman against the Jews, and so brought him to hang on the gallows that he had made for Mordecai. So he set493 those princes and administrators against Daniel, which was the utter ruin of them and their families. So in Revelation 20:7, 8, 9:494 “When the thousand years are complete, Satan will be released from his prison, and will go out to deceive the nations in the four corners of the earth—Gog and Magog—to assemble them for battle. Their number is like the sand of the seashore. And they marched across the broad expanse of the earth and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city. But fire came down from heaven and consumed them.”

Now the remedies against this device of Satan are as follows.

The first remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that none have engaged against the495 saints without being ruined by the God of the saints. Divine justice has been too hard for all who have opposed and engaged against the saints, as is evident in Saul, Pharaoh, Haman, etc. “He rebuked kings on their behalf: ‘Do not touch My anointed ones! Do no harm to My prophets!’” When men of Balaam’s spirit and principles have engaged against the saints, how the angel of the Lord has met them in the way and jostled their bones against the wall! How he has broken their backs and necks, and by his drawn sword cut them off in the prime of their days and in the height of their sins! Ah! What a harvest hell has had496 in our days of those who have engaged against the Lamb, and against those who are called, chosen and faithful! Ah, how divine justice has poured out their blood like water on the ground! How God has laid their honor and glory in the dust! In the pride and madness of their hearts they said, as Pharaoh did, “We will pursue, we will overtake, we will divide the spoil; our lusts will be satisfied on them; we will draw our sword, our hand will destroy them.” In the things in which they have spoken and acted proudly, justice has been above them. History abounds in nothing more than in examples of this kind, etc.

The second remedy against this device of Satan is to dwell for some time every morning on the following Scriptures, in which God has bound himself to stand by his people and for his people, and to make them victorious over the greatest and wisest of their enemies.497 “Huddle together” (says the Lord by the prophet) “O peoples,498 and be shattered; pay attention, all you+ distant lands; prepare for battle, and be shattered; prepare for battle, and be shattered! Devise a plan, but it will be thwarted; state a proposal, but it will not happen. For God is with us.” “Do not fear, O worm of Jacob,”499 “O few men of Israel. I will help you,” declares the Lord. “Your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel. Behold, I will make you into a threshing sledge, new and sharp, with many teeth. You will thresh the mountains and crush them, and reduce the hills to chaff.”500 “You will winnow them, and a wind will carry them away; a gale will scatter them. But you will rejoice in the Lord you will glory in the Holy One of Israel.” “No weapon formed against501 you shall prosper, and you will refute every tongue that accuses you. This is the heritage of the servants of the Lord, and their vindication is from Me,” declares the Lord. “But now many502 nations have assembled against you, saying, ‘Let her be defiled, and let us feast our eyes on Zion.’ But they do not know503 the thoughts of the Lord or understand His plan, for He has gathered them like sheaves to the threshing floor. Rise and thresh,504 O Daughter of Zion, for I will give you horns of iron and hooves of bronze to break to pieces many peoples. Then you will devote their gain to the Lord, their wealth to the Lord of all the earth.”505 “Behold, I will make Jerusalem a cup of drunkenness to all the surrounding peoples. Judah will be besieged, as well as Jerusalem. On that day, when all the nations of the earth gather against her, I will make Jerusalem a heavy stone for all the peoples; all who would heave it away will be severely injured.”

The third remedy against this device of Satan is to consider that if you+ engage against the saints, you+ must506 engage against God himself, because of that near and blessed union that is between God and them. You+ cannot be fighters against the saints without being found, when the account is cast up, to be fighters against God himself. And what greater madness is there than for weakness itself to engage against almighty strength? The near union that is between the Lord and believers is set forth by the near union that is between a husband and his wife.507 (“The two will become one flesh. This mystery is profound, but I am speaking about Christ and the church.”) “We are members of His body, of His flesh and of His bones,” says the apostle. This near union is set forth by the union that is between the head and the members, which make up one body, and by the union that is between the graft and the stock, which are made one by incision. The union between the Lord and a believer is so near that you+ cannot strike a believer without the Lord feeling it and taking it as done to himself: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?”508 “In all their distress, He too was afflicted,” etc. Ah souls! Who ever engaged against God and prospered? Who ever took up the sword against him and did not perish by it? God can speak you+ to hell, and nod you+ to hell, at his pleasure. It is your+ greatest concern to lay down your+ weapons at his feet, and to509 “kiss the Son, lest He be angry and you+ perish in your+ rebellion.”

The fourth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that510 you+ are much indebted to the saints (as instruments) for the blessings that you+ enjoy, and for the preventing and removing of many a judgment that otherwise might have been your+ ruin before this day. Were it not for the saints’ sake, God would quickly make the heavens like brass and the earth like iron; God would quickly strip you of your robes and glory, and set you on the dunghill with Job. They are the props that keep the world from falling about your ears, and that keep the iron rod from breaking your bones. “So He said He would511 destroy them—had not Moses His chosen one stood before Him in the breach to divert512 His wrath from destroying them.”

Ah! Had not the saints many a time cast themselves into the breach between God’s wrath and you+, you+ would have been cut off from the land of the living and had your+ portion with those whose names are written in the dust.513 Many a nation, many a city and many a family is surrounded with blessings for the sake of the Josephs who live in it, and is preserved from many calamities and miseries for the sake of the Moseses, the Daniels, the Noahs and the Jobs who dwell among them. That is a sweet word, Prov 10:25: “When the whirlwind passes, the wicked are no more, but the514 righteous are an everlasting foundation,” or, “are the foundation of the world.” The righteous are the foundation of the world, which but for their sakes would soon shatter and fall to ruin. So the psalmist, Ps 75:3: “When the earth and all its dwellers quake, it is I who bear up its pillars. Selah.”515

When the emperor Marcus Antoninus was in Germany with his army, he was shut in by his enemies in a dry country. They so stopped all the passages that he and his army were likely to perish for lack of water. The emperor’s lieutenant, seeing him so distressed, told him that he had heard that the Christians could obtain anything from their God by their prayers. So the emperor, having a legion of Christians in his army, asked them to pray to their God for his and the army’s deliverance out of that danger. They did so at once, and at once great thunder fell among the enemies, and abundant water on the Romans, so that their thirst was quenched and the enemies were overthrown without any fight. I shall close this last remedy with those sweet words of the psalmist: “God is known in Judah; His name is great516 in Israel. His tent is in Salem, His dwelling place in Zion. There He shattered the flaming arrows, the shield and sword and weapons of war. Selah.”

3. The Learned and the Wise

Secondly, Satan has his devices to ensnare and destroy the learned and the wise, and that sometimes

BY working on them to pride themselves517 in their talents and abilities;518 and sometimes by drawing them to rest on their talents and abilities; and sometimes by causing them to make light of and slight those who lack their talents519 and abilities, though they excel them in grace and holiness; and sometimes by drawing them to engage their talents and abilities in those ways and things that work against the honor of Christ, the joy of the Spirit, the advancement of the gospel and the liberty of the saints, etc.

Now the remedies against this device of Satan are as follows.

The first remedy against this device of Satan is to consider seriously that you+ have nothing but what you+ have received, Christ being the fountain of common gifts as well as of saving520 grace. “What do you have” (says the apostle) “that you did not receive? And if you did receive it, why do you boast as though you did not?” There are those who would hammer out their own happiness, like the spider climbing up by the thread of her own weaving. Of all the talents and abilities that are in you+, you+ may well say, as the young man did of his axe, “Oh, my master, it was borrowed!” “O Lord! All I have is only borrowed from that fountain that fills all the vessels in heaven and on earth, and yet overflows. My gifts are not so much mine521 as yours.” “From Your own hand we have given to You,” said that princely prophet, etc.

The second remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that men’s leaning and trusting on their own wits, talents and abilities has been their utter overthrow and ruin,522 as you may see in Ahithophel, in those administrators and princes who set themselves against Daniel, and in the scribes and Pharisees. God loves to confute men in their confidences. He who stands on his talents and abilities only stands on quicksand that will certainly fail him. There is nothing in the world that provokes God more to withdraw from the soul than this; and how can the soul stand when his strength has departed from him? Everything a man leans on but God will be a dart that will certainly pierce his heart through and through. Ah! how many in these days have lost their estates, their friends, their lives, their souls, by leaning on their admired talents and abilities! The saints are described523 by their leaning on their beloved, the Lord Jesus. He who leans only on the bosom of Christ lives the highest, choicest, safest and sweetest life; miseries always lie at the door of the man who leans on anything below the precious bosom of Christ. Such a man is most in danger, and this is not the least of his plagues, that he thinks himself secure. It is the greatest wisdom in the world to take the wise man’s counsel: “Trust in the Lord with all your524 heart, and lean not on your own understanding.”

The third remedy against this device of Satan is to consider that you+ do not surpass others in talents and abilities more than they surpass you+ in525 grace and holiness. There may be, and often are, great talents and abilities where there is only a little grace, indeed no grace; and there may be, and often is, a great deal of grace where there are only weak talents and abilities. You+ may be higher than others in gifts of knowledge, speech, learning, etc., and those very souls may be higher than you+ in their communion with God, in their delighting526 in God, in their dependence on God, in their affections toward God, and in their humble, holy and blameless walk before God. Is it not folly and madness in a man to make light of and slight another because he is not as rich in lead or iron as he is, when the other is a thousand thousand times richer than he in silver and gold, in jewels and pearls? And is it not madness and folly with a vengeance in those who have greater talents and abilities than others to slight them on that account, when the very persons they make light of and slight have a thousand times more grace than they? And yet, ah! how this evil spirit prevails in the world! It was the sad complaint of Augustine in his time: “The unlearned” (said527 he) “rise up and take heaven by force, and we with all our learning are thrust down to hell.” It is sad to see how many of the rabbis of these times make an idol of their talents and abilities, and with what an eye of pride, scorn and contempt they look on those who lack their talents and who do not worship the idol they have set up in their own hearts. Paul, the great teacher of the Gentiles, wonderfully surpassed the learned teachers and rabbis of our times in all talents and abilities; and yet, ah! how humbly, how tenderly, how sweetly he carries himself toward the lowliest and the528 weakest: “To the weak I became weak, to win the weak. I have become all things to all men so that by all possible means I might save some.… Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is led into sin, and I do not burn with grief?… Therefore, if what I eat causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat meat again, so that I will not cause him to stumble.” But ah! how little of this sweet spirit is to be found in the learned teachers of our age, who look sourly and speak bitterly against those who do not see as they see, and cannot speak as they speak. Sirs, the Spirit of529 the Lord (even in despised saints) will be too strong for you+, and his appearances in them in these latter days will be so full of spiritual beauty and glory that they will darken what you+ are too apt to count and call your+ glory. The Spirit of the Lord will not allow his choicest jewel, grace, to be always buried under the straw and stubble of talents and gifts.

The fourth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider that there530 is no surer way for men to have their gifts and talents blasted and withered than to pride themselves in them, to rest on them, to make light of and slight those who lack them, and to use them against those persons, ways and things on which Jesus Christ has set his heart. Ah! how God has blasted and withered the talents and abilities of many among us who were once famous shining lights! How their sun is darkened and their glory clouded! How531 the sword of the Lord is on their arm and on their right eye! How their arm is completely withered and their right eye utterly blinded! as the prophet speaks. This is matter for humbling and lamentation. Many precious, discerning saints see this and mourn for it in secret. And oh, that those men were truly aware of God’s withdrawing from them, so that they may repent, keep humble, carry themselves sweetly toward God’s jewels, and lean only on the Lord and not on their talents and understanding; so that the Lord may delight to visit them with his grace at such a rate that their faces may shine more gloriously than ever, and they may be more serviceable to the honor of Christ and the faith of the saints than they have been before, etc.

517. John 5:44.

518. 1 Kgs 22:22, 23, 24, 25. 1 Cor 1:18–29.

519. The truth of this you may see in the learned scribes and Pharisees.

520. 1 Cor 4:7. Quicquid es debes creanti, Quicquid potes debes redimenti, said Bernard: “Whatever you are, you owe to him who made you; and whatever you have, you owe to him who redeemed you.”

4. The Saints: Division

Thirdly, Satan has his devices to destroy the saints, and one great device that he has to destroy the saints is,

BY working them first to be estranged,532 then to divide, then to be bitter and suspicious, and then to be “biting and devouring one another.” Our own woeful experience is too great a proof of this. The Israelites in Egypt did not vex one another more than Christians in these days have done, which has brought a deadly consumption on some.

Now the remedies against this device of Satan are as follows.

The first remedy against this device of Satan is to dwell more on one another’s graces than on one another’s weaknesses and infirmities. It is sad to consider that saints should have533 many eyes to see one another’s infirmities, and not one eye to see each other’s graces; that they should use spectacles to look at one another’s weaknesses, rather than mirrors to look at one another’s graces. Erasmus tells of one who collected all the lame and defective verses in Homer’s works, but passed over all that were excellent. Ah, if only this were not the practice of many who will at last meet in heaven! If only they were not so careful and skillful to collect all the weaknesses of others, and to pass over all those things that are excellent in them! The Corinthians looked more at the incestuous man’s sin than at his sorrow, which was likely to have drowned him in sorrow.

Tell me, saints, is it not a sweeter, more comforting and delightful thing to look more on one another’s graces than on one another’s infirmities? Tell me, what pleasure, what delight, what comfort is there in looking on the enemies, the wounds, the sores, the sicknesses, the diseases, the nakedness of our friends? Now sin, you+ know, is the soul’s enemy, the soul’s wound, the soul’s sores, the soul’s sickness, the soul’s534 disease, the soul’s nakedness. And ah! What a heart that man has who loves to look on these! Grace is the choicest flower in all a Christian’s garden; it is the richest jewel in all his crown; it is his princely robes; it is the height of royalty; and therefore it must be the most pleasing, sweet and delightful object for a gracious eye to be fixed on. Sin is darkness, grace is light; sin is hell, grace is heaven. And what madness it is to look more at darkness than at light, more at hell than at heaven!535

Tell me, saints, does not God look more on his people’s graces than on their weaknesses? Surely he does. He looks more at David’s and Asa’s uprightness than at their infirmities, though they were great and many. He looks more at Job’s patience than at his outbursts: “Remember the patience of Job”—not a word of his impatience, etc. He who painted Alexander while he had a scar on his face painted him with his finger on the scar. God puts his finger on his people’s scars, so that no blemish may appear. Ah saints! If only you+ would make it the height of your+ glory in this to be like your+ heavenly Father! By so doing much sin would be prevented, the designs of wicked men frustrated, Satan outwitted, many wounds healed, many sad hearts cheered, and God more abundantly honored, etc.

The second remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that love and unity make most for your+ own safety and security. We will536 be insuperabiles if we are inseparabiles: invincible, if we are inseparable. The world may frown on you+ and plot against you+, but it cannot hurt you+. Unity is the best bond of safety in every church and commonwealth. And the Scythian king in Plutarch represented this vividly to his eighty sons. When he was ready to die, he ordered a bundle of arrows, bound fast together, to be given to his sons to break. They all tried to break them, but because they were bound fast together, they could not. Then he had the band cut, and then they537 broke them with ease. He applied it like this: “My sons, as long as you+ keep together, you+ will be invincible; but if the band of union between you+ is broken, you+ will easily be broken in pieces.” Pliny writes of a stone in the island of Scyrus that, if it is whole, though a large and heavy one, it floats on the water, but when it is broken, it sinks. So as long as saints keep whole, nothing will sink them; but if they break, they are in danger of sinking and drowning, etc.

The third remedy against this device of Satan is to dwell on those commands of God that require you+538 to love one another. Oh, when your+ hearts begin to rise against each other, charge the commands of God on your+ hearts, and say to your+ souls, “O our souls! Has not the eternal God commanded you+ to love those who love the Lord? And is it not life to obey, and death to rebel?” Therefore see that you+ fulfill the commands of the Lord, for his commands are not like those that are easily reversed, but like those of the Medes, which cannot be changed. Oh, ponder much on these commands of God:539 “A new commandment I give you+: Love one another. As I have loved you+, so you+ also must love one another.” It is called a new540 commandment because it is renewed in the gospel and brought home by Christ’s example, and because it is rare, choice, special and remarkable above all others. “This is My commandment, that you+ love one another as I have loved you+.” “This is My command to you+: Love one another.” “Be indebted to no one, except to one another in love. For he who loves his neighbor has541 fulfilled the law.” “Continue in brotherly love.”542 “Let us love one another, because love comes from543 God. Everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God.” “Love one another544 deeply, from a pure heart.” “Finally,545 all of you+, be like-minded and sympathetic, love as brothers, be tenderhearted and humble.” “This is the message546 you+ have heard from the beginning: We should love one another.” “And this is His547 commandment: that we should believe in the name of His Son, Jesus Christ, and we should love one another just as He commanded us.” “Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love548 one another.”

Oh, dwell much on these precious commands, so that your+ love may be549 inflamed toward one another. In the early times of the church it was much noticed by the heathen that in the depth of misery, when fathers and mothers forsook their children, Christians (otherwise strangers) stuck to one another; their love of religion proved firmer than that of nature. Ah, if only there were more of that spirit among the saints in these days! The world was once destroyed with water for the heat of lusts, and it is thought that it will be destroyed again with fire for the coldness of love.

The fourth remedy against this device of Satan is to dwell more on those choice and sweet things in which you+ agree than on those things in which you+ differ. Ah! If only you+ did this, how sinful heats would be cooled, and your+ love raised, and your+ spirits sweetened toward one another! You+ agree in most things; you+ differ in only a few. You+ agree in the greatest and weightiest, as concerning God, Christ, the Spirit, the Scripture, etc. You+ differ only in those points that have long been disputed among men of the greatest piety and gifts. You+ agree to acknowledge the Scripture, to hold to Christ the head, and to walk550 according to the laws of the new creation. Do Herod and Pilate agree? Do Turks and pagans agree? Do bears and lions, tigers and wolves, indeed, does a legion of devils agree in one body? And will not saints agree, who differ only in such things as have the least of the heart of God in them, and that will never hinder your+ meeting in heaven, etc.?

The fifth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that God delights to be called (Deus pacis) the God of peace; and Christ to be called551 (Princeps pacis) the Prince of Peace, and King of Salem, that is, King of peace; and the Spirit is a Spirit of peace. “The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace,” Gal 5:22. Oh! Why then should not the saints be children of peace? Certainly men of perverse, unquiet, fiery spirits cannot have such sweet evidence of their share in the God of peace, in the Prince of Peace and in the Spirit of peace as those precious souls have who follow after the things that make for love and peace. The very name of peace552 is sweet and comforting; its fruit and effect are pleasant and profitable, more to be desired than countless triumphs. It is a blessing that ushers in a multitude of other blessings. The ancients used to paint Peace in the form of a woman with a horn of plenty in her hand. Ah! Peace and love among the saints is what will keep them and their mercies secure at home. Indeed, it will multiply their mercies; it will move the God of mercy to crown them with the choicest mercies; and it is what will make them most fearsome, invincible and successful out in the world. Love and peace among the saints is what brings the counsels of their enemies to a standstill and makes all their enterprises miscarry. It is what most weakens their hands, wounds their hopes and kills their hearts, etc.

The sixth remedy against this device of Satan is to make it more a matter of care and conscience to keep up your+ peace553 with God. Ah Christians! I am afraid that your+ remissness here is what has caused much of the sourness, bitterness and divisions that are among you+. Ah! You+ have not kept up your+ peace with God as you+ should, and that is why you+ so dreadfully break the peace among yourselves+. The Lord has promised:554 “When a man’s ways please the Lord, He makes even the man’s enemies live at peace with him.” Ah!555 How much more, then, would God make the children of peace keep the peace among themselves, if only their ways pleased him? All created things are at his command and under his check. Laban followed Jacob with one troop and Esau met him with another, both with hostile intentions; but because Jacob’s ways pleased the Lord, God so works by his mighty power that Laban leaves him with a kiss, and Esau meets him with a kiss. He has an oath from the one, tears from the other, and peace with both. If we make it our business to keep up our league with God, God will make it his work and his glory to maintain our peace with men. But if men make light of keeping up their peace with God, it is just of God to leave them to a spirit of pride, envy, anger, contention, division and confusion; to leave them “biting and devouring one another” until they are “consumed by one another,” etc.

The seventh remedy against this device of Satan is to dwell much on that near relation and union that is between you+. This consideration had a sweet influence on Abraham’s heart: “So Abram said to Lot, ‘Please let there be556 no contention between you and me, or between your herdsmen and my herdsmen. After all, we are brothers.’” That is a sweet word of the psalmist: “Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers live together in harmony!” It is not good without being pleasant,557 or pleasant without being good, but good and pleasant. There are some things that are (bona sed non jucunda) good but not pleasant, as patience and discipline. There are some things that are pleasant but not good, as carnal pleasures, sensuality, etc. There are some things that are neither good nor pleasant, as malice, envy, worldly sorrow, etc. And there are some things that are both good and pleasant, as piety, love, peace and union among brethren. And oh, that we could see more of this among those who will one day meet (in their Father’s kingdom) and never part, etc.! And as they are brethren, so they are all fellow members:558 “Now you+ are the body of Christ, and each of you+ is a member of it.”

And again: “We are members of His body, of His flesh and of His bones.” Are559 the members of the natural body serviceable and useful to one another, and will the members of this spiritual body cut and destroy one another? Is it against the law of nature for the natural members to cut and slash one another? And is it not much more against the law of nature, and of grace, for the members of Christ’s glorious body to do so? And as you+ are all fellow members, so you+ are all fellow soldiers560 under the same captain of salvation, the Lord Jesus, fighting against the world, the flesh and the devil. And as you+ are all fellow soldiers, so you+ are all fellow sufferers under the same enemies, the devil and the561 world. And as you+ are all fellow sufferers,562 so you+ are fellow travelers toward the land of Canaan, the new Jerusalem that is above: “Here we do not have a permanent city, but we are looking for the city that is to come.” The heirs of heaven are strangers on earth. And as you+ are all fellow travelers, so you+ are all fellow heirs of563 the same crown and inheritance.

The eighth remedy against this device of Satan is to dwell on the miseries of discord. Dissolution is the564 daughter of dissension. Ah! How the name of Christ and the way of Christ suffer by the discord of saints! How many who are entering on the ways of God are hindered and saddened, and the mouths of the wicked opened and their hearts hardened against God and his ways, by the discord of his people! Remember this: the disagreement of Christians is the devil’s triumph. And what a sad thing this is, that Christians should give Satan cause to triumph! It was a notable saying of one: “Take away strife and call back peace, lest you lose a man, your friend, and the devil, an enemy, rejoice over you+ both,” etc.

The ninth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that it is no disgrace to you+ to be first in seeking peace and reconciliation, but rather an honor to you+,565 that you+ have begun to seek peace. Abraham was the elder, and worthier than Lot, both in respect of grace and of nature also (for he was Lot’s uncle), and yet he first seeks peace with his inferior, which God has recorded to his honor. Ah! How the God of peace by his Spirit and messengers pursues peace with poor mortals! God first makes offers of peace to us:566 “Therefore we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were making His appeal through us. We implore you+ on behalf of Christ: Be reconciled to God.” God’s grace first kneels to us; and who can turn their backs on such blessed and bleeding embraces, except souls in whom Satan, the god of this world, reigns as king? God is the party wronged, and yet he sues for peace with us first:567 “To a nation that did not call My name, I said, ‘Here I am! Here I am!’” Ah! How568 the sweetness, the freeness and the riches of his grace break forth and shine on poor souls! When a man goes away from the sun, the sunbeams still follow him; so when we go away from the sun of righteousness, even then the beams of his love and mercy follow us. Christ first sent to Peter, who had denied him, and to the rest, who had forsaken him: “Go, tell His disciples and Peter, ‘He is going ahead of you+ into Galilee.569 There you+ will see Him, just as He told you+.’”

Ah souls! It is not a base, low thing, but a godlike thing, though we are wronged by others, still to be the first in seeking peace. Such actions will show that much of God is with a man’s spirit, etc.

Christians! It is not a matter of liberty whether you+ will or will not pursue peace; it is a matter of duty that lies on you+. You+ are bound by express precepts to follow after peace; and though it may seem to flee from you+, still you+ must pursue it: “Pursue570 peace with everyone, as well as holiness, without which no one will see the Lord.” Peace and holiness are to be pursued with the greatest eagerness that can be imagined. So the psalmist: “Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it.” The Hebrew word that is rendered seek here is in Piel, and it means to seek earnestly, vehemently, ardently,571 studiously, industriously. And pursue it: that Hebrew word means earnestly572 to pursue, being a metaphor taken from the eagerness of wild beasts, or ravenous573 birds, which will run or fly both fast and far rather than be deprived of their prey. So the apostle presses the same duty on the Romans: “Let us pursue what leads to574 peace and to mutual edification.”

Ah! You+ perverse, sour, surly Christians, can you+ look on these commands of God without tears and blushing? I have read a remarkable story of Aristippus, though only a heathen,575 who went of his own accord to Aeschines, his enemy, and said, “Are we never to be reconciled until we become table talk to all the country?” And when Aeschines answered that he would most gladly be at peace with him, Aristippus said, “Remember then that though I was the elder and the better man, yet I sought you first.” “You are indeed,” said Aeschines, “a far better man than I; for I began the quarrel, but you the reconciliation.” My prayer is that this heathen may not rise in judgment against the flourishing professing Christians of our times,576 “who sharpen their tongues like swords and aim their bitter words like arrows.”

The tenth remedy against this device of Satan is for saints to join together and walk together in the ways of grace and holiness as far as they do agree, making the word the only touchstone and judge of their actions. That is sweet advice that the apostle gives:577 “I press on toward the goal to win the prize of God’s heavenly calling in Christ Jesus. All of us578 who are perfect” (comparatively, or in their own estimation) “should embrace this point of view. And if you+ think differently about some issue, God will reveal this to you+ as well. Nevertheless, as far as579 we have already attained, let us walk by the same rule, let us be of the same mind.”

Ah Christians! God loses much, and you+ lose much, and Satan gains much, because you+ do not, and will not, walk lovingly together as far as your+ ways lie together. It is your+ sin and shame that you+ do not, and will not, pray together, hear together, confer together, mourn together, etc., because580 in some far lesser things you+ are not agreed. What folly and madness it is in those whose way of a hundred miles lies ninety-nine together, and yet who will not walk so far together because they cannot go the other mile together! Yet such is the folly and madness of many Christians in these days, who will not do many things they may do because they cannot do everything they should do. I fear God will whip them into a better frame before he is done with them. He will break their bones and pierce their hearts; but he will cure them of this malady, etc.

And be sure you+ make the word the only touchstone and judge of all persons and actions:581 “To the law and to the testimony! If they do not speak according to this word, they have no light of dawn.” It is best and safest to make that the judge of all men and things now by which all will be judged on the last day: “The word” (says Christ)582 “that I have spoken will judge him on the last day.” Do not make your+ dim light, your+ notions, your+ fancies, your+ opinions, the judge of men’s actions, but always judge by the rule, and plead, “It is written.” When a vain, insistent soul in a dispute with a holy man cried out, “Hear me, hear me!” the holy man answered, “Let neither you hear me, nor I you, but583 let us both hear the apostle.”

Constantine, in all the disputes before him with the Arians, would always call for the word of God, as the only way, if not to convert them, yet to stop their mouths, etc.

The eleventh remedy against this device of Satan is to be much in self-judging:584 “Judge yourselves+, and you+ will not be judged by the Lord.” Ah! If Christians’585 hearts were more taken up with judging themselves and condemning themselves, they would not be so apt to judge and censure others, and to behave sourly and bitterly toward others who differ from them. There are no souls in the world so afraid to judge others as586 those who most judge themselves, nor so careful to make a righteous judgment of men or things as those who are most careful to judge themselves. There are none in the world who so tremble to think evil of others, to speak evil of others, or to do evil to others, as those who make it their business to judge themselves. There are none who put such sweet constructions and charitable interpretations on men and things as those who are best at, and most in, judging themselves. One request I have to you+ who are much in judging others and little in judging yourselves+, to you+ who are so apt and prone to judge rashly, falsely and unrighteously: that you+ will every morning dwell a little on these Scriptures.

“Do not judge, or you+ will be judged. For587 with the same judgment you+ pronounce, you+ will be judged; and with the measure you+ use, it588 will be measured to you+.” “Stop judging589 by outward appearances, and start judging justly.” “The one who does not eat everything must not judge590 the one who does, for God has accepted him.” “Why, then, do you judge your brother? Or why do you591 belittle your brother? For we will all stand before God’s judgment seat.” “Therefore let us stop judging one another. Instead,592 judge this: not to put any stumbling block or obstacle in your brother’s way.” “Judge nothing before the appointed time;593 wait until the Lord comes. He will bring to light what is hidden in darkness and will expose the motives of men’s hearts. At that time each will receive his praise from God.” “Do not slander one another” (brethren).594 “Anyone who speaks against his brother or judges him speaks against the law and judges it. And if you judge the law, you are not a practitioner of the law, but a judge of it. There is only one Lawgiver and Judge,595 the One who is able to save and destroy. But who are you to judge your neighbor?” “Who are you to judge596 someone else’s servant? To his own master he stands or falls. And he will stand, for the Lord is able to make him stand.”

One Delphidius was accusing another before Julian of something he could not prove. When the accused denied the fact, Delphidius answered, “If it is enough to deny what is laid to one’s charge, who will be found guilty?” Julian answered, “And if it is enough to be accused, who can be innocent?” You+ are wise, and know how to apply it.

The twelfth remedy against this device of Satan is this: above all, labor to be597 “clothed with humility.” Humility makes a man peaceable among brethren, fruitful in well-doing, cheerful in suffering and constant in holy walking. Humility fits a man for the highest services we owe to Christ, and yet it will not neglect598 the lowest service to the lowliest saint. Humility can feed on the plainest dish, and yet it is maintained by the choicest delicacies, such as God, Christ and glory. Humility will make a man bless the one who curses him, and pray for those who persecute him. A humble heart is a dwelling for God, a scholar599 for Christ, a companion for angels, a preserver of grace and a preparer for glory. Humility is the nurse of our graces, the preserver of our blessings and the great promoter of holy duties. Humility cannot find three things on this side of heaven: it cannot find fullness in created things, nor sweetness in sin, nor life in an ordinance without Christ. A humble soul always finds three things on this side of heaven: the soul to be empty, Christ to be full, and every mercy and duty to be sweet in which God is enjoyed. Humility can weep over other men’s weaknesses, and joy and rejoice over their graces. Humility will make a man600 quiet and content in the lowliest condition, and it will keep a man from envying others’ prosperity. Humility honors those who are strong in grace, and puts two hands601 under those who are weak in grace. Humility makes a man richer than other men, and it makes a man judge himself the poorest among men. Humility will see much good in others when it can see but little in itself. Ah Christians! Though faith is the champion of grace, and love the nurse of grace, yet humility is the beautifier of grace; it casts a general glory over all the graces in the soul. Ah! If Christians abounded more in humility,602 they would be less bitter, perverse and sour, and they would be more gentle, meek and sweet in their spirits and practices. Humility will make a man have high thoughts of others and low thoughts of himself. It will make a man see much glory and excellence in others, and much baseness and sinfulness in himself; it will make a man see others rich and himself poor, others strong and himself weak, others wise and himself foolish. Humility will make a man excellent at covering others’ infirmities, at recording their gracious services and at delighting in their graces. It makes a man rejoice in every light that outshines his own, and in every wind that blows others good. Humility is better at believing than at questioning other men’s happiness. “I judge,” says a humble soul, “that it is well with these Christians now, but it will be far better with them hereafter. They are now on the borders of the new Jerusalem, and it will be but as a day before they slide into Jerusalem.” A humble soul is more willing to say, “Heaven is that man’s,” than “It is mine”; “Christ is that Christian’s,” than “He is mine”; and “God is their God in covenant,” than “He is mine.” Ah! If Christians were more humble, there would be less fire and more love among them than there is now, etc.

5. The Ignorant

Lastly, as Satan has his devices to destroy gracious souls, so he has his devices to destroy poor ignorant souls, and that sometimes

BY drawing them to choose ignorance, and to neglect, slight and603 despise the means of knowledge. Ignorance is the mother of mistake, the cause of trouble, error and terror;604 it is the highway to hell, and it makes a man both a prisoner and a slave to the devil at once. Ignorance unmans a605 man; it makes a man a beast; indeed, it makes him more miserable than the beast that perishes. There are none so easily or so frequently taken in Satan’s snare as ignorant souls. They are easily drawn to dance with the devil all day, and to dream of supping with Christ at night, etc.

Now the remedies against this device of Satan are as follows.

The first remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that an ignorant heart is an evil heart: “Without knowledge, the mind is not good.”606

An ignorant heart is a wicked heart; it is a heart in the dark, and no607 good can come into a dark heart without passing through the understanding: “and if your eye is dark, your whole body will be full of darkness.” A leprous head and a leprous heart are inseparable companions. Ignorant hearts are so evil that they lash out on every side, and do not hold back from spitting their venom in the very face of God, as Pharaoh did when thick darkness was on him.

The second remedy against this device of Satan is to consider that ignorance is the deformity of the soul. As blindness is the deformity of the face, so ignorance is the deformity of the soul; as the lack of bodily eyes spoils the beauty of the face, so the lack of spiritual eyes spoils the beauty of the soul. A man without knowledge is like a workman without his hands, a painter without his eyes, a traveler without his legs, a ship without sails, a bird without wings, or a body without a soul.

The third remedy against this device of Satan is to consider solemnly that ignorance makes men the objects of God’s hatred and wrath. “Their hearts608 are always going astray, and they have not known My ways. So I swore on oath in My anger, ‘They shall never enter My rest.’” “This is a people without understanding. Therefore their Maker has no compassion on them.” Christ has said that he will come in blazing fire, inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God. Ignorance will end in vengeance. When you see a poor blind man here, you do not loathe him or hate him, but you pity him; oh! but soul-blindness makes you abominable in the sight of God. God has sworn that ignorant persons will never come into heaven; heaven609 itself would be a hell to ignorant souls. “My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge. Because you have rejected knowledge, I will also reject you.”

Chilo, one of the seven sages, being asked what God had done, answered, “He has exalted humble men and brought down proud, ignorant fools.”

The fourth remedy against this device of Satan is to consider that ignorance is a sin that leads to all sins. All sins are in ignorance as in their seed: “You+ are mistaken610 because you+ do not know the Scriptures.” It drives men to hate and persecute the saints: “They will hate you+ and put you+611 out of the synagogues. In fact, a time is coming when anyone who kills you+ will think612 he is offering a service to God. They will do these things because they have not known the Father or Me.” Paul lays all his cruelties to Christians at the door of his ignorance: “I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and a violent man; yet because I had acted in ignorance … I was shown mercy.” It was ignorance that drove the Jews to crucify Christ. “Father, forgive them,” says Christ of his murderers, “for they do not know613 what they are doing.” “For if the rulers of this age had understood it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.” Sin at first was the cause of ignorance, but now ignorance is the cause of all sin. “Cursing614 and lying, murder and stealing, and adultery are rampant,” says the prophet, because there is no knowledge of God in the land. There are none so frequent and so impudent in the ways of sin as ignorant souls. They do not care or heed what they do, or what they say against God, Christ, heaven, holiness and their own souls: “Our tongues615 are our own; who will be master over us?” “They mock and speak with malice; with arrogance they threaten oppression. They set their mouths against the heavens, and their tongues strut across the earth.” “Have all the616 workers of iniquity no knowledge? They devour my people like bread; they refuse to call upon the Lord.”
